essays.title: Free inquiry, firm rules for human safety

paragraphs.text: Many of the tools that define modern life, from vaccines to satellite navigation, began as research projects whose value no one could predict.
This history raises the question of how tightly governments should control the work of scientists and engineers.
I largely agree that governments should place few restrictions on scientific research and development, as long as clear rules protect the people who take part in that research.
This position rests on the unpredictable value of basic research and on the speed that open science allows, although safety rules for studies on people remain a necessary exception.
First, adopting the recommendation would be advantageous wherever the value of research cannot be judged in advance, because restrictions tend to block exactly the work that later proves essential.
For decades, Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman pursued basic research on mRNA that attracted little notice from the wider scientific community.
Yet that research allowed the COVID-19 mRNA vaccines to be developed in under a year, and the two scientists won the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
Similarly, GPS was built by the US military for its own purposes, but once it was opened to civilians, it became the basis of everyday navigation, ride-hailing and delivery apps.

This shows that in a setting where no one can foresee which line of inquiry will matter, a government that rations research by its expected usefulness would likely [[forfeit|forfeit]] its most valuable discoveries.
Second, few restrictions would be advantageous when speed and openness determine results, since bureaucratic barriers slow the sharing on which progress depends.
The Human Genome Project, a publicly funded international effort completed in 2003, made the human DNA sequence freely available to all researchers.
Because no license or special permission stood between scientists and the data, laboratories around the world could build on the sequence at once rather than wait for approval.
Similarly, smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980 after a coordinated WHO vaccination campaign that relied on countries sharing data and vaccine.

In both cases, the [[salient|salient]] feature was not the absence of government but the absence of barriers, which suggests that governments serve science best when they fund and connect researchers rather than [[impede|impede]] them.
Admittedly, there are circumstances in which adopting the recommendation would not be advantageous, most clearly when research involves people who cannot judge its risks for themselves.
Around 1960, thalidomide, a sedative given to pregnant women, caused severe birth defects in thousands of babies in Europe, while Frances Kelsey of the US FDA refused to approve it.
The US then passed stricter drug-testing rules in 1962, and few people today would call those rules an [[irksome|irksome]] burden on science.
Nevertheless, such rules govern how new products are tested on people, not which questions scientists may ask.
In my own work as an epidemiologist in Vietnam, every study involving patients must pass an ethics review, yet no committee has ever told me which disease I may study.
A government can therefore require ethics review and safety trials while still leaving the direction of inquiry free, so this exception qualifies my position rather than overturning it.
In conclusion, governments should impose few restrictions on what scientists choose to investigate, but they should not abandon their duty to protect the people who take part in research.
Basic research yields value that no one can predict, open access to data speeds progress, and the history of drug safety shows where firm limits belong.
The [[optimal|optimal]] policy is therefore freedom of inquiry paired with strict but narrow rules for human safety.

essays.title: Free questions, but regulated testing and release

paragraphs.text: Science can save millions of lives, but the same freedom that produces a cure can also produce a disaster.
For this reason, the recommendation that governments should place few, if any, restrictions on scientific research and development deserves careful scrutiny.

I mostly disagree with this recommendation: although governments should protect the freedom to ask questions, they must keep firm restrictions on how research is conducted and how its products are released.
The histories of drug safety and research ethics show why such limits are advantageous, while the success of open, publicly funded science explains where restrictions should stay light.
First, restrictions are clearly advantageous when a new product will reach large numbers of people before its risks are fully known.
Around 1960, thalidomide, a sedative given to pregnant women, caused severe birth defects in thousands of babies in Europe.
In the United States, however, Frances Kelsey of the FDA refused to approve the drug, and the country then passed stricter drug-testing rules in 1962.
Similarly, the overuse and over-the-counter sale of antibiotics, common in many countries including Vietnam, help resistant bacteria spread, so drugs that once cured infections now often fail.
As a physician, I see the result in hospitals where common infections no longer respond to standard treatment.
This shows that in a market with weak oversight, the costs of new science fall on patients who never chose to bear them, and a [[prudent|prudent]] regulator is their only protection.
Second, restrictions are advantageous wherever researchers might be tempted to place their own goals above the rights of the people they study.
In the Tuskegee syphilis study, which ran from 1932 to 1972, researchers withheld treatment from Black men without their informed consent.
The public outrage that followed led to US rules requiring ethics review boards for research on people.
In my own research on dengue in Vietnam, such a board reviews every protocol, and its questions have more than once made a study safer for participants.
These cases show that the ethical standards we now regard as [[axiomatic|axiomatic]] did not arise from the goodwill of scientists alone; governments imposed them after research went wrong.
A policy of few restrictions would invite the return of such [[egregious|egregious]] abuses.
Admittedly, heavy restrictions can [[stymie|stymie]] discovery, and some of the greatest successes of modern science came from freedom rather than control.
The COVID-19 mRNA vaccines, for example, were developed in under a year because Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman had spent decades on little-noticed basic research on mRNA.
Likewise, the Human Genome Project, completed in 2003, made the human DNA sequence freely available to all researchers.
Nevertheless, neither success depended on an absence of rules: the mRNA vaccines still passed clinical trials before reaching the public, and the genome project was itself a government effort.
The lesson, then, is that governments should restrict research lightly at the stage of ideas and firmly at the stage of human testing and public release.
In practice, this means funding bold ideas generously while requiring proof of safety before any product reaches patients.
In conclusion, removing nearly all government restrictions on research would be unwise, even though freedom of inquiry deserves strong protection.
Drug safety and research ethics reveal the harm that unchecked science can cause, while the stories of mRNA and the human genome show where rules should stay light.
Good policy, in short, does not choose between science and safety; it places each restriction where the risk to people is greatest.

essays.title: Praise the good, overlook the harmless

paragraphs.text: Anyone who has learned to ride a bicycle remembers the adult who cheered the first wobbly success more clearly than any warning.
That memory points to a common belief about teaching: praise for good actions works better than attention to bad ones.
I largely agree that the best way to teach is to praise positive actions and ignore negative ones, as long as the negative actions are minor rather than dangerous.
Praise builds the motivation that learning requires, and ignoring small mistakes keeps learners willing to try, although some errors are too serious to ignore.
First, the statement holds true because praise gives learners a reason to repeat what they did well, and repetition is how skills grow.
Consider a primary school teacher who notices a shy student finally raising her hand and thanks her warmly in front of the class.
The student is likely to speak again the next day, and each attempt makes the next one easier.
Over a semester, such small moments can turn a [[diffident|diffident]] child into an active participant.
Similarly, when I supervise young doctors, a specific comment such as "Your history-taking found the key exposure" does more to shape their habits than a long list of what they missed.
This shows that praise does more than make people feel good; it tells them precisely which behavior to [[emulate|emulate]], which is the core of effective teaching.
A teacher who notices good work, and says so specifically, gives the learner both a reason and a target.
Second, ignoring minor negative actions often works better than punishing them, because constant attention to errors can make learners afraid to try at all.
Consider a language teacher who lets small grammar slips pass during a conversation class; her students keep speaking, and many of the slips fade as they hear correct forms repeated.
Similarly, a child who spills milk while learning to pour will usually improve with practice, whereas a scolding may only teach the child to stop helping.
Many small errors simply disappear once the learner's skill improves, so correcting each one wastes the teacher's attention.
In such cases, the mistake is part of learning itself, and drawing attention to it can [[undermine|undermine]] the confidence that progress requires.
Thus, the statement holds especially true for beginners, whose mistakes are frequent, minor and largely unavoidable.
Admittedly, the statement does not hold true when a negative action threatens safety or harms other people.
A student who bullies classmates, or a junior nurse who skips hand hygiene, cannot simply be ignored, because the cost of the error falls on someone else.
Ignaz Semmelweis showed in 1847 that when doctors washed their hands in chlorinated lime, deaths from childbed fever on his ward fell sharply; a lapse in that habit is never minor.
Nevertheless, such cases are exceptions, and even then the correction works best when it is brief and paired with praise for the right behavior.
This consideration qualifies my position: teachers should ignore small, harmless mistakes, but they must address dangerous ones directly while continuing to reward progress.
In other words, the statement describes the right default for teaching, not a rule without exceptions.
In conclusion, praising positive actions while overlooking minor negative ones is, in most situations, the most effective way to teach.
Praise shows learners what to repeat, and ignoring small mistakes protects their willingness to try, yet harmful behavior always requires a direct response.
The best teachers, therefore, are generous with praise and [[judicious|judicious]] with criticism, saving it for the errors that truly matter.

words.meaning_here: copy in order to match or equal
showing good judgment; careful in choosing when to act

essays.task_note: Bodies 1-2 show ways the statement holds true (praise guides repetition; ignoring minor errors protects confidence), and Body 3 shows where it does not hold (dangerous errors), explaining how that limits the position to harmless mistakes.

essays.title: Good teaching both praises and corrects

paragraphs.text: A thermometer that reports only good news would be useless to a doctor.
Feedback in teaching works in a similar way, which is why the statement that the best way to teach is to praise positive actions and ignore negative ones is troubling.
I mostly disagree with this statement: praise is valuable, but the best teaching also corrects negative actions clearly, kindly and promptly.
Learners cannot fix errors they do not know about, and ignored mistakes often become habits, even though praise remains essential for motivation.
First, the statement does not hold true because learners usually cannot see their own errors, so a teacher's silence leaves them uninformed.
Consider a medical student who repeatedly misreads electrocardiograms while her supervisor praises only her bedside manner.
She may finish her training confident and well liked, yet unable to recognize a heart attack, an error that her future patients would pay for.
Ignoring her errors would be kind in the moment but [[deleterious|deleterious]] in the long run.

Similarly, in 2015 a large collaboration tried to repeat 100 published psychology studies and reproduced the results of only about a third, a reminder that even experts need criticism to find their mistakes.
This shows that correction is not the opposite of good teaching but a part of it, since it [[elucidates|elucidate]] the gaps that praise alone leaves hidden.
A supervisor who stays silent about such errors is not protecting the learner but postponing the cost of the mistake.
Second, negative actions that are ignored rarely disappear; more often, they harden into habits that are far harder to change later.
Antibiotic use in Vietnam offers a clear case: when overuse and over-the-counter sales of antibiotics go unchallenged, resistant bacteria spread.
Today, drugs that once cured infections often fail, and reversing the habit now requires far more effort than early correction would have.
As a physician, I have also seen how a clinic that tolerates small lapses in hygiene often finds those lapses copied by new staff members.
Likewise, a child who is never told that lying is wrong may conclude that dishonesty carries no cost.
In each case, silence is not neutral; learners [[construe|construe]] it as permission, so ignoring bad actions can teach the very behavior a teacher hopes to prevent.
Correcting a mistake early, before it becomes [[ingrained|ingrained]], is therefore both kinder and more efficient.
Admittedly, the statement holds some truth, because praise motivates learners more effectively than constant criticism.
A shy student whose first attempts are met only with corrections may stop raising her hand altogether.
Finland, which relies far less on standardized testing than many countries, also suggests that schools can succeed without a constant focus on ranking students' failures.
Nevertheless, the lesson of such cases is to correct with care, not to stop correcting.
A teacher can praise what a student did well and, in the same conversation, point out one specific error to fix next time, a balance that preserves both motivation and accuracy.
Thus, the value of praise refines my position rather than reverses it.
In conclusion, the best teaching does not ignore negative actions; it combines generous praise with honest, timely correction.
Learners need to know what they are doing wrong, ignored mistakes tend to become habits, and praise works best as a partner to correction rather than a substitute for it.
A teacher who only praises may be liked, but a teacher who both praises and corrects is the one students remember as having truly taught them.

words.meaning_here: interpret or understand in a particular way
firmly fixed and difficult to change

essays.task_note: Bodies 1-2 show ways the statement fails (unseen errors, ignored errors becoming habits), and Body 3 grants where it holds (praise motivates), explaining how this refines rather than reverses the position.

essays.title: Free tuition, if well funded

paragraphs.text: In many families, the price of a degree decides whether a talented child becomes an engineer or leaves school to work.
Some argue that governments can remove this barrier by offering college and university education free of charge to all students.
I largely agree with this recommendation, provided that free tuition is paired with adequate funding and high standards for admission and teaching.
Free education widens the pool of talent a country can draw on and repays its cost through a more productive workforce, although in poorer countries the policy must be phased in carefully.
First, adopting the recommendation would be advantageous in a society where talent is spread widely but money is not, because tuition fees waste the abilities of poor students.
Consider a rural district in Vietnam where a top student's parents earn their living from rice farming.
If a university charges fees equal to several years of the family's income, that student may abandon her studies, and the country loses a future doctor or teacher.

Similarly, Marie Curie won Nobel Prizes in both physics and chemistry despite the barriers women faced in science at the time, a reminder of how much talent lies outside the groups that traditionally enter universities.
This shows that free tuition does not simply reward individuals; it allows a nation to [[garner|garner]] talent from every [[stratum|stratum]] of society.
A country that leaves such students behind wastes the very resource that public education is meant to develop.
Second, the recommendation would be advantageous where the economy depends on skilled workers, since public spending on education returns to society in many forms.

Vietnam's Doi Moi reforms of 1986 helped a country that had faced food shortages become one of the world's largest rice exporters, and sustaining such growth increasingly requires engineers, doctors and managers.
A government that makes university education free is, in effect, investing in the workers who will sustain that growth and pay taxes for decades.
Likewise, Finland, which requires schoolteachers to hold a master's degree, shows how advanced education can turn an ordinary job into a respected and selective profession.
Thus, in a growing economy, free higher education is less a cost than an investment whose benefits are [[pervasive|pervasive]] across the whole society.
Seen this way, tuition fees are a tax on the future rather than a saving for the present.
Admittedly, adopting the recommendation would not be advantageous in a country whose budget cannot support it, because free tuition without enough funding lowers quality.
Consider a government that abolishes fees but does not increase funding; enrollment might double while classrooms, laboratories and teachers stay the same.
The result would be crowded lectures and [[lackluster|lackluster]] degrees that employers no longer trust, so the students the policy was meant to help would receive a weaker education than before.
Nevertheless, this problem argues for introducing free tuition gradually and funding it properly, not for rejecting the idea.
A poorer country might begin by making public medical and teacher-training programs free and then expand the policy as its revenue grows.
Such caution qualifies my support but does not reverse it.
In conclusion, governments should offer free college education to all students when they can fund it well and keep standards high.
Free tuition draws talent from every family and repays its cost through a skilled workforce, but without adequate funding it can dilute the quality it was meant to spread.
The real question, then, is not whether free education is desirable but how [[prudently|prudent]] a government can pay for it.

words.meaning_here: carefully and sensibly, with attention to future costs

essays.task_note: Bodies 1-2 describe circumstances (wide talent but unequal wealth; a growing economy) where free tuition is advantageous, and Body 3 describes an underfunded system where it is not, explaining how this makes support conditional on funding.

essays.title: Targeted aid beats free tuition for all

paragraphs.text: A gift given to everyone is often a gift that helps the people who need it least.
This principle applies to the recommendation that governments should offer college and university education free of charge to all students.
I mostly disagree with this recommendation: although no qualified student should be turned away for lack of money, free tuition for everyone is a costly and poorly targeted way to reach that goal.
Universal free tuition largely benefits families who could already pay, and it diverts funds from earlier stages of education, even though it can be advantageous in a few special circumstances.

First, adopting the recommendation would not be advantageous in a society where university students come mostly from wealthier families, because free tuition would then transfer public money to those who need it least.
Consider a city where most university entrants attended private high schools and expensive tutoring centers.

If the government abolished fees there, the largest share of the benefit would go to families who were already prepared to pay, while poor students who never qualified for university would gain nothing.
A system of need-based scholarships could spend the same money far more [[equitably|equitable]], covering tuition and living costs for the students who would otherwise be shut out.
This shows that the aim behind the recommendation is [[laudable|laudable]], but the policy itself is too blunt to achieve it.
Fairness requires helping those who face barriers, not helping everyone equally.

Second, the recommendation would be disadvantageous in a country with a limited budget, since money spent on free university places is money not spent on the earlier schooling that decides who reaches university at all.

Finland offers a useful contrast: it requires schoolteachers to hold a master's degree and makes teaching a respected and selective profession, which strengthens schools long before students apply to college.

Now consider a developing country where many rural primary schools lack well-trained teachers; a dollar spent there may change more lives than a dollar spent on tuition for a student already admitted to university.
Thus, where resources are scarce, universal free tuition can [[exacerbate|exacerbate]] inequality by funding the end of the educational pipeline while its beginning remains weak.
Admittedly, there are circumstances in which free tuition would be advantageous, especially in fields where society faces a shortage of trained professionals.
A government that needs more rural doctors, for instance, might offer free medical training to students who agree to serve in remote districts for several years.
Such a program would address a [[pressing|pressing]] need, since in many countries the shortage of physicians is most severe outside the cities.
Nevertheless, such targeted programs are not the same as free tuition for all; they attach public money to public needs.
Free tuition for every student in every subject, by contrast, would spread the same budget so thinly that the most urgent needs might remain unmet.
This circumstance therefore supports my position rather than challenging it, because it shows that tuition support works best when it is aimed rather than universal.
In conclusion, governments should not make college free for every student, but they should make sure that no capable student is excluded by cost.
Universal free tuition favors the already advantaged and drains funds from basic schooling, whereas targeted aid can meet real shortages without these costs.
The wiser policy is to spend public money where it changes the most lives, not where it simply lowers the bill for everyone.

essays.task_note: Bodies 1-2 describe circumstances (wealth-skewed enrollment, limited budgets) where free tuition is disadvantageous, and Body 3 describes a shortage field where it would help, explaining why that case favors targeted aid.

essays.title: Comfort weakens those who stop striving

paragraphs.text: A muscle that is never used grows weak, and the same may be true of character.
This idea lies behind the statement that the luxuries and conveniences of contemporary life prevent people from developing into truly strong and independent individuals.
I largely agree with this statement, although I believe convenience weakens people only when they rely on it without effort or reflection.
Comfort removes the struggles that build resilience, and easy tools can replace skills people once had to master, even though conveniences also free time for more demanding work.
First, the statement holds true because strength grows from struggle, and modern comforts remove many of the struggles that once trained people to persevere.

The Wright brothers, bicycle makers without college degrees, achieved the first powered airplane flight in 1903 only after years of careful experiments with gliders and a wind tunnel they built themselves.
Their success depended on patience with failure, a quality that is hard to develop when every problem can be solved with a quick search.
Similarly, a student who has always had a tutor to answer each question may grow [[complacent|complacent]] and struggle when she meets her first problem with no ready answer.
This suggests that when comfort becomes [[ubiquitous|ubiquitous]], people lose the small, daily challenges that once made them [[hardy|hardy]] and self-reliant.
Struggle, in this sense, is not a misfortune to be avoided but a form of training that comfort quietly removes.
Second, conveniences can weaken independence because tools that perform a task for us often replace the skill we once needed to perform it ourselves.
GPS, for example, was built by the US military and became the basis of everyday navigation once it was opened to civilians.
Today, many drivers follow their phones without any sense of where they are, and when the signal fails, they cannot find their way home.

Likewise, smartphones and social media spread information instantly, but they also spread misinformation faster than corrections can follow, so people who rely on them uncritically may lose the habit of judging sources for themselves.
In these cases, convenience does not merely save effort; it gradually [[supplants|supplant]] the abilities that make a person independent.
A person who cannot navigate, calculate or evaluate information without a device is convenient to serve but hard to call independent.
Admittedly, the statement does not hold true in every case, because conveniences can also free people to pursue more demanding goals.

In the past, many people spent much of their lives fighting illness or hunger; today, antibiotics and reliable food supplies allow far more of them to study, build careers and serve their communities.
As a physician, I know that a healthy patient has far more energy for independent achievement than one who is constantly sick.
Nevertheless, this benefit depends on how people use the time that convenience gives them.

Someone who fills that time with new challenges grows stronger, while someone who fills it only with more comfort becomes more dependent, so the statement is true for passive users of convenience rather than for everyone.
My position, then, is qualified rather than absolute.
In conclusion, modern luxuries and conveniences often do prevent people from becoming strong and independent, but mainly when they are used to avoid effort.
Comfort removes the struggles that build character and tools can replace real skills, yet the same conveniences can free people for harder and more meaningful work.
Strength in a comfortable age, therefore, has to be chosen deliberately, because life no longer forces it upon us.

essays.title: Convenience frees people for harder challenges

paragraphs.text: Every generation seems to believe that the next one has grown soft.

The statement that the luxuries and conveniences of contemporary life prevent people from developing into truly strong and independent individuals is a modern version of this [[perennial|perennial]] complaint.
I mostly disagree with this statement: conveniences can weaken people who use them passively, but on the whole they make strength and independence more achievable, not less.
Modern tools give individuals more control over their own lives, and freedom from basic hardship lets people take on harder challenges, even though some conveniences do encourage dependence.
First, the statement does not hold true for many people, because modern conveniences give individuals the power to act on their own rather than rely on others.
Wikipedia, launched in 2001 and written by unpaid volunteers, grew into the largest encyclopedia in history, allowing anyone with an internet connection to teach themselves almost any subject.
A student in a remote province of Vietnam no longer needs a well-stocked library to learn about genetics or economics.
She can master the basics on her own and arrive at university already curious.
Similarly, smartphones and social media let activists organize quickly during the Arab Spring of 2011, giving ordinary citizens a voice that had once belonged mainly to governments and newspapers.
This shows that conveniences can [[bolster|bolster]] independence by placing knowledge and influence directly in the hands of individuals.
A person who can learn, publish and organize without anyone's permission is more independent than earlier generations could ever be.
Second, relief from basic hardship does not make people weak; rather, it allows them to direct their strength toward more ambitious goals.
After Vietnam's Doi Moi reforms of 1986, a country that had faced food shortages became one of the world's largest rice exporters, and poverty fell dramatically over the following decades.
Families who no longer worry about their next meal can send children to school, start businesses and take risks that hunger once made impossible.
Likewise, in my work, I meet young Vietnamese doctors whose grandparents lived through food shortages; free of that daily struggle, they can devote years to [[arduous|arduous]] research training.
In other words, comfort removes the struggle for mere survival so that people can face chosen challenges, which are a truer test of strength and independence.
Admittedly, the statement holds true in some cases, since certain conveniences encourage people to stop thinking for themselves.
Smartphones and social media spread misinformation faster than corrections can follow, and users who accept whatever appears on their screens become dependent on others' judgment.
Similarly, a driver who relies entirely on GPS may be lost the moment the signal fails.
Nevertheless, these problems come from how people use conveniences, not from the conveniences themselves.
The same phone that spreads rumors can also lead a reader to the original source, and the same GPS that makes one driver [[complacent|complacent]] lets a delivery worker build an independent living.
Thus, these cases qualify my position by showing that independence requires discipline, but they do not show that comfort itself is the enemy.
In conclusion, the luxuries and conveniences of modern life do not, on the whole, prevent people from becoming strong and independent.
They put knowledge and influence in individual hands and free people from the hardships of survival, although passive users can still become dependent on them.
Whether convenience weakens or strengthens us depends less on the tools we have than on the effort we choose to make with them.

too satisfied to make further effort

essays.title: Fresh eyes often see what experts miss

paragraphs.text: Some of history's most important discoveries were made by people who did not know what was supposed to be impossible.
This observation supports the statement that, in any field of inquiry, the beginner is more likely than the expert to make important contributions.
I largely agree with this statement, especially in fields where experts have grown attached to accepted ideas, though not in fields that demand years of technical training.
Beginners are free from the assumptions that blind experts, and they often bring methods from outside the field, although expertise remains essential where knowledge is highly specialized.
First, the statement holds true because newcomers are not bound by the assumptions that experts have learned to accept.
In 1847, Ignaz Semmelweis had doctors in Vienna wash their hands in chlorinated lime, and deaths from childbed fever on his ward fell sharply.
Yet most of his colleagues, many of them experienced physicians, rejected his idea, which germ theory vindicated only years after his death.

Similarly, consider a first-year resident who asks why a ward routine exists and discovers that senior doctors have not checked its value in years; her question, not their experience, prompts the change.
These cases show that expertise can harden into [[dogma|dogma]], and the person most likely to challenge it is often someone who has not yet learned to accept it.
Expertise is valuable, but it can also teach people what not to question.
Second, beginners often contribute by bringing skills from other fields, which experts inside a discipline may never think to use.
The Wright brothers, bicycle makers without college degrees, achieved the first powered airplane flight in 1903.

They succeeded through years of careful experiments with gliders and a wind tunnel they built themselves, applying a mechanic's [[empirical|empirical]] habits to a problem that had long defeated others.
Similarly, Wikipedia, written by unpaid volunteers rather than professional scholars, grew into the largest encyclopedia in history.
In my own field, I have seen junior researchers trained in computer science propose analyses of dengue data that senior epidemiologists, myself included, had never considered.
This shows that newcomers can reshape a field precisely because they do not approach it in the [[orthodox|orthodox]] way.
An outsider's lack of training, in other words, can become a strength when the experts have run out of new approaches.
Admittedly, the statement does not hold true in fields where progress requires deep technical knowledge that takes years to acquire.
The COVID-19 mRNA vaccines, for instance, were developed in under a year only because Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman had spent decades on basic research on mRNA.
No beginner could have supplied that foundation.
Nevertheless, even in such fields, experts make their greatest contributions when they keep the openness of a beginner.

Karikó and Weissman pursued research that attracted little notice at the time, which suggests that their success came from a willingness to work outside the mainstream rather than from experience alone.
This consideration narrows my position: the beginner's advantage lies less in a lack of knowledge than in a fresh perspective that experts can also choose to keep.
In conclusion, beginners are often more likely than experts to make important contributions, particularly in fields where accepted ideas have gone unquestioned.
They see past the assumptions that limit experts and bring methods from other fields, although highly technical fields still depend on years of expertise.
The most valuable mind, it seems, combines the knowledge of an expert with the curiosity of a [[neophyte|neophyte]].

words.meaning_here: a belief accepted as true without question

essays.title: Important discoveries usually require expertise

paragraphs.text: Stories of amateurs who outsmart professionals are appealing, but they are popular partly because they are rare.
This tension lies at the heart of the statement that, in any field of inquiry, the beginner is more likely than the expert to make important contributions.
I mostly disagree with this statement: although newcomers occasionally offer fresh insights, important contributions usually depend on the knowledge and judgment that only experience provides.
Most major discoveries build on long expertise, and experts are better able to recognize what truly matters, even though beginners sometimes challenge ideas that experts take for granted.
First, the statement does not hold true for most fields, because important contributions usually rest on years of accumulated knowledge.
The COVID-19 mRNA vaccines were developed in under a year, but only because Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman had spent decades on earlier, little-noticed basic research on mRNA.
Their 2023 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine rewarded a lifetime of expertise, not a beginner's lucky insight.
Similarly, Marie Curie won Nobel Prizes in physics in 1903 and in chemistry in 1911, a record that reflects years of [[assiduous|assiduous]] work rather than a single fresh idea.
This shows that in modern science, the questions worth answering are often visible only to those who already know the field deeply.
A beginner may ask a bold question, but without such knowledge he rarely has the tools to answer it.
Second, experts are more likely to contribute because they can recognize which observations are important and which are mere accidents.
In 1928, Alexander Fleming noticed that mold killed bacteria on a culture plate, an event a beginner might have [[dismissed|dismiss]] as a spoiled experiment.
Moreover, penicillin became a usable drug only when Howard Florey and Ernst Chain's team developed it during World War II, a task that required deep expertise in chemistry.
Likewise, in my own work, an experienced field epidemiologist can often tell from a few case reports whether a dengue cluster is a real outbreak or a reporting error.
A newcomer looking at the same reports would see only numbers.
This shows that a [[discerning|discerning]] expert does not simply collect facts but knows which facts deserve attention.
In Fleming's case, expertise turned a lucky observation into a lasting contribution.
Admittedly, there are cases in which beginners do make important contributions, especially when experts cling to [[obsolete|obsolete]] ideas.
The Wright brothers, bicycle makers without college degrees, achieved the first powered airplane flight in 1903.
Their achievement is often cited as proof that amateurs can outperform trained scientists.
Nevertheless, even this famous case supports the value of expertise more than it denies it.
The brothers succeeded only after years of careful experiments with gliders and a wind tunnel they built themselves; by the time they flew, they had become experts in their own right.
Their story suggests that what matters is not formal credentials but deep, hard-won knowledge, which is exactly what a true beginner lacks.
This consideration refines my position: experts need not hold degrees, but important contributions almost always come from people who have mastered their subject.
In conclusion, experts, not beginners, are more likely to make important contributions in most fields of inquiry.
Major discoveries build on long study, experts can tell meaningful observations from accidents, and even celebrated amateurs usually became experts before they succeeded.
Fresh eyes have value, but important discoveries usually belong to those who have earned their knowledge through years of patient, disciplined work.

words.meaning_here: showing great care and steady effort
showing good judgment about what matters
out of date; no longer useful

essays.task_note: Bodies 1-2 show ways the statement fails (discoveries built on long study, expert recognition), and Body 3 considers where it seems to hold (the Wright brothers), explaining how this refines the position to mastery rather than credentials.

essays.title: Welfare is the surest sign of greatness

paragraphs.text: Visitors often judge a country by its monuments, museums and famous names.
Yet the statement under discussion argues that the surest indicator of a great nation is not the achievements of its rulers, artists or scientists but the general welfare of its people.
I largely agree with this statement, because achievements matter most when they improve ordinary lives, although some achievements deserve recognition in their own right.

The welfare of a population reflects the quality of its leadership, and even scientific achievements are best measured by their effect on ordinary people, though some artistic accomplishments have lasting value beyond welfare.
First, the statement holds true because the welfare of ordinary people is the clearest evidence of whether a nation's leaders have governed well.
Vietnam's Doi Moi reforms of 1986 replaced central planning with market incentives, and a country that had faced food shortages became one of the world's largest rice exporters.
Poverty fell dramatically over the following decades, which is a far more convincing sign of national progress than any single leader's speech or monument.
Similarly, Singapore's government housing program now houses about 80% of the country's residents, most of whom own their flats.
These cases show that a ruler's achievement is best judged not by its [[ostentatious|ostentatious]] symbols but by the security and opportunity it brings to the general population.
A government that builds grand monuments while its citizens go hungry has achieved little that matters.
Second, even the achievements of scientists are most meaningful when they raise the general welfare of the people.
Smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980 after a coordinated global WHO vaccination campaign that relied on countries sharing data and vaccine.
The discovery of vaccination mattered because it was turned into protection for whole populations.
Likewise, Vietnam's 2007 law requiring motorbike helmets raised helmet use from low levels to over 90% within months and reduced head injuries and deaths.
As an epidemiologist, I see such outcomes as the real measure of public health: not the number of papers a country publishes, but the number of lives it saves.
This shows that scientific greatness and national welfare are not rivals; science [[redounds|redound]] to a nation's credit chiefly through the welfare it creates.
Admittedly, the statement does not hold true in every respect, because some achievements of artists and scientists have value beyond the welfare of a single generation.
Vincent van Gogh sold very few paintings during his lifetime, yet he is now regarded as one of the greatest painters in history, and his work enriches people far beyond his own country.
Likewise, Marie Curie's Nobel Prizes in physics and chemistry are still celebrated more than a century later.
Nevertheless, a nation whose people are poor or unhealthy cannot claim greatness merely because it produced a famous painter.
Art and science may add to a nation's glory, but they cannot [[offset|offset]] widespread suffering; greatness requires both a high peak of achievement and a broad base of welfare.
This consideration qualifies my view: achievements are a valuable sign of greatness, but welfare is the surest one.
In conclusion, the general welfare of a nation's people is a more reliable sign of greatness than the achievements of its most famous citizens.
Welfare shows whether leaders have governed well and whether scientific progress has reached ordinary lives, although art also has lasting value of its own.
A truly great nation, then, is one whose achievements are [[manifest|manifest]] not only in museums and laboratories but also in the daily lives of its people.

words.meaning_here: designed to impress or attract notice

essays.title: Achievements, not welfare alone, reveal greatness

paragraphs.text: When we remember ancient civilizations, we usually recall their thinkers, builders and artists rather than their average incomes.
This habit challenges the statement that the surest indicator of a great nation is the general welfare of its people rather than the achievements of its rulers, artists or scientists.
I mostly disagree with this statement: welfare is essential, but a nation's greatness is shown most clearly by achievements that benefit people beyond its own borders and generation.
Great achievements create welfare rather than merely reflect it, and their influence outlasts any measure of living standards, even though a nation that neglects its people cannot be called great.
First, the statement does not hold true because the achievements of rulers and scientists are often the source of general welfare, not a separate matter.
The Human Genome Project, a publicly funded international effort completed in 2003, made the human DNA sequence freely available to all researchers.
Its benefits did not stay within the countries that paid for it; scientists everywhere could build on it.
A nation that produces such work raises the welfare of people it will never govern.
Similarly, GPS was built by the US military, and once it was opened to civilians, it became the basis of everyday navigation, ride-hailing and delivery apps.
This shows that the welfare of ordinary people is frequently [[derivative|derivative]] of extraordinary achievements, so judging a nation by welfare alone mistakes the result for the cause.
Without such achievements, there would be far less welfare to measure.
Second, achievements are a surer sign of greatness because their influence lasts far longer than any level of material comfort.
Vincent van Gogh sold very few paintings during his lifetime, yet he is now regarded as one of the greatest painters in history.
Similarly, the leadership of Abraham Lincoln, who appointed political rivals such as William Seward to his cabinet, is still studied as a model of choosing able critics over loyal followers.
Living standards rise and fall with economic cycles, but such contributions remain part of a nation's identity for generations.
A visitor to any great city learns more about its past from its [[landmark|landmark]] buildings and books than from old income statistics.
Thus, welfare is a snapshot of a nation at one moment, whereas achievements are the lasting [[hallmark|hallmark]] of its character.
Admittedly, the statement contains an important truth, because a nation that neglects the welfare of its people cannot be considered truly great.

Vietnam's Doi Moi reforms of 1986 replaced central planning with market incentives, and poverty fell dramatically over the following decades; few would deny that this change made the country stronger.
Likewise, Singapore's housing program, which now houses about 80% of residents, is a genuine national accomplishment.
Nevertheless, these examples present welfare as the product of wise policy, which is itself an achievement of rulers.
The reforms and the housing program are admired precisely because leaders designed them, so they support the view that achievement, rather than welfare alone, reveals greatness.
Welfare, in other words, is not an alternative to achievement but one of its most important forms.
In conclusion, the general welfare of a nation's people is necessary for greatness, but it is not the surest indicator of it.
Great achievements often create welfare, they last far longer than living standards, and even successful welfare policies are themselves the achievements of capable rulers.
A nation is best judged, therefore, by what it contributes to humanity, with the welfare of its own people as a [[cardinal|cardinal]] condition.

essays.task_note: Bodies 1-2 show ways the statement fails (achievements create welfare and outlast it), and Body 3 shows where it holds (neglected welfare disqualifies greatness), explaining how welfare policies themselves count as achievements.

essays.title: Praise teaches; criticism only for real danger

paragraphs.text: People rarely work harder for a critic than for someone who notices what they do well.
This observation supports the claim that the best way to teach, whether as an educator, employer or parent, is to praise positive actions and ignore negative ones.
I largely agree with this claim for most everyday situations, although actions that cause serious harm must still be addressed.

Praise builds the trust that makes people receptive to learning, and it directs attention toward the behavior worth repeating, even though critics rightly point out that some mistakes cannot be ignored.
First, praise is the best way to teach because it builds the trust and confidence that make people willing to learn.
Abraham Lincoln, for example, appointed his political rivals, including William Seward, to his cabinet, choosing able critics over loyal followers.
By recognizing their strengths rather than dwelling on past opposition, Lincoln made a [[magnanimous|magnanimous]] choice that turned former opponents into capable partners.
In the workplace, a manager who thanks a new employee for a well-prepared report is more likely to receive a second good report than one who comments only on its typing errors.
This shows that recognition, whether from a leader, employer or parent, creates the goodwill on which real learning depends, while constant criticism tends to [[alienate|alienate]] the learner.
People who feel valued are more willing to accept guidance, and guidance is useless if no one is willing to accept it.
Second, praise teaches more efficiently than criticism because it points directly to the behavior that the learner should repeat.
Consider a parent teaching a young child to share toys.

If the parent praises each act of sharing and pays little attention to occasional grabbing, the child learns that sharing earns attention, whereas scolding may teach that grabbing is a reliable way to get it.
The child soon begins to share without being asked.
Similarly, when I supervise junior researchers, specific praise such as "This table is clear and complete" is more [[efficacious|efficacious]] than a long list of corrections.
In each case, praise gives the learner a clear model to follow, whereas attention to errors can [[inadvertently|inadvertent]] reward the very behavior it aims to stop.
Over time, learners who know what success looks like begin to seek it on their own, which is the real aim of teaching.
Admittedly, the most compelling challenge to this view is that some negative actions are too dangerous to ignore.

When Ignaz Semmelweis had doctors in Vienna wash their hands in chlorinated lime in 1847, deaths from childbed fever on his ward fell sharply, so a hospital that ignored a doctor's failure to wash would put lives at risk.
Likewise, a parent cannot ignore a child who runs into traffic.
Nevertheless, these cases are exceptions that call for a clear, immediate rule rather than a general habit of criticism.
Even in a hospital, the best way to build lasting hand-washing habits is to correct the dangerous lapse briefly and then praise every instance of compliance.
Thus, the challenge limits the claim to harmless mistakes but does not overturn it.
In conclusion, praising positive actions while overlooking minor negative ones is usually the best way to teach in classrooms, workplaces and homes.
Praise builds trust and shows learners exactly what to repeat, while the danger of ignoring serious errors requires only a narrow exception.
A good teacher, employer or parent should therefore be generous with praise and reserve criticism for the moments when real harm is at stake.

words.meaning_here: generous toward a rival or someone less powerful
make someone feel distant or unfriendly
effective in producing the intended result

essays.task_note: Body 3 states the strongest challenge (dangerous errors cannot be ignored) with two examples, then answers it by limiting the claim to harmless mistakes rather than abandoning it.

essays.title: Ignored mistakes grow; feedback needs both

paragraphs.text: A coach who never mentions a player's mistakes may be pleasant company, but the team is unlikely to win.
This image raises doubts about the claim that the best way to teach, whether as an educator, employer or parent, is to praise positive actions and ignore negative ones.
I mostly disagree with this claim: praise is a powerful tool, but effective teaching also requires honest attention to negative actions.

Ignored mistakes do not disappear, and people and organizations that cannot hear criticism make costly errors, although the strongest objection to my view, the motivating power of praise, deserves careful attention.
First, ignoring negative actions fails because mistakes that go uncorrected tend to grow rather than fade.
Kodak engineer Steven Sasson invented the digital camera in 1975, yet Kodak, protecting its profitable film business, was slow to embrace digital photography and filed for bankruptcy in 2012.
A company culture that rewarded success in film while ignoring the warning signs allowed a manageable problem to become fatal.
Had its leaders treated the threat as a mistake to correct early, the company might have adapted in time.
Similarly, a parent who overlooks a teenager's first small lies may find that dishonesty has become a habit by the time it causes real trouble.
This shows that silence about errors is not neutral; it allows them to [[fester|fester]] until correction is far more painful than it would have been at the start.
Ignoring a negative action, in other words, is itself a choice, and often an expensive one.
Second, learners and organizations improve fastest when criticism is welcomed rather than avoided.
Abraham Lincoln appointed his political rivals, including William Seward, to his cabinet, choosing able critics over loyal followers.
He understood that a leader surrounded only by praise would hear only what he wished to hear.

Likewise, in 2015 a large collaboration tried to repeat 100 published psychology studies and reproduced the results of only about a third of them, a finding that has made researchers more [[circumspect|circumspect]] about single studies.
In my own field, peer review is valuable precisely because reviewers identify flaws that authors cannot see in their own work.
In politics and science alike, then, progress depends on people who are willing to point out negative actions, not merely praise positive ones.
Admittedly, the most compelling challenge to my position is that praise motivates people far more than criticism, and harsh correction can make learners give up.
A child who hears only about her mistakes in piano practice may decide she has no talent and stop playing altogether.
Similarly, an employee who is criticized in front of colleagues may become [[timorous|timorous]] and stop offering ideas.
Nevertheless, this objection argues against harsh criticism, not against addressing negative actions at all.
A teacher can correct a wrong note gently and then praise the passage played well, and a manager can discuss an error privately while acknowledging the employee's effort.
The real choice is not between praise and criticism but between careless and careful feedback, and careful feedback includes both.
In conclusion, the best way to teach is not to ignore negative actions but to address them with [[candid|candid]], thoughtful feedback alongside generous praise.
Ignored mistakes tend to grow, and people and institutions improve when criticism is welcome, although the value of praise means that correction must be delivered with care.
Educators, employers and parents who combine both forms of feedback will produce learners who are confident as well as competent.

words.meaning_here: grow worse over time when left untreated
cautious; careful before trusting or acting

essays.task_note: Body 3 states the strongest challenge (praise motivates and harsh criticism discourages) with two examples, then answers it by distinguishing harsh criticism from careful correction.

essays.title: Pay teachers for measured student progress

paragraphs.text: In most professions, from sales to surgery, people who produce better results expect to earn more than those who do not.
Applying this principle to education, some argue that teachers' salaries should be based on their students' academic performance.
I largely agree with this claim, provided that performance is measured by students' progress over time rather than by raw test scores.

Linking pay to results rewards effective teaching and helps schools attract and keep talented teachers, even though critics raise serious concerns about fairness that a well-designed system must answer.
First, basing salaries on student performance would reward teachers for the outcome that matters most: how much their students learn.
Consider two mathematics teachers in the same Hanoi school who begin the year with similar classes.
If one teacher's students improve their scores by twenty points while the other's barely improve, paying both the same salary sends the message that results are irrelevant.
Similarly, in public health we judge a policy such as Vietnam's 2007 motorbike helmet law by its results: helmet use rose to over 90% within months, and head injuries and deaths fell.
This shows that measuring outcomes, rather than effort or years of service alone, can [[galvanize|galvanize]] professionals to focus on what truly helps the people they serve.
When pay ignores results, the most effective teachers have little reason to stay, and the least effective have little reason to improve.
Second, performance-based pay would help schools attract and keep talented teachers, who might otherwise leave for better-paid careers.
Finland shows that the status of teaching shapes who enters it: by requiring a master's degree, it makes teaching a respected and selective profession.
A salary system that rewards excellent results would add a financial reason to the professional respect that draws capable people into classrooms.
Consider a country where teachers' fixed salaries are so low that the most able graduates choose other fields; performance pay would give such graduates a reason to choose teaching instead.
Thus, tying pay to results can raise both the [[standing|standing]] of the profession and the quality of the people within it.
Students would be the ultimate beneficiaries, because the best teachers would remain in the classroom rather than leave it.
Admittedly, the most compelling challenge to this claim is that student performance depends on factors teachers cannot control, such as poverty, family support and prior schooling.
A teacher in a poor rural district may work harder than a colleague in a wealthy city school yet see lower test scores, and a crude system would punish her for her students' disadvantages.
Pay based on scores might also tempt teachers to drill students for tests rather than teach them to think.
Nevertheless, these problems argue for measuring progress fairly, not for abandoning the link between pay and performance.
A system that compares each student's growth from the start of the year, and that adds classroom observations to test results, would [[mitigate|mitigate]] both risks.
With such safeguards, the teacher in the poor district would be rewarded for her students' growth rather than punished for their starting point.
In conclusion, teachers' salaries should reflect their students' academic performance, as long as that performance is measured as fair, long-term progress.
Such a system rewards the results that matter and draws talented people into teaching, while careful design answers the strongest objections about fairness and narrow test preparation.
Paying teachers for real learning, rather than for time served, would treat teaching as the [[estimable|estimable]] profession it deserves to be.

essays.task_note: Body 3 states the strongest challenge (scores reflect factors outside teachers' control and invite test drilling), then answers it by proposing progress-based measurement rather than abandoning the claim.

essays.title: Hold teachers accountable without score-based pay

paragraphs.text: Some of the most important things a teacher gives students, such as curiosity and character, never appear on a test.
This fact makes me doubt the claim that teachers' salaries should be based on their students' academic performance.
I mostly disagree with this claim: although teachers should be accountable for their work, tying pay to student results would be unfair and would distort teaching.

Student performance depends heavily on factors outside a teacher's control, and pay linked to scores encourages narrow test preparation, even though the strongest argument for the claim, the need for accountability, deserves a serious answer.
First, basing salaries on student performance is unfair because scores reflect students' backgrounds as much as their teachers' skill.
Consider a teacher in a remote district of Vietnam whose students often miss school during the harvest and have no books at home.
Even if she teaches with great skill, her students may score below those of an average teacher in a wealthy city, and a performance-based system would pay her less for taking the harder job.
Similarly, in epidemiology we never judge a hospital by its raw death rate without adjusting for how sick its patients were on arrival.
This shows that a salary system based on raw results would [[marginalize|marginalize]] the very teachers who serve the neediest students and push them toward easier schools.
Over time, the students who most need skilled teachers would be the least likely to have them.
Second, pay tied to performance encourages teachers to teach for the test rather than for real understanding.
Finland relies far less on standardized testing than many countries, and it instead invests in teachers by requiring a master's degree and making teaching a respected and selective profession.
Its approach suggests that a nation can trust teachers' professional judgment rather than reduce their work to a single [[aggregate|aggregate]] score.

By contrast, a teacher whose salary depends on test results has every reason to spend weeks drilling past exam questions instead of encouraging the curiosity that leads students to learn on their own.
Thus, performance pay may raise scores in the short term while leaving students [[bereft|bereft]] of the deeper skills that education should develop.
Qualities that cannot be measured easily, such as curiosity and character, would simply stop being taught.
Admittedly, the most compelling argument for the claim is that teachers, like other professionals, should be accountable for results, and fixed salaries can protect ineffective teachers.
Parents whose children spend a year with a careless teacher have a fair complaint if that teacher earns exactly the same as a dedicated colleague.
Nevertheless, accountability does not require linking salaries to test scores.

Schools can evaluate teachers through classroom observation, peer review and student progress over several years, and they can provide training or, if necessary, dismissal when a teacher repeatedly fails.
Medicine offers a useful model: doctors are held to professional standards and reviewed by colleagues, yet few people suggest paying them according to whether their patients recover.
This challenge therefore shows the need for evaluation, not for performance-based pay.
In conclusion, teachers' salaries should not be tied to their students' academic performance, even though teachers must be held accountable for their work.
Scores reflect students' circumstances as much as teaching quality, and performance pay rewards test preparation over real learning, while better tools exist to ensure accountability.
Paying teachers fairly and evaluating them [[judiciously|judicious]] would serve students far better than turning every classroom into a contest of scores.

formed by combining many parts into one total

essays.task_note: Body 3 states the strongest argument for the claim (accountability and protection of weak teachers), then answers it by showing that evaluation, not score-based pay, meets that need.

essays.title: Human-caused threats create a clear duty

paragraphs.text: Every year, conservation agencies must decide which of thousands of threatened species will receive their limited money and attention.
The policy under discussion offers a simple rule for these choices: society should make efforts to save endangered species only when human activities are the cause of their potential extinction.
I largely support this policy, as long as "human activities" is read broadly enough to include indirect harms such as climate change and introduced diseases.

This position rests on three considerations: the policy assigns responsibility fairly, it directs scarce resources where they are most likely to work, and its main weakness, though real, can be managed.
First, implementing the policy would place the burden of rescue on those who created the danger, a principle we already accept in other areas of life.
When a factory pollutes a river, we do not ask the fishermen downstream to clean it; we require the factory to stop and to repair the damage.

Likewise, when logging, hunting or the illegal wildlife trade pushes an animal toward extinction, it is reasonable to ask society, which [[reaps|reap]] the benefits of those activities, to pay for the recovery.

Similarly, a country that drains a wetland for rice farming has a stronger duty to protect the birds that lived there than a country whose birds are disappearing because of a natural shift in climate.
This shows that the policy's central condition is not arbitrary: it links the duty to act with the act that caused the harm, which makes the duty easier to justify and to enforce.
Second, the policy would likely make conservation more effective, because threats caused by humans are usually threats that humans can remove.
When a species is declining because of overhunting or habitat loss, the remedy is clear: ban the hunting, protect the forest, and the population often recovers.

By contrast, when a species is fading because of slow natural processes, such as competition with a better-adapted rival, even a large budget may only delay the end, and spending on such cases can be [[futile|futile]].
Medicine offers a parallel: in my work as an epidemiologist, we direct resources first to causes we can modify, such as unsafe water, rather than to risks we cannot change.
Consequently, the policy acts like a triage rule, and in a world of limited funds, triage based on what can be fixed is a [[prudent|prudent]] choice rather than a cold one.
Admittedly, the policy has a serious weakness: in practice, it is often difficult to separate human causes from natural ones.

A frog species may be dying from a fungal disease, which looks natural, yet the fungus may have spread around the world through the human pet trade; likewise, a coral reef may be bleaching because of warming seas that human emissions helped to cause.
Nevertheless, this difficulty argues for a careful definition of human activity, not for abandoning the policy.
If agencies count indirect effects such as introduced diseases and climate change, the rule will cover most of the species now at risk, and the few truly natural declines can be judged case by case.

In other words, the [[ambiguous|ambiguous]] cases [[qualify|qualify]] my support rather than overturn it: the policy is sound only if it is applied with scientific judgment instead of a narrow legal reading.
In conclusion, I support the policy of focusing conservation efforts on species threatened by human activity, provided that the term is defined broadly.
Such a policy matches responsibility to cause, concentrates limited resources on threats that can actually be removed, and can handle unclear cases through sound scientific assessment.
Applied in this way, the policy would not make society [[indifferent|indifferent]] to nature; it would make society accountable for its own impact on nature.

essays.title: Species are worth saving whatever the cause

paragraphs.text: A species that disappears cannot be brought back, whatever the reason it disappeared.
The policy under discussion would nonetheless limit conservation to species whose potential extinction results from human activities.
I largely oppose this policy, because the value of a species does not depend on what threatens it, although I accept that human-caused threats deserve priority when funds are scarce.

Three consequences shape this position: the policy would force agencies into a slow search for causes, it would allow the loss of species whose value we cannot yet foresee, and it is not needed to set sensible priorities.
First, implementing the policy would delay action, because agencies would have to prove the cause of a decline before they could respond.
In ecology, as in epidemiology, causes are rarely simple.
A bird population may shrink because of a disease, a drought and the loss of a few nesting sites all at once, and scientists may argue for years about which factor matters most.
Under this policy, each argument would become a legal question, and while experts debated, the population could fall below the point of recovery.
Similarly, in outbreak response, we do not wait to confirm the exact source of an epidemic before we start protecting people, because delay is the most [[pernicious|pernicious]] error we can make.
This shows that a rule tied to the cause of extinction would [[impede|impede]] the very thing conservation needs most: early, decisive action.
Second, the policy would allow the loss of species that may prove valuable in ways we cannot predict, regardless of why they are declining.
Penicillin offers a clear illustration.
In 1928, Alexander Fleming noticed that mold killed bacteria on a culture plate, and that chance observation eventually led to one of the most important drugs in history.
Nature is full of organisms whose useful chemicals or genes remain [[latent|latent]] until someone studies them.
A plant that is disappearing because of a natural change in rainfall may hold a compound as useful as the one in Fleming's mold, but under the proposed policy, no one would be obliged to save it.
Thus, the policy asks the wrong question: what matters is not who caused the threat, but what society would lose if the species were gone.
Admittedly, supporters of the policy make a strong point: resources for conservation are limited, and humans have a special duty to repair the damage they themselves have done.
When logging or poaching drives an animal toward extinction, society clearly owes that species a response, and such threats are also easier to remove than natural ones.
Nevertheless, this argument supports giving human-caused cases priority, not making them the only cases that count.
A hospital, for instance, treats the most urgent patients first, but it does not refuse care to others simply because their illness was not caused by an accident.

In the same way, a [[judicious|judicious]] conservation policy can rank species by urgency, cost and cause without declaring any species unworthy of help, so the consequence I fear is not prioritization but exclusion.
In conclusion, I oppose a rule that limits conservation strictly to species endangered by human activity, although human causes may reasonably come first.
Such a rule would slow responses while causes are debated, would risk the loss of species with unknown value, and is not needed to set sensible priorities.
Society should try to prevent every extinction it can prevent, whatever the cause, and let responsibility shape the order of action rather than its limits.

words.meaning_here: harmful in a gradual or hidden but serious way
present but hidden and not yet developed or noticed

essays.task_note: Body 1-2 trace two harmful consequences of implementing the policy (delayed action, lost species), Body 3 weighs the supporters' strongest consequence, and the essay explains how these consequences lead to opposing exclusion but accepting prioritization.

essays.title: Job prospects deserve a central role

paragraphs.text: For many young people, choosing a major is the first large financial decision of their lives.
Because university education costs years of time and often large debts, some argue that college students should base their choice of a field of study on the availability of jobs in that field.
I largely agree with this claim, as long as job availability is treated as the main factor in the choice rather than the only one.

Job prospects matter because they protect students from financial hardship and because they connect education to the needs of society, and the strongest objection, that passion drives success, can be met within this approach.
First, students should weigh job availability heavily because a degree without a job market can leave them in a [[precarious|precarious]] position for years.
In Vietnam, many families borrow money or sell land to send a child to university in Hanoi or Ho Chi Minh City.
When that graduate studies a field with few openings, the family's sacrifice may produce years of underemployment instead of security.
By contrast, a graduate in a field with many openings can usually start earning, repay the family and build a career.
Similarly, a graduate with heavy student loans in the United States has little freedom to wait for an ideal job; the debt requires an income now.
This shows that job availability is not a shallow concern; for most students, it determines whether education becomes a path out of hardship or a new source of it.
Moreover, choosing fields with strong demand helps society as well as the individual, since job openings often signal unmet social needs.
Consider a country facing a shortage of doctors and nurses in rural districts.
When students respond to that demand by entering the health professions, they gain stable careers, and patients in underserved areas finally receive care.
In my own field, the demand for epidemiologists grew sharply during the COVID-19 pandemic, and those trained in data analysis could [[alleviate|alleviate]] a real public problem.
Likewise, once GPS was opened to civilians, it became the basis of ride-hailing and delivery apps, and students who studied software engineering helped build services that millions now use.
Thus, when students let the labor market guide them, they are not merely protecting themselves; they are directing their talent to where society needs it most.
Admittedly, the most compelling challenge to my position is that passion and ability, not job counts, are what lead people to excel.

Vincent van Gogh sold very few paintings during his lifetime and is now regarded as one of the greatest painters in history; had he chosen a career by market demand, the world would have lost his work.
Nevertheless, such cases are rare, and most students are not choosing between greatness and a paycheck but between a stable career and an uncertain one.
Moreover, interest and demand often overlap: a student who loves art can study design, and one who loves biology can enter public health.

This challenge therefore refines my position rather than [[refuting|refute]] it: job availability should lead the decision, but students should look for the in-demand field that best fits their interests.
In conclusion, I largely agree that college students should base their choice of field mainly on the availability of jobs.
Doing so protects them from financial insecurity and directs their skills toward society's needs, and it need not crush personal interest if students choose wisely within growing fields.
The wisest choice is rarely passion alone or demand alone, but a [[pragmatic|pragmatic]] match between the two, with demand setting the boundaries.
