essays.title: Learn first, question next

paragraphs.text: Doubt is a powerful tool, but like any tool, it can be misused.
This is why I hesitate to endorse the statement that students should always question what they are taught instead of accepting it passively.

I mostly disagree with the statement as written, because its demand that students always question ignores the need to build a foundation first, although critical thinking remains an essential goal of education.

Learners need trusted knowledge before they can question well, uninformed doubt can spread falsehoods rather than truth, and the real value of questioning appears mainly after students have mastered the basics.
First, the statement does not hold for beginners, because meaningful questions require knowledge that [[neophytes|neophyte]] do not yet have.
A first-year medical student who doubts every page of a pharmacology textbook will learn very little; she must first accept established facts about how drugs act before she can judge a new study.
In my experience teaching young doctors, the most useful questions come from those who have mastered the basics, not from those who challenge everything from the start.
Similarly, a child learning to read must accept the sounds of the letters before she can analyze a poem.
Accepting such basics is not the same as believing blindly; it is a reasonable choice to trust a discipline's accumulated evidence for a while.
Trust at this stage is not passivity; it is the [[rudimentary|rudimentary]] foundation on which all later questioning depends.
Asking students to question everything before they know anything would simply leave them confused.
Second, questioning without knowledge can spread falsehoods rather than correct them.
During the Arab Spring of 2011, smartphones and social media let activists organize quickly, but the same tools also spread misinformation faster than corrections could follow.
Distrust of official sources does not automatically produce truth; it can simply transfer belief to less reliable voices.
In my own work, I have met parents who doubted what they had been taught about vaccines, yet accepted [[specious|specious]] claims from online videos without any doubt.
Without the knowledge to evaluate evidence, such doubt is not critical thinking; it is merely a different form of trust.
These cases show that questioning has value only when it is guided by evidence and method, which students must first be taught to accept.
A school that urges constant questioning without teaching method may therefore produce students who distrust experts but are easily misled by others.
Admittedly, the statement holds true in important cases, since passive acceptance can preserve serious errors.
In 2015, a large collaboration tried to repeat 100 published psychology studies and reproduced the results of only about a third of them, showing that even published research can mislead.
Nevertheless, those errors were exposed by trained scientists who had first mastered their field, not by students who doubted everything from the beginning.

Ignaz Semmelweis, too, could challenge his colleagues' views only because he was a physician who saw deaths from childbed fever on his own ward fall sharply after doctors washed their hands in chlorinated lime.
Such experts questioned received ideas from a position of knowledge, which is what made their doubts productive.
This consideration shapes my position: questioning is the [[zenith|zenith]] of education, not its starting point.
Students must earn the right to question by first understanding what they are questioning.
In conclusion, I mostly disagree that students should always question what they are taught, although critical thinking should be a central aim of every school.
Beginners need a foundation of trusted knowledge, uninformed doubt can spread falsehoods, and the most valuable challenges to accepted ideas come from those who first learned them well.
Students should therefore learn first, question next, and always [[ascertain|ascertain]] whether their doubts rest on evidence.

essays.title: Speed creates more problems than it solves

paragraphs.text: Modern life often feels [[frenetic|frenetic]], like a race in which no one remembers where the finish line is.
This feeling underlies the statement that the increasingly rapid pace of life today causes more problems than it solves.
I largely agree with this statement, although speed has brought undeniable benefits in fields where time saves lives.

A faster pace encourages hasty decisions with long-term costs, it allows false information to outrun the truth, and while rapid innovation has solved some urgent problems, those gains depend on slow work that a hurried culture tends to undervalue.
First, the statement holds true because a faster pace pushes people toward quick fixes that create larger problems later.
Antibiotic resistance offers a clear case.
Patients who want to recover immediately often buy antibiotics over the counter, a practice common in many countries including Vietnam, and doctors under time pressure prescribe them too readily.
As a result, resistant bacteria spread, and drugs that once cured infections now often fail.
Alexander Fleming foresaw this danger; in his 1945 Nobel lecture, he warned that misuse would breed resistant bacteria.
In my own work, I have also seen patients stop their antibiotics as soon as they feel better, which worsens the problem.
The demand for speed thus [[exacerbates|exacerbate]] a problem far more serious than the inconvenience it was meant to remove.
What looks like efficiency in the moment becomes a burden for an entire health system.
Second, the rapid pace of communication allows misinformation to spread faster than it can be corrected.
During the Arab Spring of 2011, smartphones and social media let activists organize quickly, but they also spread misinformation faster than corrections could follow.
In public health, I have seen the same pattern: a false rumor about a vaccine can travel across a province in a day, while a careful correction takes weeks to prepare.
Similarly, a busy reader who scrolls through dozens of headlines each morning rarely stops to check a single source.
Speed also leaves less time for reflection, so people react to news before they understand it.
When speed rewards the first message rather than the accurate one, falsehoods [[proliferate|proliferate]] and public trust is [[undermined|undermine]].
A society that cannot pause to verify information makes poorer decisions about health, politics and everyday life.
Admittedly, the statement does not hold in every field, since speed has sometimes solved urgent problems.
The COVID-19 mRNA vaccines were developed in under a year and protected many people during a global emergency.
Nevertheless, that speed was possible only because of decades of earlier, little-noticed basic research on mRNA by Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman.
In other words, a rapid result rested on exactly the kind of slow, patient work that a hurried culture tends to undervalue.
Without that long, quiet preparation, no amount of urgency could have produced a vaccine so quickly.
This consideration [[qualifies|qualify]] my position: speed is beneficial when it is built on careful foundations, but a society that values only speed will gradually lose those foundations.
The benefits of speed, in short, are borrowed from patience, and a culture that rejects patience will eventually run out of credit.
In conclusion, I largely agree that the accelerating pace of modern life creates more problems than it solves.
Haste encourages harmful shortcuts and spreads misinformation, and even the genuine successes of speed depend on the slow, careful work that a rushed society neglects.
The wiser goal is not to slow down everything, but to be [[judicious|judicious]] about when speed truly serves us.

essays.title: A faster world solves more than it breaks

paragraphs.text: Many people complain that life moves too fast, yet few would give up the speed that saves time and lives.
This tension lies at the center of the statement that the increasingly rapid pace of life today causes more problems than it solves.
I mostly disagree with the statement, because the speed of modern life has solved serious problems in health and economic life, although it creates real costs that demand attention.

Rapid innovation responds to emergencies in ways that were once impossible, fast economic change has reduced poverty dramatically, and the genuine harms of speed, such as misinformation, call for better management rather than a return to a slower age.
First, the statement does not hold in medicine and technology, where a faster pace of innovation has solved problems that once seemed [[intractable|intractable]].
The COVID-19 mRNA vaccines were developed in under a year, an [[unprecedented|unprecedented]] speed made possible by decades of earlier basic research by Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman.
Rapid development allowed health systems to protect vulnerable people while the pandemic was still spreading.
Similarly, once GPS, first built by the US military, was opened to civilians, it became the basis of everyday navigation, ride-hailing and delivery apps that save ordinary people countless hours.
In these cases, speed was not a source of problems but the solution itself.
A slower world would have faced the same emergencies with far fewer tools.
Second, a faster pace of economic life has improved living standards on a vast scale.
Vietnam's Doi Moi reforms of 1986 replaced central planning with market incentives, and a country that had faced food shortages became one of the world's largest rice exporters.
Over the following decades, poverty fell dramatically as markets, trade and communication accelerated.
In my own field, likewise, faster digital reporting now lets district health officers in Vietnam detect a dengue outbreak within days rather than weeks.
Faster communication also lets farmers check prices and families send money home within minutes.
Such gains [[outstrip|outstrip]] the inconveniences of a busy life, and they show that speed often serves human welfare.
For many ordinary families, a faster pace has meant not stress but opportunity, and speed has served as an engine of development rather than a source of harm.
Admittedly, the statement holds true in some respects, because speed also spreads harm.
During the Arab Spring of 2011, smartphones and social media helped activists organize quickly but also spread misinformation faster than corrections could follow.
Nevertheless, this problem arises from how people use fast tools, not from speed itself, and it can be [[mitigated|mitigate]].
Public health agencies, for instance, can answer rumors through the same rapid channels, and schools can teach students to check sources before sharing.
In my experience, a health message shared quickly by trusted local officials often reaches people before a rumor takes hold.
This consideration shapes my position: the costs of a rapid pace are real, but they are manageable side effects of a change that has solved far larger problems.
Rejecting speed because of misinformation would be like rejecting medicine because of side effects.
In conclusion, I mostly disagree that the rapid pace of modern life creates more problems than it solves.
Speed has transformed medicine and helped lift many families out of poverty, and its most visible harm, the spread of misinformation, can be reduced without giving up these benefits.
Rather than [[lament|lament]] the speed of modern life, we should learn to direct it wisely.

essays.title: Media scrutiny makes living heroes rare

paragraphs.text: Heroes once lived at a distance, known through stories rather than through daily news.

Today, constant coverage has led some to claim that it is no longer possible for a society to regard any living man or woman as a hero, for the reason that the reputation of anyone subjected to media scrutiny will eventually be diminished.
I largely agree with both the claim and the reason, although I would weaken the claim from "impossible" to "very difficult."

The claim reflects how modern media expose every flaw, the reason is supported by the way online platforms reward criticism, and the most compelling counterexample, a pair of widely admired living scientists, shows only that heroism today is narrower and more fragile.
First, the claim is largely accurate because modern media leave almost no part of a public figure's life private.
Consider a hypothetical surgeon who becomes a national hero after leading her team through a hospital crisis.
Within weeks, journalists and online users examine her old social media posts, her finances and her family, and any small [[peccadillo|peccadillo]] becomes headline news.
Abraham Lincoln, by contrast, could appoint political rivals such as William Seward to his cabinet without every private word being instantly published and judged.
Earlier heroes were not necessarily better people; they were simply seen from farther away.
Because scrutiny today is constant and [[exhaustive|exhaustive]], the distance that once protected heroic reputations has largely disappeared.
Even a genuinely heroic act cannot protect a reputation for long when every minor flaw becomes public.
Second, the reason on which the claim rests is persuasive, because media platforms reward stories that diminish reputations.
During the Arab Spring of 2011, smartphones and social media helped people organize quickly, but they also spread misinformation faster than corrections could follow.
A false accusation against a public figure can therefore reach a huge audience before any correction appears.
In public health, I have watched respected doctors become targets of online [[vitriol|vitriol]] simply for recommending vaccines.
Corrections rarely travel as far as the original accusation, so damage often remains even after the truth is known.

The reason is thus not only true but also explains the claim: if scrutiny inevitably [[sullies|sully]] reputations, a living person can hardly keep the spotless image that heroism has traditionally required.
Under such conditions, the diminishing of reputations is less a possibility than a pattern.
Admittedly, the strongest challenge to my position is that some living people are still widely admired.

Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman, whose decades of little-noticed research made the COVID-19 mRNA vaccines possible, won the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine and are celebrated by many as heroes of the pandemic.
Nevertheless, their admiration is largely limited to certain communities, and in a [[polarized|polarized]] media environment many people who distrust vaccines would refuse to call them heroes.
Their case shows that a living hero can still exist, but usually for one group rather than for a whole society.
This counterexample weakens the absolute form of the claim without overturning its central point: a hero admired by an entire society is now extremely rare.
The claim overstates the case, but only slightly.
In conclusion, I largely agree that media scrutiny makes it very difficult for a society to regard any living person as a hero.
Constant exposure strips away the distance that heroism needs, platforms reward damage to reputations, and even admired figures are now heroes only to part of the public.
A society should therefore look for heroic acts rather than heroic people, admiring what someone has done without expecting a flawless life.

essays.title: Living heroes can survive scrutiny

paragraphs.text: Every era seems to believe that its heroes are smaller than those of the past.

Our own era expresses this belief in the claim that it is no longer possible for a society to regard any living man or woman as a hero, based on the reason that the reputation of anyone subjected to media scrutiny will eventually be diminished.
I mostly disagree with both the claim and the reason, although I accept that scrutiny makes heroism more fragile than it once was.

The claim is contradicted by living people whom societies admire today, the reason ignores scrutiny that reveals true merit, and the real danger of media attacks requires us to judge heroes more carefully rather than to abandon the idea.
First, the claim is refuted by living people whom whole societies continue to admire.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, frontline health workers in Vietnam were widely celebrated as heroes, and many of my colleagues who worked in isolation wards are still remembered with gratitude in their communities.

Similarly, Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman, whose decades of little-noticed research made the COVID-19 mRNA vaccines possible, received the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine and wide public admiration.
Their reputations have survived years of public attention precisely because their work was real.
These examples show that heroism has not disappeared; it has simply shifted toward people whose [[intrepid|intrepid]] or patient work serves others.
A society that can still name such people has clearly not lost its capacity for heroes.
Second, the reason is flawed because media scrutiny does not always diminish reputations; it often confirms or even creates them.
Frances Kelsey of the US FDA refused to approve thalidomide, a sedative given to pregnant women around 1960 that caused severe birth defects in thousands of babies in Europe.
Public attention to her decision turned her into a widely admired figure, and the US then passed stricter drug-testing rules in 1962.
Likewise, the Montgomery bus boycott, in which Black residents refused for over a year to ride segregated buses, drew national attention that elevated its participants rather than diminishing them.
Scrutiny is a test that people of genuine [[probity|probity]] can pass, and the reason wrongly assumes that every reputation conceals a scandal waiting to be found.
In many cases, the more closely the public looks, the stronger a deserving reputation becomes.
Admittedly, the strongest point on the other side is that modern media can damage reputations unfairly.
As the Arab Spring of 2011 showed, smartphones and social media can spread misinformation faster than corrections can follow, so a false accusation may harm a good person before the truth emerges.
Nevertheless, the existence of unfair attacks shows that heroes are vulnerable, not that they are impossible.
A hero's reputation may be [[assailed|assail]] for a time, yet careful reporting and the judgment of those who know the facts can restore it.
In Vietnam, doctors who faced false rumors online during the pandemic often regained public trust once their work became known.
This concession shapes my position: societies should be more [[discerning|discerning]] in choosing heroes, but they need not stop choosing them.
Heroism today may require more courage than before, since heroes must endure attention that earlier figures never faced.
In conclusion, I mostly disagree that media scrutiny has made living heroes impossible.

Societies still admire living people whose actions serve others, scrutiny often confirms merit rather than destroying it, and the risk of unfair attacks calls for careful judgment rather than a [[cynical|cynical]] refusal to admire anyone.
A hero who survives the bright light of modern media may, in fact, deserve the title more than any hero of the past.

essays.task_note: Body 1 explicitly refutes the claim and Body 2 explicitly tests the reason, showing that scrutiny can confirm merit, while Body 3 concedes the strongest opposing point about unfair media attacks.

essays.title: Grade competition narrows real learning

paragraphs.text: Students quickly learn that the grade, not the knowledge, is what gets rewarded.
This lesson lies behind the statement that competition for high grades seriously limits the quality of learning at all levels of education.
I largely agree with this statement, although competition can help when it rewards genuine mastery.

Grade competition encourages memorization over understanding, it discourages the curiosity and risk-taking that deep learning requires, and while it can motivate some students, its benefits depend on assessments that rarely exist in practice.
First, the statement holds true because competition for grades pushes students to memorize rather than understand.
In Vietnam, where exam culture is deeply [[ingrained|ingrained]], many students attend extra classes in the evenings to practice test questions.
When I taught young doctors, I often found that top scorers could recite treatment guidelines but struggled to explain why a treatment works or when it should not be used.
Such students are not lazy; they are responding rationally to a system that rewards correct answers rather than understanding.

Finland, by contrast, relies far less on standardized testing than many countries and requires its schoolteachers to hold a master's degree, showing that a school system need not revolve around exam scores.
These cases suggest that when grades become the goal, learning shrinks to whatever the test measures, and understanding becomes [[peripheral|peripheral]] to the real competition.
The competition, in effect, teaches students to perform for examiners rather than to think for themselves.
Second, grade competition discourages the curiosity and willingness to fail that real learning requires.
The Wright brothers achieved the first powered flight in 1903 only after years of careful experiments with gliders and a wind tunnel they built themselves, a process full of failed attempts.
A student competing for a perfect grade point average has every incentive to avoid such risky projects and choose the safest course.

A similar pressure appears in research: in 2015, a large collaboration reproduced the results of only about a third of 100 published psychology studies, a sign of how competition to publish striking findings can [[undermine|undermine]] quality.
Curiosity rarely survives when every question outside the syllabus seems like a waste of valuable study time.
When mistakes carry a heavy cost, students learn to [[eschew|eschew]] the experiments through which deep understanding grows.
A system that punishes failure, therefore, also punishes the very process by which people learn, and students begin to confuse a high grade with real mastery.
Admittedly, the statement does not hold in every case, since competition can motivate students to work harder.
A medical licensing exam, for instance, pushes future doctors to master essential knowledge on which patients depend.
Nevertheless, such competition improves learning only when the test truly measures understanding, and most grading systems fall short of that standard.
A multiple-choice test can reward a student who has memorized facts as highly as one who can use them.
In that case, the competition rewards memory, not skill, and the quality of learning suffers.
This consideration [[qualifies|qualify]] my position: competition itself is not harmful, but competition for grades that measure the wrong things seriously limits learning.
This limitation applies at every level, from primary school to professional training, wherever grades become the main goal.
In conclusion, I largely agree that the race for high grades damages the quality of learning across education.
It rewards memorization, discourages curiosity and risk, and offers real benefits only when assessments measure understanding, which they seldom do.
Schools that want better learning should therefore change what grades reward, not simply ask students to care less about them.

essays.title: Grade competition often raises standards

paragraphs.text: Few people run as fast alone as they do in a race.
Yet some argue that competition for high grades seriously limits the quality of learning at all levels of education.
I mostly disagree with this statement, because grade competition often raises effort and standards, although it can harm learning when grades are poorly designed or pressure becomes excessive.

Competition motivates students to master demanding material, it helps institutions select capable people for roles where competence matters, and its real harms appear only in particular settings rather than at all levels.
First, the statement does not hold in many settings, because competition for grades motivates students to work harder on difficult material.
In Vietnam, entrance to medical school is fiercely competitive, and students preparing for it master chemistry and biology to a level that few would reach without that pressure.
When I meet first-year medical students, their knowledge of basic science is often impressive, and it gives them a solid base for clinical training.
Competition did not limit their learning; it gave them a reason to reach a higher standard.
Similarly, a student who knows that only the best performers in a class will win a scholarship is likely to study far more [[assiduously|assiduous]] than one with nothing at stake.
In these cases, competition raises the quality of learning by turning vague intentions into concrete, daily effort.
Without a clear goal, many students would study far less and learn far less.
Second, grade competition serves a valuable purpose by identifying people who have truly mastered a field.
Finland requires schoolteachers to hold a master's degree and makes teaching a respected and selective profession, so only strong candidates who compete successfully for places become teachers.
Likewise, patients benefit when only medical graduates who have shown clinical [[acumen|acumen]] in [[exacting|exacting]] examinations are allowed to practice.
In Vietnam, too, competitive selection into residency programs helps ensure that young specialists have mastered their fields before treating patients.
At the higher levels of education, competition for grades therefore protects the public by ensuring that grades [[denote|denote]] real skill.

Without competition, grades would lose their meaning, and employers and patients would have no reliable signal of competence; at advanced levels, competition is the very mechanism that guarantees quality.
Admittedly, the statement holds true in some circumstances, especially for young children and for tests that reward memorization.
A primary school pupil who is ranked against classmates every week may learn to fear mistakes rather than enjoy discovery.
Similarly, students who compete on multiple-choice tests often memorize facts without understanding them.
Nevertheless, these problems come from poor assessment design and excessive pressure, not from competition itself.
A teacher who replaces weekly rankings with feedback, or a school that uses projects instead of multiple-choice tests, can keep motivation high without these harms.
This consideration shapes my position: competition should be reduced for young learners and paired with better tests, but it should not be blamed for limiting learning at all levels.
The statement's claim about all levels of education is therefore too broad to accept.
In conclusion, I mostly disagree that competition for high grades seriously limits the quality of learning throughout education.

Competition motivates students to master difficult material and helps identify those who are truly competent, while its genuine harms are confined to particular settings that can be [[ameliorated|ameliorate]].
The task for educators is not to abolish grade competition but to make sure that the grades worth competing for reward real understanding.

words.meaning_here: carefully, persistently and with hard work
the ability to make good judgments quickly

essays.title: Breadth makes specialists better

paragraphs.text: Many of the most important problems of our time do not fit neatly inside one academic department.
This is why the recommendation that universities should require every student to take a variety of courses outside the student's field of study deserves serious attention.
I largely agree with this recommendation, provided that the requirement is modest enough not to weaken training in the student's main field.

Adopting it would be advantageous when solutions depend on combining knowledge from several fields and when specialists must communicate with a wider public, though it would be less advantageous in programs that are already overloaded.
First, the recommendation is advantageous in settings where solutions require knowledge from several fields, because students exposed to other disciplines learn to connect ideas.
The Wolbachia method of dengue control illustrates this well.

Releasing mosquitoes that carry Wolbachia bacteria, which block dengue transmission, cut dengue cases by 77% in a randomized trial in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, and the method has also been tested in Vietnam.
This success required entomology, microbiology and epidemiology to work together.
Scientists trained in only one discipline might never have imagined using bacteria to stop a virus carried by mosquitoes.
Similarly, the Wright brothers drew on their experience as bicycle makers when they achieved the first powered airplane flight in 1903.
Such cases show that breadth is not a distraction from expertise; it is often the [[catalyst|catalyst]] for discoveries that no single field could produce.
A student who has taken courses in several fields is more likely to see such connections.
Second, the recommendation is advantageous because specialists must explain their work to people outside their field.
In my work as an epidemiologist in Vietnam, I have seen excellent analyses fail to influence policy because their authors could not explain them to officials without technical training.
Colleagues who had studied economics or communication, by contrast, could [[articulate|articulate]] the same findings in terms that decision makers understood.

Likewise, Vietnam's 2007 motorbike helmet law raised helmet use from low levels to over 90% within months, a result that depended not only on medical evidence but also on law, enforcement and public persuasion.
The law succeeded because people from different fields could understand one another's arguments.
Courses outside one's major therefore build an [[eclectic|eclectic]] set of skills that most careers now demand, rather than an [[insular|insular]] expertise.
Without such skills, even the best research may remain unread and unused.
Admittedly, the recommendation would not be advantageous in every program.

Consider a medical school that must already cover anatomy, pharmacology and years of clinical practice; adding several unrelated courses could crowd out essential training and lengthen an already [[arduous|arduous]] path.
Nevertheless, this circumstance argues for a smaller requirement, not for none at all.
Even a single course in ethics can change how a doctor practices, as the Tuskegee syphilis study, which withheld treatment from Black men without their informed consent, makes clear.
This exception shapes my position: universities should require breadth, but they should adjust its size to the demands of each field.
For most programs, a few well-chosen courses outside the major would bring large benefits at a modest cost.
In conclusion, I largely agree that universities should require students to take courses beyond their major.
Breadth helps students combine ideas from different fields and communicate with a wider audience, and the burden on crowded programs calls for a flexible requirement rather than its rejection.
A university that produces specialists who can think and speak beyond their field serves both its students and the society that depends on them.

essays.title: Let students choose depth over breadth

paragraphs.text: Time is the scarcest resource in any university education.
For this reason, I question the recommendation that universities should require every student to take a variety of courses outside the student's field of study.

I mostly disagree with this recommendation as a universal requirement, because in many circumstances it would cost students time and money without clear benefit, although breadth can be valuable when students choose it.

A mandatory breadth requirement would be disadvantageous in demanding professional programs and for students under financial pressure, but it could be advantageous where real problems demand collaboration across fields.
First, a breadth requirement would not be advantageous in demanding professional programs, because every extra course takes time from essential training.
Consider medical training in Vietnam, which is already long and packed with anatomy, pharmacology and clinical rotations.

When I teach young doctors, I find that many still lack confidence in [[rudimentary|rudimentary]] statistics, a core skill for reading research; requiring them to spend semesters on unrelated subjects would only widen such gaps.
Similarly, an engineering student forced to take literature and art history may simply memorize enough to pass, gaining little while losing time for core design skills.
Professional programs already include the related subjects their students need, such as ethics in medicine.
In such programs, a mandatory variety of courses is less an enrichment than an [[extraneous|extraneous]] burden.
Depth in one's own field, not a scattering of unrelated courses, is what patients and clients will depend on.
Second, the recommendation would be disadvantageous for students under financial pressure, because breadth requirements raise the cost of a degree.

For a student from a low-income family, each additional semester means more tuition and lost earnings, and required courses outside the major can delay graduation until the added cost becomes [[prohibitive|prohibitive]].
Such a student would reasonably regard a compulsory art history course as a luxury she cannot afford.
Moreover, required courses often produce reluctant students; anyone who has taught a mandatory class knows how quickly [[apathy|apathy]] can fill a room.
When breadth is forced rather than chosen, its benefits shrink while its costs remain, so the requirement fails the students it is meant to help.
A voluntary system would let motivated students explore widely while protecting those who cannot afford to.
Admittedly, there are circumstances in which courses outside one's field would be advantageous.

Releasing mosquitoes that carry Wolbachia bacteria, which block dengue transmission, cut dengue cases by 77% in a randomized trial in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, a success that depended on combining knowledge from several fields.
Nevertheless, such collaboration usually brings together deep specialists from different disciplines rather than individuals who took a few introductory courses outside their own.
Likewise, the Human Genome Project, a publicly funded international effort completed in 2003, succeeded by uniting many specialized teams.
In my own research, I rely on statisticians and entomologists rather than trying to master their fields myself.
This consideration shapes my position: universities should offer and encourage breadth, especially in the first year, but should not impose it on every student.
Breadth gained through teamwork later in a career can be more useful than breadth required during a crowded degree.
In conclusion, I mostly disagree that universities should require every student to take a variety of courses outside the major.
Such a requirement burdens demanding professional programs and financially stretched students, while the real benefits of breadth come mostly from collaboration among well-trained specialists.
A [[pragmatic|pragmatic]] university would make breadth an open door that students may choose to walk through, not a requirement that every student must pass.

so high that it prevents people from doing something

essays.task_note: Each body paragraph describes a circumstance (dense professional programs, students under financial pressure) in which a universal requirement would not be advantageous, and the concession describes where breadth would be, explaining how it shapes the position.

essays.title: Ask students, but keep experts in charge

paragraphs.text: Most people remember at least one class that felt pointless, and one reason is that no one ever asked them what they needed to learn.
This common experience lies behind the recommendation that educators should find out what students want included in the curriculum and then offer it to them.
I largely agree with this recommendation, as long as student wishes are treated as one important input rather than the final word.

Asking students is most advantageous for adult learners who know their own needs and for any class in which interest fuels effort, although it can backfire when essential but difficult subjects are at stake.
First, adopting the recommendation is clearly advantageous in settings where students are adults who understand the demands of their work.
In my work training district doctors in Vietnam, our early courses on antibiotic use followed a fixed textbook outline, and attendance was poor.

When we surveyed the doctors first, they asked for practical cases on treating common infections without laboratory tests, and once we offered those cases, attendance rose and the discussions became far livelier.
Similarly, a company that asks its engineers which software tools they need will spend its training budget more wisely than one that simply guesses.
This shows that when learners already know what their work requires, finding out what they want is not a surrender to taste but a [[pragmatic|pragmatic]] route to useful knowledge.
In such settings, the learners' own requests are the best available map of the gaps that a course should fill.
Second, offering students what they want is advantageous because interest is a powerful engine of effort, even among younger learners.
Consider a secondary school whose students find biology dull until a teacher asks them which health problems worry them most.

When the class chooses to study dengue, which affects many of their families each rainy season, the students survey standing water in their own neighborhoods and learn the mosquito's life cycle with real [[zeal|zeal]].
Likewise, a university statistics course that lets students analyze data from their own majors will usually hold their attention better than one that recycles the same textbook examples every year.
This shows that student preferences, when taken seriously, can [[kindle|kindle]] the motivation without which even the best-designed curriculum fails.
A teacher who ignores those preferences may cover every required topic and still leave most students unchanged.
Admittedly, adopting the recommendation would not be advantageous where students do not yet know what they will need.
Many young students, if asked, would gladly drop algebra or grammar, yet these subjects are the foundation for nearly every later course and career.
They are not foolish; they simply cannot yet see where those subjects lead.
Nevertheless, this risk argues for limits on student choice, not for ignoring students altogether.
A school can keep core subjects compulsory while asking students which topics, projects or examples should be used to teach them, and which electives should be added.
In this way, educators remain the [[arbiters|arbiter]] of what is essential, while students help decide how it is taught, so this circumstance qualifies my agreement rather than reversing it.
In conclusion, educators should listen to what students want and act on it, but they should not hand over the curriculum entirely.
Student input is most advantageous for adult learners with clear goals and for classes in which interest drives effort, whereas it needs firm limits when essential skills are involved.
The best curriculum, therefore, is built with students rather than simply for them or by them.

words.meaning_here: practical and focused on real results
to stir up or arouse a feeling
those with the final authority to decide

essays.task_note: Each body paragraph is framed as a specific circumstance (adult learners, motivation-driven classes, core skills) where adopting the recommendation would or would not be advantageous, and the concession explains how the third circumstance limits the position.

essays.title: Curricula should follow needs, not wants

paragraphs.text: Children, if given the choice, would happily eat dessert before every meal.
A similar worry arises from the recommendation that educators should find out what students want included in the curriculum and then offer it to them.
I mostly disagree with this recommendation, because students' wishes are an unreliable guide to what they actually need, although their input is valuable in limited ways.
Adopting it would be disadvantageous when essential but unpopular subjects are at stake and when popular demand chases passing trends, though it can help in elective and adult courses.
First, adopting the recommendation would be harmful in any setting where the most important subjects are also the least popular.
In Vietnamese medical schools, for instance, many students would happily drop biostatistics and research methods, which seem dry next to clinical work.
Yet in my career as an epidemiologist, those were exactly the skills that allowed me to judge whether a new treatment truly worked or whether a published result was merely a [[fluke|fluke]].

Similarly, when a large collaboration in 2015 tried to repeat 100 published psychology studies and reproduced only about a third of them, it reminded everyone how much training in sound methods matters.
This shows that students often cannot see the value of a subject until long after they have studied it, so asking them in advance produces a [[myopic|myopic]] curriculum.
A survey of first-year students, in other words, measures their present comfort rather than their future needs.
Second, a curriculum built on student demand would chase fashions that may prove [[ephemeral|ephemeral]].
Consider a university that, responding to a survey, replaces its introductory economics course with a class on building a social media following.
Within a few years the platforms students loved may have changed or disappeared, while the principles of supply, demand and incentives remain as useful as ever.
Likewise, Kodak, protecting its profitable film business, was slow to embrace the digital camera its own engineer had invented in 1975 and filed for bankruptcy in 2012.

Just as a company that clings to today's demand can miss tomorrow's needs, a school that teaches only what is popular can leave graduates unprepared, which is why educators who can see further ahead should decide.
Students may resent such decisions at first, but most later value the durable skills they were required to learn.
Admittedly, ignoring students entirely would also be a mistake, especially in elective courses and adult education.
A course for working nurses on diabetes care, for example, will be far more useful if the teachers first ask which problems the nurses face on their wards.
Adults with years of practice know their own gaps, and a course that ignores them wastes valuable time.
Nevertheless, such cases involve learners who already have a strong foundation and clear professional goals.
Even for younger students, letting the class choose the novels for one unit can stir interest in reading without removing literature from the program.
In other words, students can [[inform|inform]] the curriculum without controlling it, which limits but does not overturn my position.
Their wishes deserve a voice, but the final decision belongs to those who can see the whole curriculum.
In conclusion, educators should not simply offer students whatever they ask for, even though student views deserve a hearing.
Unpopular subjects are often the most essential, popular demand tends to follow short-lived trends, and student input works best within a structure that experts design.
Educators should therefore consult their students but [[maintain|maintain]] responsibility for what every graduate must know.

words.meaning_here: a result produced by chance rather than a real effect
shortsighted; unable to see long-term needs
to shape or give character to
to keep or continue to hold

essays.task_note: The essay describes circumstances where adopting the recommendation would be disadvantageous (unpopular essential subjects, passing trends) and one where it would be advantageous (adult and elective courses), and explains how each shapes the position.

essays.title: Concepts first make facts meaningful

paragraphs.text: A list of dates or drug names is easy to forget, but a story that connects them can last a lifetime.
This difference underlies the recommendation that educators should teach facts only after their students have studied the ideas, trends and concepts that help explain those facts.
I largely agree with this recommendation, particularly in subjects where facts are numerous and change over time, although beginners need some basic facts first.

Teaching concepts first is advantageous because it helps students organize and remember facts and because it prepares them for new facts, even though complete beginners need a few facts before any concept makes sense.
First, adopting the recommendation is advantageous in fact-heavy subjects because a concept gives students a framework on which to hang details.
When I studied pharmacology, memorizing dozens of antibiotics one by one was [[arduous|arduous]] and largely [[futile|futile]], since I forgot most names within weeks.
Once a teacher [[elucidated|elucidate]] how bacteria build their cell walls and how each drug class attacks a different step, the same facts became easy to recall because each one had a place.

Similarly, a student who first understands the idea of market incentives can make sense of why Vietnam's Doi Moi reforms of 1986 turned a country with food shortages into one of the world's largest rice exporters.
This shows that concepts turn scattered facts into a connected system, which is exactly why teaching ideas first is more efficient.
Without the concept, each new fact is one more item to memorize; with it, each fact confirms and enriches an idea.
Second, studying concepts first is advantageous because it prepares students for facts that do not yet exist.
Antibiotic resistance is a clear case: drugs that once cured infections now often fail, so a list of effective drugs memorized by a medical student today may be [[obsolete|obsolete]] within a decade.
A physician who understands natural selection, however, can predict that overuse will breed resistance, just as Alexander Fleming warned in his 1945 Nobel lecture.
Likewise, a programmer who grasps general principles of logic can learn any new language, while one who has memorized commands for a single tool is lost when it changes.
This shows that concepts, unlike isolated facts, transfer to new situations, and preparing students for new situations is the real goal of education.
Facts learned in school will age, but a sound concept keeps paying returns long after graduation.
Admittedly, the recommendation would not be advantageous for complete beginners, who need some facts before ideas mean anything.
A child cannot grasp the concept of a food chain without first knowing that rabbits eat grass and foxes eat rabbits, and a medical student cannot understand disease before learning basic anatomy.
Nevertheless, this objection argues for a short foundation of facts, not for teaching facts in isolation for years.
Good teachers introduce a few key facts, use them to build a concept, and then present the remaining details within that framework.
Thus the word "only" in the recommendation is too strict, but its [[gist|gist]], that ideas should guide the learning of facts, remains sound.
In conclusion, educators are generally wise to teach the ideas and trends that explain facts before asking students to master the facts themselves.
Concepts make facts easier to remember and prepare students for facts that will change, although beginners need a small base of facts to start.
The best sequence, therefore, is a few facts, then the concept, and then the rest of the facts in light of it.

words.meaning_here: requiring great effort; hard and tiring
out of date and no longer useful
the main point or essential meaning

essays.task_note: The essay presents circumstances where teaching concepts first is advantageous (fact-heavy and fast-changing fields) and one where it is not (complete beginners), and explains that this last case softens the word "only" without overturning the recommendation.

essays.title: Facts should come before concepts

paragraphs.text: No one can admire the shape of a building before its bricks are laid.
Yet the recommendation that educators should teach facts only after students have studied the ideas, trends and concepts that explain them asks students to do something similar.
I mostly disagree with this recommendation, because in most subjects facts are the raw material from which concepts are built, although concepts can guide learning once a foundation exists.
Teaching facts first is advantageous for beginners and essential for testing ideas against evidence, while a concepts-first approach helps mainly advanced students.
First, insisting on concepts before facts would be disadvantageous for beginners, who have nothing to attach an abstract idea to.
Consider a first-year nursing class asked to study the concept of herd immunity before learning what a vaccine is, how infection spreads, or what smallpox was.

The idea would remain [[opaque|opaque]], but students who first learn that smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980 after a global vaccination campaign can then see why protecting enough people protects everyone.
Similarly, children learn multiplication tables before they study functions, and language learners memorize words before they analyze grammar.
In each case, the abstract idea makes sense only because concrete examples have already been stored in memory.
This shows that for novices, facts are not the end of learning but its starting point, so delaying them makes concepts harder, not easier, to grasp.
Teachers who reverse this order often find that students can repeat a definition without being able to apply it.
Second, teaching concepts first risks producing students who accept ideas without checking them against evidence.
Ignaz Semmelweis offers a warning: in 1847 he had doctors in Vienna wash their hands in chlorinated lime, and deaths from childbed fever on his ward fell sharply.
Yet most of his colleagues rejected his idea, and the [[empirical|empirical]] results in front of them were [[dismissed|dismiss]] because they did not fit what they already believed.
Likewise, a student taught a neat theory of economic trends may ignore data that [[contravene|contravene]] it rather than question the theory.
This shows that students who learn facts first are more likely to treat concepts as hypotheses to be tested, which is the habit of mind good education should build.
Concepts should earn their place by explaining facts, not by excusing students from looking at them.
Admittedly, for advanced students, concepts can make the learning of facts far more efficient.
A resident who already understands how bacteria develop resistance can absorb the details of a new antibiotic quickly, because the concept tells her what to look for.
For her, a lecture that opens with the general mechanism is far more efficient than a list of drug names.
Nevertheless, such students acquired their concepts by first learning many facts in earlier years.
Her framework rests on years of memorized anatomy, microbiology and pharmacology, without which the concept of resistance would mean little.
Thus the recommendation may suit the final stage of education, but as a general rule it reverses the natural order in which understanding [[burgeons|burgeon]].
Before that stage, facts should lead and concepts should follow.
In conclusion, educators should not wait to teach facts until students have studied the concepts that explain them.
Facts give beginners something concrete to build on and keep students honest when theories conflict with evidence, even if concepts later speed up learning for advanced students.
The wiser approach is to move back and forth, letting facts suggest concepts and concepts organize facts.

essays.task_note: The essay describes circumstances where the recommendation would be disadvantageous (beginners, testing ideas against evidence) and one where it would be advantageous (advanced students), and explains why that exception does not change the general position.

essays.title: Shared views make learning easier at first

paragraphs.text: Most of us learn our first lessons from parents, teachers and friends who see the world much as we do.

This familiar pattern supports the claim that we can usually learn much more from people whose views we share than from those whose views contradict our own, a claim based on the reason that disagreement can cause stress and inhibit learning.
I partly agree with both the claim and the reason, especially for beginners and for learning practical skills, although disagreement remains valuable at later stages.
Shared assumptions let people build knowledge efficiently, and hostile conflict often does block learning, even though some of the most important lessons come from critics.
First, the claim holds in many settings because people who share a basic framework can build on each other's ideas instead of arguing over first principles.
The Human Genome Project, completed in 2003, was a publicly funded international effort in which researchers shared a common goal and could therefore divide the work and combine their results.
Because they agreed on what mattered, each team could build on the others' findings, and the project made the human DNA sequence freely available to all researchers.
Similarly, a junior doctor learns surgery fastest from a mentor who shares her basic approach to patient safety, since every lesson adds to what she already accepts.
If her mentor instead challenged every basic assumption, she would spend her energy defending herself rather than learning to operate.
This shows that agreement on fundamentals often [[facilitates|facilitate]] learning, which supports the claim in many practical situations.
Time that would be spent defending basic assumptions can instead be spent learning new material.
Second, the reason offered for the claim is largely true: disagreement, especially when it is hostile, can create stress that inhibits learning.

In my experience teaching epidemiology, students who were [[berated|berate]] by a [[caustic|caustic]] supervisor for questioning a study design stopped asking questions altogether, and their progress slowed.
When the same students joined a supportive group with similar views, they made [[candid|candid]] comments about their doubts and learned more.
Likewise, online arguments about vaccines often turn into insults, and few participants come away better informed.
In such exchanges, people defend their pride rather than examine the evidence.
This shows that the reason has real force, though it applies mainly to disagreement delivered with hostility rather than to disagreement itself.
A frightened learner, after all, cannot think clearly, however valuable the criticism may be in principle.
Admittedly, the strongest objection to the claim is that many crucial lessons come only from people who contradict us.
Abraham Lincoln appointed political rivals such as William Seward to his cabinet, choosing able critics over loyal followers.
Their objections forced him to test his plans against the strongest arguments available.
Nevertheless, Lincoln could learn from his rivals because he already had a firm foundation and the confidence to handle conflict.
A first-year student facing constant contradiction, by contrast, may feel lost rather than enlightened and may stop trying.
Thus disagreement is most useful for experienced learners, which [[qualifies|qualify]] rather than overturns my partial agreement with the claim and its reason.
Beginners first need a secure base, which shared views provide; later, they can turn to critics.
In conclusion, I accept the claim and its reason in part, since people who share our views often help us learn more efficiently and hostile disagreement can hinder learning.
Shared frameworks speed cooperation, stress can inhibit learning, and yet critics remain essential once learners are secure.
The practical lesson is to learn the basics among allies and then seek out thoughtful critics.

essays.task_note: Body 1 evaluates the claim, Body 2 evaluates the reason, and Body 3 concedes the strongest point for the other side (learning from rivals), naming "the claim" and "the reason" explicitly.

essays.title: Disagreement teaches more than agreement

paragraphs.text: An echo can repeat our words, but it can never teach us anything new.

That is the weakness of the claim that we can usually learn much more from people whose views we share than from those who contradict us, a claim based on the reason that disagreement can cause stress and inhibit learning.
I largely disagree with both the claim and the reason, because disagreement is often the main source of new knowledge, and the stress it causes is usually manageable and even useful.
Contrary views expose our errors, moderate stress can sharpen learning, and only hostile conflict truly inhibits it.
First, the claim is mistaken because people who share our views mostly confirm what we already believe, whereas critics reveal our errors.

When Ignaz Semmelweis had doctors in Vienna wash their hands in chlorinated lime in 1847, deaths from childbed fever on his ward fell sharply, yet colleagues who shared the same assumptions rejected his idea.
Medicine learned the lesson only when germ theory, which contradicted their beliefs, vindicated him years after his death.
Similarly, the 2015 effort that reproduced only about a third of 100 published psychology studies came from researchers willing to question findings their own field accepted.

This shows that groups of like-minded people easily grow [[complacent|complacent]], and that progress often depends on hearing the views we least want to hear, which [[undermines|undermine]] the claim.
A community that hears only agreement has no way to discover what it has gotten wrong.
Second, the reason is only partly true, and even where it is true, it does not support the claim.

Disagreement can certainly cause stress, but moderate stress often focuses attention; a young doctor who must defend her diagnosis to a [[skeptic|skeptic]] on the ward examines the evidence more carefully than one whose colleagues simply nod.
In my own research, the reviewer comments that stung most also improved my papers most.
Likewise, Abraham Lincoln chose able critics such as William Seward for his cabinet rather than loyal followers.
He accepted friction within his own government as the price of hearing objections that loyal followers would never raise.
This shows that the discomfort of disagreement is often a sign that learning is happening, not that it is being blocked.
Stress, in other words, is not always the enemy of learning; often it is the feeling of an old belief being tested.
Admittedly, the most compelling support for the reason is that hostile, personal disagreement can make people defensive and stop them from learning at all.
On social media, where misinformation spreads faster than corrections can follow, angry debates often [[polarize|polarize]] users rather than inform them.
In these settings, users often leave an argument more certain of their original views than before.
Nevertheless, the problem in such cases is the manner of the disagreement, not the fact of it.
When critics argue respectfully, as in a well-run journal club where colleagues test each other's interpretations, contrary views teach far more than polite agreement.
Thus the stress the reason describes calls for better ways of disagreeing rather than for retreating to people who think as we do.
Even if hostile disagreement inhibits learning, the claim does not follow, because respectful disagreement remains the richest source of new ideas.
In conclusion, we usually learn more from people who challenge our views than from those who share them.
Critics reveal errors that allies miss, moderate stress sharpens rather than blocks thinking, and the harm of hostile conflict can be reduced by civility.
The wise learner, therefore, seeks out disagreement instead of avoiding it.

essays.title: Officials should judge, not simply obey

paragraphs.text: A doctor who prescribed whatever patients demanded would soon do more harm than good.
A similar logic applies to the recommendation that government officials should rely on their own judgment rather than unquestioningly carry out the will of the people they serve.
I largely agree with this recommendation, especially when officials have expert knowledge that the public lacks, provided that they explain their decisions and remain accountable.
Independent judgment is advantageous when experts understand hidden risks and when a majority would harm a minority, but it becomes dangerous when officials stop listening to citizens.
First, relying on judgment is advantageous in situations where experts understand risks that the public cannot easily see.
Around 1960, thalidomide, a sedative given to pregnant women, caused severe birth defects in thousands of babies in Europe.
Frances Kelsey of the US FDA refused to approve it, and the United States then passed stricter drug-testing rules in 1962.
Had she treated approval as a formality, many American families might have suffered the same tragedy.
Similarly, Vietnam's 2007 law requiring motorbike helmets was not welcomed by every rider, yet it raised helmet use from low levels to over 90% within months and reduced head injuries and deaths.
This shows that blind [[deference|deference]] to public demand can cost lives, while officials who use informed judgment can save them.
In such circumstances, the public interest is served precisely when officials refuse to treat popularity as proof of safety.
Second, independent judgment is advantageous when the majority's will would harm a minority.
In Montgomery in the 1950s, segregated buses reflected the wishes of the local majority, and Black residents had to refuse for over a year to ride them before bus segregation ended in that city.
An official who unquestioningly carried out the majority's will would simply have defended that [[iniquity|iniquity]].
Likewise, a health official in a town where most residents oppose a clinic for HIV patients should still open it, because those patients have an equal right to care.
Fear of a disease does not give neighbors the right to deny care to patients.
This shows that the will of the people is not always the will of all the people, and judgment is needed to protect those who are outvoted.
Majorities can be wrong about the rights of others, and officials swear to serve everyone, not merely the largest group.
Admittedly, adopting the recommendation would not be advantageous when officials [[arrogate|arrogate]] to themselves decisions that belong to citizens.
A mayor who builds an expensive highway through a neighborhood whose residents wanted a park may claim superior wisdom while simply serving powerful interests.
Residents would rightly see such a decision as arrogance rather than leadership.
Nevertheless, the remedy for such abuse is accountability, not obedience.
Elections, a free press and public explanation of decisions allow citizens to check officials without dictating every choice.
An official who must defend each major decision in public is far less likely to confuse personal interest with sound judgment.
Thus the danger of arrogant officials qualifies my position: judgment should be independent but never [[covert|covert]], so that citizens can see and challenge the reasons behind it.
In conclusion, government officials should generally rely on their own judgment rather than simply follow public demands.
Expert judgment prevents harm when risks are hidden and protects minorities from the majority, although it must stay open to scrutiny so that it does not become arrogance.
The best officials, therefore, listen carefully to the people but decide according to evidence and principle.

to take or claim something without the right to it

essays.task_note: Each body paragraph presents a specific circumstance (expert risk assessment, protecting minorities) where relying on judgment is advantageous, and Body 3 presents one where it is not (arrogant officials), explaining how it adds a condition of accountability.

essays.title: Officials should usually follow the people

paragraphs.text: In a democracy, power is lent to officials, not given to them.
That principle is challenged by the recommendation that government officials should rely on their own judgment rather than unquestioningly carry out the will of the people they serve.

I mostly disagree with this recommendation, because officials who override the public too readily make costly mistakes and lose trust, although expert judgment is needed when lives are clearly at stake.

Following the people's will is advantageous because citizens often know local conditions better and because policies they support are more likely to succeed, even if officials must occasionally lead against opinion.
First, carrying out the people's will is advantageous in settings where citizens understand local needs better than distant officials.
Before 1986, Vietnam relied on central planning, in which officials rather than farmers decided how the economy should work, and the country faced food shortages.

The Doi Moi reforms replaced central planning with market incentives that let people act on their own choices, and Vietnam became one of the world's largest rice exporters as poverty fell dramatically.
Similarly, in dengue control I have seen campaigns designed without community input fail because they ignored how residents actually store water.
Residents knew which containers mattered and which did not, and plans that respected that knowledge worked far better.
This shows that the people's will often carries knowledge that officials lack, so overriding it is rarely as [[sagacious|sagacious]] as it appears.
Officials who claim superior judgment often have less information about daily life, not more.
Second, following the public's will is advantageous because policies that people support are far easier to carry out.
Releasing mosquitoes carrying Wolbachia bacteria cut dengue cases by 77% in a randomized trial in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, but such releases take place in people's own neighborhoods.
Officials who imposed them on unwilling communities would invite resistance that could [[stymie|stymie]] even a proven intervention.
Community acceptance, rather than official judgment alone, is what allows a sound intervention to reach the people it is meant to protect.
Likewise, the Tuskegee syphilis study withheld treatment from Black men without their informed consent, and the public outrage forced new rules requiring ethics review boards for research on people.

This shows that officials who ignore the people they serve risk losing the trust on which every public program depends, whereas those who [[accede|accede]] to reasonable public wishes gain cooperation.
A policy that is correct on paper but rejected in practice protects no one.
Admittedly, there are cases, especially when lives are at stake, in which officials must act against popular opinion.
Vietnam's 2007 helmet law was not universally welcomed by riders, yet it raised helmet use to over 90% within months and reduced head injuries and deaths.
Nevertheless, such cases are exceptions that require strong evidence, and an official who claims special knowledge should be able to show it publicly.
Without that requirement, any leader could describe an unpopular personal preference as expert judgment.
History offers many leaders who justified unpopular and harmful policies by claiming to know better than the people.
Thus independent judgment should be a rare, [[circumscribed|circumscribe]] power rather than the normal way of governing.
Even then, officials should explain their reasons openly and remain answerable to the public for the results.
In conclusion, officials should usually carry out the will of the people they serve rather than substitute their own judgment.
Citizens often understand local conditions better, and policies with public support are far more likely to succeed, even though rare cases of clear danger justify leading against opinion.
Officials should therefore treat overriding the public as an exception to be justified, never as a habit.

essays.title: Long-term goals outlast quick fame

paragraphs.text: Social media has made it possible to become famous overnight and to be forgotten just as quickly.
In this climate, the recommendation that young people should be encouraged to pursue long-term, realistic goals rather than seek immediate fame and recognition is more relevant than ever.
I largely agree with this recommendation, as long as it is not taken to mean that young people should reject every form of early recognition.
Long-term goals are advantageous because lasting achievement requires sustained effort and because fame-seeking distorts choices, although some young people benefit from early recognition.
First, encouraging long-term goals is advantageous because most valuable achievements require years of patient work.

Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman spent decades on basic research on mRNA that attracted little notice, yet that work allowed COVID-19 vaccines to be developed in under a year and earned them the 2023 Nobel Prize.
Had they chased quick recognition, they would likely have abandoned such an unfashionable field long before it paid off.
Similarly, the Wright brothers spent years on careful experiments with gliders and a wind tunnel they built themselves before their first powered flight in 1903.
They were bicycle makers without college degrees, and no one was applauding their slow, repetitive work.
This shows that [[assiduous|assiduous]] effort toward a distant goal, not a hunt for applause, produces work of lasting value.
Recognition, when it came, was the result of their patience rather than its goal.
Second, the recommendation is advantageous because the pursuit of immediate fame tends to distort young people's choices.
Consider a talented student who could become a public health researcher but instead spends her late teens chasing followers with ever more [[lurid|lurid]] videos.
When the attention fades, as it usually does, she may find herself without skills, qualifications or a clear path.
Her peers who spent those years studying, meanwhile, will have built careers that do not depend on the next viral post.

Likewise, a junior scientist eager for headlines may rush out a striking but weak study, and the 2015 effort that reproduced only about a third of 100 psychology studies shows how often single findings mislead.
This shows that fame is [[ephemeral|ephemeral]] and that chasing it can [[undermine|undermine]] the very work that would bring lasting respect.
A realistic, long-term goal, by contrast, gives young people a reason to build skills that remain valuable after the spotlight moves on.
Admittedly, there are circumstances in which early recognition is advantageous, especially in fields such as music or sports where careers begin early.
A teenage athlete who wins a national title may gain sponsors and coaching that would otherwise be out of reach.
For such a young person, refusing all recognition in the name of long-term goals would mean losing real opportunities.
Nevertheless, such recognition is valuable only when it serves a longer goal rather than replacing it.
The athlete who treats a first title as one step in a long career is likely to last far longer than one who treats it as the [[zenith|zenith]] of success.
This exception therefore refines rather than overturns my position, since recognition is welcome as a by-product of long-term goals but not as a goal in itself.
Even the most talented athletes need a plan for the years after their competitive careers end.
In conclusion, young people should be encouraged to pursue long-term goals rather than immediate fame.
Lasting achievements require years of work, and fame-seeking distorts choices, although early recognition can help when it serves a longer plan.
The best advice, then, is to aim high, plan realistically, work patiently and let recognition follow.

shocking and sensational in order to attract attention

essays.title: Bold goals and recognition deserve encouragement

paragraphs.text: Many of the people we now admire were once told that their goals were unrealistic.
That history should make us cautious about the recommendation that young people should be encouraged to pursue long-term, realistic goals rather than seek immediate fame and recognition.

I partly disagree with this recommendation, because its emphasis on "realistic" goals can discourage bold ambition and because early recognition often helps young people succeed, although fame for its own sake is a poor goal.
Seemingly unrealistic dreams have driven major achievements, early recognition can open doors, and only empty fame-seeking deserves discouragement.
First, encouraging only realistic goals would be disadvantageous for young people with unusual talents or ambitions.
The Wright brothers were bicycle makers without college degrees, and powered flight must have seemed an unrealistic goal for such men.
Yet after years of careful experiments with gliders and a wind tunnel they built themselves, they achieved the first powered airplane flight in 1903.
Similarly, Marie Curie won Nobel Prizes in both physics and chemistry despite the barriers women faced in science at the time, barriers that made her ambitions look far from realistic.
Had the Wright brothers or Curie been encouraged only toward realistic goals, they might have chosen safer, more ordinary careers.
This shows that advice to be "realistic" can [[squelch|squelch]] exactly the ambition that produces breakthroughs.
For a gifted young person, the most realistic goal is sometimes the one that seems unrealistic to everyone else.
Second, seeking early recognition is advantageous in circumstances where visibility creates opportunity.
Consider a young Vietnamese researcher who presents her dengue study at an international conference while still a student.
The recognition she gains may bring a scholarship, a mentor and funding that a quieter path would take a decade to produce.
Without such early visibility, talented students from modest backgrounds may never be noticed by the people who could help them.
By contrast, Vincent van Gogh sold very few paintings during his lifetime, and his [[posthumous|posthumous]] fame, though enormous, could not support the artist while he lived.
This shows that recognition is not merely vanity, since it is often the [[catalyst|catalyst]] that turns talent into a sustainable career.
Encouraging young people to avoid it entirely would remove one of the main ladders by which talent rises.
Admittedly, the recommendation is right that fame pursued for its own sake is a poor goal.
Young people who chase online popularity with [[meretricious|meretricious]] stunts often gain attention that vanishes within weeks and leaves them with nothing of value.
The recommendation is a useful warning against this kind of empty attention.
Nevertheless, the remedy is to encourage meaningful recognition, not to discourage recognition altogether.
A student who hopes to win a science fair or publish an article is seeking recognition, yet this is a healthy motive that rewards real work.
Such recognition often encourages further effort and attracts the support needed for long-term success.
Thus the recommendation rests on a false [[dichotomy|dichotomy]] between long-term goals and recognition, since the best kind of recognition usually marks progress toward a long-term goal.
Young people should be taught to distinguish fame that rewards real work from fame that replaces it.
In conclusion, I only partly accept the advice that young people should pursue realistic long-term goals instead of immediate recognition.
Bold, seemingly unrealistic goals have produced great achievements, and early recognition often opens doors, even though empty fame is worth little.
Young people should therefore be encouraged to dream boldly and to seek recognition for real accomplishments.

attractive on the surface but without real value
a division into two sharply opposed parts
