essays.title: Praise teaches better than scolding

paragraphs.text: Anyone who has trained a puppy knows that a reward often works better than a scolding.
Teachers face a similar choice, which is why some recommend that the best way to teach is to praise positive actions and ignore negative ones.
I largely agree with this recommendation for minor misbehavior and for young or anxious learners, though serious or dangerous errors cannot be ignored.
Praise builds the confidence and motivation that learners need, and ignoring minor faults denies them the attention they seek, but harmful mistakes require correction.
First, praising positive actions is advantageous because it builds confidence, especially in learners who fear failure.
When I supervised junior health workers collecting dengue data in rural Vietnam, those who were praised for careful records soon became the most [[meticulous|meticulous]] members of the team.
Those who were mainly criticized grew [[timorous|timorous]], hid their errors and asked fewer questions.
Because they feared blame, they also reported problems later, which made the data harder to correct.
Similarly, a primary school teacher who praises a shy child for one correct answer often sees the child raise a hand again the next day.
One small success, noticed and praised, gives the child a reason to risk another attempt.
This shows that praise does more than reward, since it tells learners what to repeat and gives them the courage to try.
Criticism, by contrast, tells learners only what to avoid, and fearful learners often respond by avoiding effort altogether.
Second, ignoring minor negative actions is advantageous in classrooms where misbehavior is a bid for attention.
Consider a student who makes jokes during a lesson to draw a reaction from his classmates.
If the teacher scolds him, he gains the attention he wanted, but if the teacher ignores the jokes and praises him when he contributes seriously, the behavior often [[subsides|subside]].
Likewise, parents who respond calmly to a toddler's tantrum, rather than with anger, often find that the tantrums become less frequent.
The behavior loses its purpose once it no longer produces the reaction it was meant to provoke.
This shows that attention itself is a reward, so ignoring trivial faults can teach as effectively as punishment and without its side effects.
Constant scolding, moreover, can damage the relationship between teacher and student that makes other learning possible.
Admittedly, ignoring negative actions would be harmful when an error is serious or dangerous.
A surgical trainee who fails to wash her hands cannot simply be ignored, because Semmelweis showed in 1847 that hand-washing sharply reduced deaths from childbed fever.
A teacher who stayed silent in that situation would be failing both the trainee and her future patients.
Nevertheless, such cases call for clear correction, not for abandoning praise as the main method of teaching.
Even in an operating room, a supervisor can correct a lapse firmly and then praise the trainee when she follows the right procedure.
In this way, the trainee learns the rule without losing the confidence she needs to keep improving.
Thus the recommendation should be [[qualified|qualify]] so that teachers ignore minor faults, correct dangerous ones, and praise generously throughout.
Praise should remain the main tool, while correction is reserved for the errors that truly matter.
In conclusion, praising good actions and ignoring minor bad ones is usually the best way to teach.
Praise builds confidence and shows learners what to repeat, and ignoring attention-seeking behavior removes its reward, although serious errors must be corrected.
A good teacher, therefore, is generous with praise and [[judicious|judicious]] about criticism.

words.meaning_here: limited or modified to be more accurate

essays.task_note: The essay gives circumstances where praising good actions and ignoring bad ones is advantageous (anxious learners, attention-seeking behavior) and one where it is not (dangerous errors), and explains how that case qualifies the recommendation.

essays.title: Ignoring mistakes leaves learners uninformed

paragraphs.text: A map that showed only the right roads, but never the dead ends, would still leave travelers lost.
This is the problem with the recommendation that the best way to teach is to praise positive actions and ignore negative ones.
I mostly disagree with this recommendation, because learners need to know what they are doing wrong, although praise should remain a central part of teaching.
Ignoring errors leaves them uncorrected, praise alone can produce [[complacent|complacent]] learners, and only for trivial misbehavior is silence the wise response.
First, ignoring negative actions would be disadvantageous in any field where mistakes have serious consequences for other people.
Antibiotic resistance offers a clear case, since overuse and over-the-counter sales of antibiotics, common in many countries including Vietnam, help resistant bacteria spread.
As a result, drugs that once cured infections now often fail.
A medical teacher who praised students' correct prescriptions but ignored their unnecessary ones would be helping to create this problem.
Similarly, a driving instructor who ignored a student's failure to check mirrors would be [[abetting|abet]] a future accident.
The student would leave the course confident but dangerous, because no one had ever named the habit that needed to change.
This shows that silence about errors is not neutral, because it lets [[pernicious|pernicious]] habits take root.
Learners cannot fix a mistake that they do not know they are making.
Second, praise without correction is disadvantageous because it can make learners overconfident and unprepared for honest criticism.

In my experience reviewing manuscripts by young researchers, those who had received only encouragement from their supervisors often submitted papers with basic statistical errors and were shocked by reviewers' criticism.
Students who had been given [[candid|candid]] feedback earlier handled peer review far better.
They had learned early that criticism was a normal part of improvement rather than a personal attack.

Likewise, the 2015 finding that only about a third of 100 published psychology studies could be reproduced suggests that a field which rewards striking results without examining weaknesses can mislead itself.
Praise for exciting results is useful only when it is balanced by careful attention to what may be wrong.
This shows that criticism, delivered well, is a form of respect, since it assumes the learner can improve.
Withholding it, however kindly meant, leaves learners to discover their weaknesses later, when the cost is higher.
Admittedly, ignoring negative actions is sensible for minor misbehavior meant to attract attention.
A child who makes noise to provoke the teacher may stop sooner if the noise draws no reaction and quiet work earns praise.
In this narrow case, attention is the reward, and withholding it can change behavior.
Nevertheless, this strategy works only for trivial, attention-seeking behavior, not for errors of understanding or safety.
A student who misunderstands how vaccines work will not correct the error simply because it is ignored; she needs to be shown her mistake patiently rather than [[admonished|admonish]].
Thus the recommendation describes one useful classroom tactic, but it cannot be the best general way to teach.
Praise should remain central, but it must be paired with clear, specific correction whenever an error affects understanding or safety.
In conclusion, praising positive actions while ignoring negative ones is not the best way to teach, even though praise itself is valuable.
Ignored errors persist, praise alone breeds complacency, and only trivial, attention-seeking misbehavior is best met with silence.
The best teachers, therefore, combine generous praise with clear and respectful correction.

words.meaning_here: overly satisfied and unaware of one's weaknesses
harmful in a gradual or hidden way

essays.task_note: The essay describes circumstances where the recommendation would be disadvantageous (consequential errors, praise-only training) and one where it would be advantageous (attention-seeking misbehavior), and explains why that case does not make it the best general method.

essays.title: Worthy goals can justify costly means

paragraphs.text: Few great achievements have come without someone paying a price.
This fact gives some force to the statement that if a goal is worthy, then any means taken to attain it are justifiable.
I agree with this statement to a considerable extent, since worthy goals often justify difficult, unpopular or costly means, although the word "any" goes too far when the means destroy basic rights.

The statement holds when public health measures restrict freedom or demand sacrifice to save lives and when disruptive action ends injustice or hardship, but it fails when the means violate human dignity.
First, the statement holds in public health, where the goal of saving lives justifies measures that limit freedom or demand sacrifice.
Vietnam's 2007 law requiring motorbike helmets restricted riders' choices, yet it raised helmet use from low levels to over 90% within months and reduced head injuries and deaths.
Few people today would call that restriction unjustified, because the goal was so clearly worthy.

Similarly, the coordinated global WHO vaccination campaign that ended with smallpox being declared eradicated in 1980 relied on countries sharing data and vaccine, setting aside narrow national interests for a common good.
No single country could have achieved that goal alone, and the cooperation it demanded was a price worth paying.
This shows that when a goal is worthy, means that would seem [[onerous|onerous]] in ordinary times become justifiable.
The worthier and more urgent the goal, the heavier the burden that can fairly be imposed to reach it.
Second, the statement holds when a worthy goal requires disrupting an unjust or failing order.
During the Montgomery bus boycott of 1955-1956, Black residents refused for over a year to ride segregated buses, accepting great inconvenience in their own daily lives.
The boycott helped end bus segregation in that city, and its goal of equal treatment clearly justified the hardship.
Those who walked or found other ways to travel for months chose a hard path, but few would now say they were wrong to do so.

Likewise, under Vietnam's Doi Moi reforms of 1986, market incentives [[supplanted|supplant]] central planning; the change was sweeping, yet a country that had faced food shortages became one of the world's largest rice exporters.
This shows that worthy goals can justify means that are costly, disruptive and even [[contentious|contentious]] at the time.
Had the boycotters or the reformers waited for a painless path, the injustice or hardship they faced might have continued for years.
Admittedly, the statement does not hold when the means violate basic human rights.
In the Tuskegee syphilis study, which ran from 1932 to 1972, researchers withheld treatment from Black men without their informed consent.
No goal could justify deceiving sick men and denying them care.
Nevertheless, this case limits rather than refutes my position, because the problem was that the means destroyed the very dignity medicine exists to protect.
The public outrage that followed led to US rules requiring ethics review boards, showing that societies accept costly means for worthy goals but draw a firm line at deception and harm.
Thus I accept the statement for means that impose fair costs, but not for means that [[abase|abase]] the people they are supposed to help.
The statement is therefore largely true for costly means but false for cruel ones.
In conclusion, a worthy goal can justify a wide range of difficult means, though not literally any means.
Public health laws and protests against injustice show how worthy aims justify restrictions and disruption, while the Tuskegee study shows where the statement breaks down.
The test, then, is whether the means respect the people they are meant to serve.

essays.task_note: Body 1 and Body 2 show ways the statement holds (public health measures, disruptive protest and reform), and Body 3 shows where it does not hold (rights violations), explaining that this limits the word "any."

essays.title: Noble ends cannot excuse cruel means

paragraphs.text: Many of history's worst abuses were committed by people who believed their goals were good.
That is why the statement that if a goal is worthy, then any means taken to attain it are justifiable is so dangerous.
I strongly disagree with this statement, because unjust means harm real people and often defeat the goal itself, although worthy goals can justify some proportionate costs.
The statement fails when means violate rights and when bad means destroy the trust a goal depends on, and it holds only partly for fair, limited sacrifices.
First, the statement does not hold when the means violate the rights of the people involved.
The Tuskegee syphilis study, which ran from 1932 to 1972, withheld treatment from Black men without their informed consent in the name of medical knowledge.
Knowledge about disease is a worthy goal, yet no one today would argue that it justified deceiving and harming those men.
The men were treated as sources of data rather than as patients with a right to choose.

Similarly, thalidomide was given to pregnant women around 1960 as a sedative, and it caused severe birth defects in thousands of babies in Europe; the hope of helping patients could not excuse giving them a drug before its risks were understood.
This shows that a worthy goal cannot [[exonerate|exonerate]] means that treat people as tools.
The more worthy the goal, in fact, the more carefully we should guard against the temptation to cut corners in pursuing it.
Second, the statement fails because unjust means often [[undermine|undermine]] the very goal they serve.
In my work on dengue control, communities cooperate only when they trust health workers.
A campaign that forced its way into homes to destroy water containers might reduce mosquitoes this season, but it would lose the cooperation needed in every season that follows.
Residents who felt invaded would stop reporting fever cases and hide containers from inspectors.
Likewise, a government that pursued lower crime through torture would teach citizens that the law itself cannot be trusted.
Each forced confession would weaken the very respect for law on which lasting order depends.
This shows that means and ends are linked, because corrupt means [[vitiate|vitiate]] the ends they claim to serve.
A goal reached by unjust means is often not truly reached at all.
Admittedly, the statement holds partly when the means impose fair, limited costs for a clearly worthy goal.
Vietnam's 2007 helmet law restricted riders' freedom, yet it raised helmet use to over 90% within months and reduced head injuries and deaths.
Nevertheless, this case shows only that some costly means are justifiable, not that any means are.
The helmet law applied equally to everyone and was [[commensurate|commensurate]] with the danger it addressed.
It did not single out a vulnerable group, deceive anyone or cause harm beyond a small loss of choice.
Thus the real question is never simply whether a goal is worthy but whether the means are proportionate and respectful, which is why I reject the statement as written.
A goal can be worthy and still be pursued in ways that no decent person could accept.
In conclusion, a worthy goal does not make any means justifiable.
Means that violate rights cannot be excused, unjust means tend to defeat their own goals, and even justified sacrifices must be proportionate.
We should judge every plan, therefore, by its methods as well as by its aims.

words.meaning_here: in proportion to; matching in size

essays.task_note: Body 1 and Body 2 show ways the statement fails (rights violations, self-defeating means), and Body 3 considers how it partly holds (proportionate costs) before explaining why that case still rejects the word "any."

essays.title: Literature makes better professionals

paragraphs.text: A good novel lets a reader live, for a few hours, inside someone else's mind.

That experience lies behind the recommendation that, in order to become well-rounded individuals, all college students should be required to take courses in which they read poetry, novels, mythology and other imaginative literature.
I largely agree with this recommendation, provided the requirement is modest in size and flexible in content.

Such courses are advantageous because they build empathy in future professionals and because they sharpen the reading and writing skills every field needs, even though they compete for time in demanding programs.
First, requiring literature is advantageous for students entering professions that serve people, because imaginative reading builds empathy.
As a physician, I learned the facts of disease from textbooks, but novels about families coping with illness taught me what a diagnosis feels like to a patient.
That understanding made me more patient with frightened families during dengue outbreaks, when hospitals were crowded and tempers were short.
No statistics table could have given me that insight as vividly as a well-told story did.

Similarly, an engineer designing public housing benefits from stories about how ordinary people live, since a program like Singapore's, which now houses about 80% of residents, must serve real families rather than abstract numbers.
This shows that imaginative literature can [[imbue|imbue]] students with the empathy that well-rounded professionals need.
Professionals who serve people need to understand those people, and fiction offers practice in doing so.
Second, literature courses are advantageous because they sharpen the ability to read closely and write clearly.
Consider a computer science student who must interpret a difficult poem and defend her reading in an essay.
She learns to notice [[nuance|nuance]], weigh evidence and express a complex idea in plain words, skills she will later use in writing reports and explaining her work to clients.
Likewise, many scientists struggle to explain their findings to the public, and close reading of stories could help them make research [[intelligible|intelligible]] to ordinary readers.
Public trust in research depends partly on whether ordinary readers can follow it.
This shows that reading imaginative literature is not a luxury but practical training in thinking and communication.
Even students who never read another poem after graduation will keep the habits of careful reading the course built.
Admittedly, a literature requirement would not be advantageous in programs already crowded with essential technical courses.
A medical or engineering student who must master a heavy load of required subjects may find an extra reading course an [[irksome|irksome]] burden that takes time from clinical or laboratory training.
For such students, a large requirement could mean less practice in the skills their future patients and clients depend on.
Nevertheless, this problem argues for a modest, flexible requirement rather than none at all.
A single course, or a choice among short courses on mythology, poetry or novels, would cost little time while giving every student some exposure.
Students could even choose works connected to their own fields, such as novels about illness for future doctors.
Thus the circumstances of demanding programs shape how the requirement should be designed, not whether it should exist.
A small, well-chosen requirement keeps the benefits of literature while respecting the demands of technical training.
In conclusion, colleges should require all students to read some imaginative literature.
Such courses build empathy and sharpen communication, although the requirement must stay small enough to fit demanding programs.
A modest dose of poetry and fiction, therefore, can produce better professionals and fuller human beings.

words.meaning_here: to fill or inspire with a quality

essays.task_note: The essay gives circumstances where a literature requirement is advantageous (people-serving professions, communication skills) and one where it is not (crowded technical programs), and explains how that case shapes the design of the requirement.

essays.title: Require breadth, not literature specifically

paragraphs.text: There are many roads to a well-rounded mind.

That is why I question the recommendation that, in order to become well-rounded individuals, all college students should be required to take courses in which they read poetry, novels, mythology and other imaginative literature.
I mostly disagree with this recommendation, because a single required subject cannot suit every student, although some exposure to the humanities is worthwhile.
A mandatory literature course is disadvantageous when students can gain breadth in other ways and when forced reading breeds resentment, though it can help students who would otherwise never read.
First, the requirement would be disadvantageous because students can become well-rounded through many fields besides imaginative literature.

A public health student who studies history, for instance, may learn as much about human nature from the Tuskegee syphilis study, which withheld treatment from Black men without their informed consent, as from any novel.
Studying that case teaches ethics, empathy and the dangers of power in a form directly relevant to her future work.
Such a case can build moral imagination just as effectively as a story, while also teaching real history.
Similarly, a literature student who takes a course in statistics gains a kind of breadth that poetry cannot give, yet few would argue that statistics should be required of everyone.

This shows that well-roundedness depends on breadth, not on any one [[canonical|canonical]] subject, so colleges should encourage an [[eclectic|eclectic]] mix of courses rather than literature in particular.
Second, compulsory literature courses can be disadvantageous when they turn reading into a chore.
Consider an engineering student forced to read long novels on a strict schedule while also preparing for difficult technical exams.
Rather than learning to love fiction, he may skim summaries, write [[perfunctory|perfunctory]] essays and leave college determined never to open a novel again.
Likewise, students in a required ethics course often memorize theories for the exam and forget them soon after, while those who choose the course tend to engage more deeply.
Requirements guarantee attendance, but they cannot guarantee interest or understanding.
This shows that imposing literature on unwilling students may [[alienate|alienate]] them from the very reading the requirement hopes to encourage.
A love of reading is more likely to grow from choice than from compulsion.
Admittedly, a requirement would be advantageous for students who would otherwise never encounter imaginative literature.
A student from a family without books, studying a technical subject, might discover in a mythology course a lifelong interest she would never have found on her own.
For her, the requirement would open a door that might otherwise stay closed for life.
Nevertheless, this benefit can be achieved by a broader humanities requirement in which literature is one option among history, philosophy and the arts.
A student like her could still choose the mythology course, while classmates with other interests could pursue history or philosophy instead.
This case therefore qualifies my position but does not reverse it, because breadth, not literature alone, is the real goal.
The goal of introducing new readers to great stories can be met without making one subject mandatory for all.
In conclusion, colleges should not require all students to read imaginative literature in order to become well-rounded.
Breadth can come from many fields, and forced reading can breed resentment, although exposure to the humanities helps students who would otherwise miss it.
A flexible humanities requirement, therefore, serves the goal of well-rounded graduates better than a single mandatory literature course.

words.meaning_here: drawn from a wide variety of sources
done quickly and without real effort or interest
to make someone feel unfriendly or distant toward something

essays.task_note: The essay describes circumstances where the requirement would be disadvantageous (other routes to breadth, forced reading) and one where it would be advantageous (students who would never read otherwise), and explains how that case leads to a broader humanities requirement instead.

essays.title: Art earns merit by being understood

paragraphs.text: Art has always been one of the main ways that people share feelings and ideas with one another.
This shared purpose raises the question of whether a film, novel, poem or song must be understandable to most people in order to have merit.

I largely agree that a work of art needs to be understandable to most people to have real merit, as long as "understandable" means that ordinary audiences can grasp its emotional core, not every technical detail.
Three considerations shape this view: art exists to communicate, accessible art can change how communities behave, and some great works are understood only after a delay.
First, a work of art has merit largely because it communicates, and a work that almost no one can understand fails at its most basic task.
Consider a novel about a family surviving a famine, written in plain language and told through a single child's eyes.
Readers who have never experienced hunger can still feel the child's fear and hope, and many of them may finish the book with a new sympathy for the poor.
Its merit lies precisely in this transfer of feeling from the writer to a wide audience.
Similarly, a love song with a simple melody can move listeners in many countries, even those who do not know the language in which it is sung.
These cases show that the value of art is not hidden inside the object; it is realized when people understand it.
A work that remains [[opaque|opaque]] to nearly everyone may display skill, but it has not yet achieved the purpose for which art exists.
Second, art that most people can understand has a greater capacity to change behavior and strengthen communities.
In my work on dengue control in Vietnam, I have seen a short song broadcast over commune loudspeakers do more than our printed leaflets.
The song explained, in simple and catchy lines, why families should empty standing water every week, and residents soon repeated it to their children.
It was not sophisticated, yet its clarity allowed it to [[permeate|permeate]] daily life in a way that a technical lecture never could.
Likewise, a film with a clear story about a social injustice can [[galvanize|galvanize]] viewers to discuss a problem they had previously ignored.
This shows that being understandable is not a weakness that lowers artistic value; it is often the very quality that allows a work to matter beyond a small circle of experts.
Admittedly, the statement does not hold true in every case, because some works are valuable long before most people understand them.
Vincent van Gogh sold very few paintings during his lifetime, yet he is now regarded as one of the greatest painters in history.
If his merit had depended on the approval of his contemporaries, we would have to conclude that his work had little value, which is clearly [[erroneous|erroneous]].
Nevertheless, this case refines rather than refutes my position.
Van Gogh's paintings did eventually become understandable to ordinary viewers, and their recognized merit grew together with that understanding.
The lesson, then, is that the test of understandability should be applied over time, not only at the moment a work is created.
A work that remains [[esoteric|esoteric]] forever, appreciated only by a few specialists, has a weaker claim to merit than one that eventually reaches a broad audience.
In conclusion, I largely agree that art must be understandable to most people to have merit, provided that understanding refers to its emotional core and is allowed to develop over time.
Art earns its value by communicating, by shaping how communities think and act, and, as van Gogh's case shows, sometimes by waiting for audiences to catch up.
Artists, therefore, should not fear clarity, because clarity is often what turns private skill into public value.

essays.task_note: Bodies 1-2 show where the statement holds (communication, social impact) and Body 3 uses van Gogh as a case where it does not, explaining that it refines the position to understanding over time.

essays.title: Merit does not require mass understanding

paragraphs.text: Some of the works that people treasure most today were once ignored or misunderstood.
This history challenges the claim that a film, novel, poem or song must be understandable to most people in order to have merit.

I largely disagree with this statement, because merit depends on the quality, originality and depth of a work rather than on its immediate popularity, although broad understanding can add to a work's value.
Merit is often recognized before the public catches up, difficult art serves important audiences, and accessibility matters mainly when art has a practical goal.
First, the statement does not hold true because the merit of a work often exists long before most people understand it.
Vincent van Gogh sold very few paintings during his lifetime, which suggests that most people of his era did not value his work.
Today, however, he is regarded as one of the greatest painters in history.
His paintings did not change; what changed was the public's ability to see their worth.

A similar pattern appears outside art: when Ignaz Semmelweis asked doctors in Vienna to wash their hands, most colleagues [[dismissed|dismiss]] his idea, which germ theory vindicated only years after his death.
These cases show that the judgment of the majority at any moment is an unreliable measure of value.
If merit required broad understanding, we would have to deny merit to many works that later generations rightly [[venerate|venerate]].
Second, difficult art has merit because it serves audiences who are willing to work for meaning, and that effort is part of its value.
Consider a dense poem that uses unusual images and broken syntax to capture the confusion of grief.
A casual reader may find it [[arcane|arcane]], but a reader who has lost a parent may recognize in its fractured lines an honest picture of mourning that a simple rhyme could never offer.
Similarly, an experimental film may confuse most viewers while inspiring a small group of young directors, who later borrow its techniques for films that reach a mass audience.
This shows that a work can have merit by deepening the experience of a few readers or by influencing other artists, even if most people never understand it directly.
Requiring every work to be easy would push artists toward safe and [[banal|banal]] choices.
Admittedly, the statement contains some truth, since art that almost no one can understand risks becoming self-indulgent rather than meaningful.
Consider a children's film about friendship: if most children cannot follow its plot, it has failed, whatever its technical brilliance.
Similarly, a song written for a public health campaign must be clear, or families will not change their behavior.
Nevertheless, these examples concern art with a practical purpose, not art in general.

The [[salient|salient]] question is what a work is trying to do: a campaign song should be judged by how many people it reaches, but a novel or poem may be judged by its depth, honesty and originality.
Therefore, broad understanding is one possible source of merit, not a requirement for it.
In conclusion, I largely disagree that a work of art needs to be understood by most people in order to have merit.
Great works are often recognized only later, difficult art can deeply affect a smaller audience, and accessibility, though valuable, matters most when art serves a practical goal.
We should therefore judge art by what it achieves, not merely by how many people grasp it at first sight.

words.meaning_here: rejected as not worth serious consideration
regard with great respect and admiration
mysterious and understood by few people
dull and unoriginal because too common

essays.task_note: Bodies 1-2 show where the statement fails (delayed recognition, difficult art) and Body 3 grants where it holds (practical art), explaining how that limits the position.

essays.title: Discovery often answers a different question

paragraphs.text: Many people imagine that great discoveries come from a lone genius who sets out to solve a problem and succeeds.
The statement challenges this picture by claiming that important discoveries and creations are often accidental, found while we search for the answer to a different question.
I largely agree with this statement, as long as "accidental" means unexpected rather than unearned, because chance rewards only those who are already working hard.
Unexpected findings in medicine, unplanned uses of technology, and the limits of pure luck each shape this position.
First, the statement holds true in medicine, where several landmark discoveries arose while researchers were pursuing other goals.
In 1928, Alexander Fleming noticed that mold had killed bacteria on a culture plate.
He was not searching for a new drug at that moment, yet this [[fortuitous|fortuitous]] observation eventually led to penicillin.
Had he discarded the plate as spoiled, the opportunity might have been lost.
Even then, penicillin became a usable drug only when Howard Florey and Ernst Chain's team developed it during World War II.
Similarly, in my work as an epidemiologist, I have seen [[empirical|empirical]] studies designed to answer one question produce an unexpected finding that later became the main result.
These cases show that the path to discovery is rarely a straight line.
Researchers seek one answer, and their data often hand them another, which is exactly what the statement describes.
Second, the statement also holds true for creations, because inventions built for one purpose often find their greatest value in another.
GPS was built by the US military to serve military needs.
Once it was opened to civilians, however, it became the basis of everyday navigation, ride-hailing and delivery apps, uses far removed from its original purpose.
Likewise, a hospital that installs a text-message system to remind patients about appointments may discover that the same system is ideal for warning residents about a dengue outbreak.
This shows that the answer to one question, such as how to guide soldiers, can turn out to answer a different and larger question, such as how ordinary people move through their cities.
Much of a creation's value is therefore [[latent|latent]] until people apply it in unforeseen ways.
Admittedly, not every important discovery is accidental, and treating luck as the main cause would make discovery sound like a [[fluke|fluke]].

The Wright brothers, bicycle makers without college degrees, achieved the first powered airplane flight in 1903 only after years of careful experiments with gliders and a wind tunnel they built themselves.
Their achievement was planned step by step, and luck played only a minor part in it.
Nevertheless, such planned successes qualify the statement rather than refute it.
Even a lucky observation in a laboratory becomes a discovery only if a [[meticulous|meticulous]] researcher notices it and understands why it matters.
Accident supplies the surprise, but discipline supplies the ability to recognize it.
For this reason, I accept the statement for the moment of discovery, while insisting that the work surrounding that moment is anything but accidental.
In conclusion, I largely agree that many important discoveries and creations are accidental, since researchers often find one answer while seeking another.
Penicillin, the civilian uses of GPS and the deliberate work of the Wright brothers together show that chance plays a large role, but only within a framework of effort.
Institutions that want more discoveries should therefore fund curious, careful researchers rather than demand that every project find exactly what it promised.

words.meaning_here: based on observation and data rather than theory
present but hidden and not yet developed
very careful and attentive to detail

essays.task_note: Bodies 1-2 show where the statement holds (penicillin, GPS) and Body 3 considers a deliberate discovery (Wright brothers) and explains how it qualifies the position.

essays.title: Most breakthroughs come from deliberate work

paragraphs.text: Stories of lucky accidents are popular because they are dramatic and easy to remember.
Perhaps for this reason, the statement claims that important discoveries and creations are usually accidental, found while seeking the answer to a different question.
I largely disagree with this statement, because most important advances result from long, deliberate work aimed at a specific problem, even though chance occasionally plays a role.
Planned medical breakthroughs, the methodical nature of invention, and the real but limited role of accidents such as penicillin shape my position.
First, the statement does not hold true for many major medical advances, which came from research aimed squarely at the problem it solved.
The COVID-19 mRNA vaccines were developed in under a year, but this speed depended on decades of earlier, little-noticed basic research on mRNA by Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman.
Their [[assiduous|assiduous]] work, recognized with the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, was no accident; it was a long effort to make mRNA useful in medicine.
Similarly, researchers who released mosquitoes carrying Wolbachia bacteria, which block dengue transmission, cut dengue cases by 77% in a randomized trial in Yogyakarta, Indonesia.
That result came from a clear question and a carefully designed test, not from stumbling on an answer to something else.
These cases show that major discoveries usually come from asking the right question and pursuing it for years.
Second, important creations are typically the result of methodical experimentation rather than fortunate surprises.
The Wright brothers, bicycle makers without college degrees, achieved the first powered airplane flight in 1903.
They did not stumble on flight while trying to solve another problem; they pursued it directly and patiently.
Their success came after years of careful experiments with gliders and a wind tunnel they built themselves, each test bringing them closer to controlled flight.
Likewise, smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980 only after a coordinated global WHO vaccination campaign that relied on countries sharing data and vaccine.
Nothing about this victory was accidental; it was planned, measured and revised.
This shows that when the stakes are high, progress comes from [[indefatigable|indefatigable]] effort rather than from [[flukes|fluke]].
In my own work as an epidemiologist, too, useful findings almost always come from a clear question and a well-planned study.
Admittedly, some important discoveries were genuinely unexpected, and the statement captures these cases well.
In 1928, Alexander Fleming noticed that mold had killed bacteria on a culture plate, a [[fortuitous|fortuitous]] observation he had not planned to make.
Nevertheless, even this famous accident required years of deliberate work before it mattered.
Penicillin became a usable drug only when Howard Florey and Ernst Chain's team developed it during World War II.
Without that team's years of focused effort, the observation might have remained a curiosity in a laboratory.
The accidental moment was real, but it was a small part of a much longer, intentional process.
Such stories are memorable precisely because they are [[anomalies|anomaly]], not the rule; in most fields, accidents provide only occasional sparks, while planned, patient work provides the fire.
In conclusion, I largely disagree that important discoveries and creations are usually accidental.

The mRNA vaccines, the Wolbachia trial, the Wright brothers' flight and the eradication of smallpox all came from focused effort, and even penicillin needed years of planned development after its lucky start.
Chance may open a door, but only sustained and purposeful work carries a discovery through it.

words.meaning_here: unusual cases that do not fit the normal pattern

essays.title: History shows we are not so different

paragraphs.text: It is tempting to believe that we are wiser than the people who came before us.
The statement claims that the main benefit of studying history is to dispel this illusion by showing that people living now are not significantly different from people in earlier times.
I largely agree with this statement, because history repeatedly reveals the same human strengths and weaknesses, although it also teaches valuable lessons about how institutions improve.
The persistent human resistance to new ideas, the recurring misuse of powerful discoveries, and the real progress in our institutions shape this view.
First, history shows that people today resist uncomfortable evidence in much the same way earlier generations did.
In 1847, Ignaz Semmelweis had doctors in Vienna wash their hands in chlorinated lime, and deaths from childbed fever on his ward fell sharply.
Yet most colleagues rejected his idea, which germ theory vindicated only years after his death.
Similarly, Galileo was forced by the Church in 1633 to recant his support for the idea that the Earth moves around the sun.
In both cases, people in authority rejected sound ideas because those ideas challenged their beliefs.
It would be comforting to view these episodes as relics of a less enlightened age, but modern professionals still [[dismiss|dismiss]] findings that threaten their habits or status.
Studying such cases [[disabuses|disabuse]] us of the [[complacent|complacent]] belief that we are immune to the same pride and fear.
Second, history reveals that people repeatedly misuse powerful tools, which suggests that human nature has changed little.
In his 1945 Nobel lecture, Alexander Fleming warned that misuse of penicillin would breed resistant bacteria.
Today, overuse and over-the-counter sales of antibiotics, common in many countries including Vietnam, help resistant bacteria spread, so drugs that once cured infections now often fail.
As a physician working on antimicrobial resistance in Vietnam, I see this pattern regularly, as patients and sellers choose quick relief over long-term safety.
Many patients still request antibiotics for viral illnesses, thinking little about the long-term risk to their community.
This shows that the same [[myopic|myopic]] reasoning that worried Fleming persists today, despite all our scientific progress.
History is useful precisely because it lets us recognize this weakness in ourselves before its consequences grow worse.
Admittedly, the statement overlooks the fact that history also records real change, especially in the rules that govern how people behave.
After the Tuskegee syphilis study (1932-1972) withheld treatment from Black men without their informed consent, public outrage led to US rules requiring ethics review boards for research on people.
Today, researchers in many countries cannot begin a study on people without such approval.
Nevertheless, this progress actually supports my position rather than weakening it.
Ethics boards exist because societies learned that researchers, then and now, can be tempted to treat people as a means to an end.
In other words, our institutions improved precisely because we accepted that human nature had not.
Calling this the "main" benefit may slightly overstate the case, but it is the benefit on which most other historical lessons depend.
In conclusion, I largely agree that the chief value of history is to show that we are not fundamentally different from earlier generations.
Our resistance to new evidence, our misuse of powerful tools, and even the safeguards we have built all point to a human nature that remains largely [[immutable|immutable]].
Students of history should therefore read the past not as a record of foolish strangers, but as a mirror.

essays.title: History mainly teaches how societies change

paragraphs.text: Every society looks to its past for guidance, but people disagree about what the past can teach.
The statement claims that the main benefit of studying history is to dispel the illusion that people living now are significantly different from those who lived earlier.
I largely disagree, because the most valuable lesson of history is how societies change their conditions and institutions, although history does remind us that basic human nature is stable.
History's record of reform after disaster, its evidence that policy can transform lives, and its reminder of our unchanging flaws together shape this position.
First, the greatest benefit of history is that it shows how societies learn from their mistakes and build better systems.
Thalidomide, a sedative given to pregnant women around 1960, caused severe birth defects in thousands of babies in Europe.
Frances Kelsey of the US FDA refused to approve it, and the US then passed stricter drug-testing rules in 1962.
Her caution is remembered precisely because it changed how new medicines are tested.
Similarly, after the [[egregious|egregious]] Tuskegee syphilis study withheld treatment from Black men without their informed consent, public outrage led to US rules requiring ethics review boards.
These cases show that history matters most as a record of [[remedial|remedial]] action: it explains why our institutions look the way they do.
A patient today is protected by rules that did not exist a century ago, so in this sense people now really do live differently.
Second, history demonstrates that people's lives can change dramatically when their circumstances change, which is the opposite of what the statement suggests.
Before its Doi Moi reforms of 1986, Vietnam relied on central planning and faced food shortages.
After the reforms replaced central planning with market incentives, Vietnam became one of the world's largest rice exporters, and poverty fell dramatically over the following decades.
Likewise, Singapore's government housing program now houses about 80% of the country's residents, most of whom own their flats.
Vietnamese farmers before and after 1986 were not different kinds of people, but the contrast between their lives was [[stark|stark]].
Studying such reforms gives citizens and leaders a [[pragmatic|pragmatic]] guide to what works, which is far more useful than the claim that people never change.
Admittedly, history does reveal that certain [[ingrained|ingrained]] human weaknesses persist across centuries.
Galileo was forced by the Church in 1633 to recant his support for the idea that the Earth moves around the sun, and powerful groups still sometimes try to silence inconvenient truths.
In this sense, the statement is right that people in earlier times were not so different from us.
Nevertheless, recognizing this continuity is only a starting point, not the main benefit.
Knowing that people resist new ideas is useful mainly because it helps us design protections, such as open scientific debate, that reduce the damage of that resistance.
Thus, the stability of human nature is a background fact; the real value of history lies in what we do about it.
A hospital that builds hand-washing into its daily rules does more good than one whose staff merely know that colleagues once rejected Ignaz Semmelweis.
In conclusion, I largely disagree that the main purpose of history is to show that we resemble earlier generations.
Reforms after thalidomide and Tuskegee, the transformation brought by Doi Moi, and even the lesson of Galileo all show that history is most useful as a guide to change.
We study the past not only to see ourselves in it, but to avoid repeating it.

essays.title: Discipline, not school, drives learning

paragraphs.text: Two students can sit in the same classroom, hear the same lectures and still leave with very different knowledge.
This common observation supports the statement that learning is primarily a matter of personal discipline and that schools or colleges alone cannot motivate students.
I largely agree with this statement, because lasting learning depends mainly on a student's own effort, although good schools can strengthen that effort.
The achievements of self-driven learners, the limits of external pressure, and the real influence of excellent school systems shape this view.
First, the statement holds true because some of the most impressive learners in history relied on self-discipline far more than on any school or college.
The Wright brothers were bicycle makers without college degrees, yet they achieved the first powered airplane flight in 1903.
Their success came after years of careful experiments with gliders and a wind tunnel they built themselves, a program of study that no school had assigned to them.
Similarly, Marie Curie won Nobel Prizes in both physics and chemistry despite the barriers women faced in science at the time.
No institution handed her success; she earned it through years of persistent work.
These cases show that discipline can carry a learner far beyond what institutions offer, and even past barriers that [[impede|impede]] progress.
The driving force in each case was internal, not institutional: schools can offer tools, but only the learner decides to use them every day.
Second, external pressure from schools can produce compliance, but it rarely produces genuine learning without personal commitment.
In medical school in Vietnam, I watched classmates face the same demanding exams.
Some memorized material the night before and forgot it within weeks, while others reviewed patiently every day and could still apply that knowledge years later on the ward.
The school, the teachers and the stakes were identical; the difference lay in each student's habits.
Those who succeeded had built routines that no professor could impose on them.
Likewise, a [[lethargic|lethargic]] employee sent to a mandatory training course may attend every session and still learn almost nothing.
This shows that institutions can create opportunities and deadlines, but they cannot force a mind to engage.
Real learning requires the kind of [[assiduous|assiduous]] practice that only the learner can supply.
Admittedly, the statement may underestimate how much a well-designed school system can [[kindle|kindle]] motivation.
Finland requires schoolteachers to hold a master's degree, makes teaching a respected and selective profession, and relies far less on standardized testing than many countries.
Such a system may well make students more curious and less anxious than one driven by constant exams.
Nevertheless, even the best teachers can only spark interest; they cannot keep it alive for the student.
A student in an excellent classroom who never practices outside it will still fall behind.
Once a student leaves the classroom, the hours of practice that turn interest into skill depend on personal discipline, so good schools [[augment|augment]] motivation but do not replace it.
For this reason, the statement, while not completely true, captures the most important part of the picture.
In conclusion, I largely agree that learning is mainly a matter of personal discipline and that schools alone cannot motivate students.
Self-taught achievers like the Wright brothers, the gap between disciplined and careless students, and even Finland's excellent schools all point to the learner as the decisive factor.
Schools should therefore aim not only to teach content but also to build the habits of self-discipline that learning ultimately requires.

essays.title: Good schools can create motivation

paragraphs.text: Most people can remember one teacher who changed the way they thought about a subject.
Such memories challenge the statement that learning is primarily a matter of personal discipline and that schools or colleges cannot motivate students on their own.
I largely disagree with this statement, because well-designed schools can create motivation where little existed, although personal discipline remains important.
The influence of strong teaching systems, the role of mentors and learning environments, and the undeniable value of self-discipline shape this position.
First, the statement does not hold true in countries whose school systems are deliberately built to motivate students.
Finland requires schoolteachers to hold a master's degree, makes teaching a respected and selective profession, and relies far less on standardized testing than many countries.
In such a system, highly trained teachers have more freedom to design lessons around students' curiosity instead of around exam scores.
Students in such classrooms are more likely to see learning as interesting rather than as a series of tests to survive.
These students are not born with more discipline than children elsewhere; they are taught in a system that makes effort feel worthwhile.
Conversely, a school that offers only rote memorization and frequent high-stakes tests can fill even a curious child with [[apathy|apathy]].
These contrasting cases show that motivation is not simply an [[inborn|inborn]] trait; it is shaped by the institution in which a student learns.
If schools can destroy motivation, they can also build it.
Second, mentors and learning environments can turn indifferent students into committed learners.
Early in my medical training in Vietnam, I had little interest in statistics, which seemed dry and [[arcane|arcane]].

A professor who taught epidemiology through real outbreak investigations, including dengue cases in our own region, changed that attitude completely, and the subject later became the center of my career.
Similarly, a hospital that holds regular case discussions encourages young doctors to keep reading, because they know colleagues will ask hard questions.
By contrast, a young doctor in a hospital without such discussions may lose the habit of reading within a year or two.
In both examples, the institution supplied the spark and the structure that personal discipline later sustained.
Without that external [[catalyst|catalyst]], many learners never discover what they might care about; motivation is often borrowed from a teacher before it becomes one's own.
Admittedly, personal discipline matters, and some people learn remarkably well with little help from schools.

The Wright brothers, bicycle makers without college degrees, achieved the first powered airplane flight in 1903 after years of careful experiments with gliders and a wind tunnel they built themselves.
Nevertheless, such self-taught achievers are exceptional, and an education system cannot be designed around exceptions.
Most students, especially children, have not yet developed the habits needed to study alone for years.
Children who grow up in homes without books or quiet study space depend even more on what schools provide.
For them, a good school is not a supplement to discipline but the place where discipline is first [[inculcated|inculcate]].
This consideration qualifies my position: discipline is necessary, but schools are often its source.
In conclusion, I largely disagree that learning depends primarily on personal discipline and that schools cannot motivate students on their own.
Finland's teaching system, the influence of good mentors and the rarity of truly self-taught learners all show that institutions shape motivation.
Instead of blaming unmotivated students, societies should invest in schools that make learning worth the effort.

essays.title: Prioritize research that helps the most people

paragraphs.text: Research money, time and talent are always limited, so every scientific agenda involves hard choices.
The recommendation that researchers should focus on areas likely to benefit the greatest number of people offers one rule for making those choices.
I largely agree with this recommendation, especially where resources are scarce and the burden of disease is heavy, but I would not apply it so strictly that basic research is neglected.
The advantages of targeting widespread health threats, the value of research that guides national policy, and the risk to basic science shape this position.
First, in circumstances where a few problems cause most of the harm, adopting this recommendation would be clearly advantageous.
Consider dengue, which is [[endemic|endemic]] in much of Southeast Asia, including Vietnam.

Researchers who released mosquitoes carrying Wolbachia bacteria, which block dengue transmission, cut dengue cases by 77% in a randomized trial in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, and the method has also been tested in Vietnam.
Research of this kind can protect entire cities at once.
Similarly, studies on antibiotic resistance address a threat to nearly everyone, since overuse and over-the-counter sales of antibiotics help resistant bacteria spread.
Because resistant infections threaten anyone who needs surgery, childbirth care or cancer treatment, progress in this field protects a very large population.
These examples show that when a country must choose, research aimed at widespread problems offers the largest return on [[scant|scant]] resources.
Second, the recommendation is advantageous when research can be translated quickly into policies that reach whole populations.
Vietnam's 2007 law requiring motorbike helmets raised helmet use from low levels to over 90% within months and reduced head injuries and deaths.
Research on the causes of road injuries is exactly the kind of work that supports laws like this, whose benefits reach almost everyone who rides a motorbike.

In my own work as an epidemiologist, I have seen how a single well-designed study of a common infection can change treatment guidelines across a country, while a study of a rare condition seldom changes practice beyond a few hospitals.
For a country with limited budgets, such research offers both scientific value and immediate public benefit.
This shows that research focused on common problems does not merely produce knowledge; it can [[galvanize|galvanize]] action that improves many lives at once.
Admittedly, there are circumstances in which adopting this recommendation would not be advantageous, especially in basic science.
The COVID-19 mRNA vaccines were developed in under a year because of decades of earlier, little-noticed basic research on mRNA by Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman.
For years, their work did not appear likely to benefit many people, and a strict version of this rule might have cut its funding.
A committee asking only how many people a project would help might have ranked it near the bottom.
Nevertheless, this example argues for a balanced portfolio, not for abandoning the recommendation.
Funders can reserve part of their budgets for curiosity-driven research while directing most of their money toward pressing, widespread problems.
In this way, the recommendation serves as a sound default rather than a rigid [[dogma|dogma]], capturing most of its benefits while limiting its risks.
In conclusion, I largely agree that researchers should prioritize areas likely to benefit the greatest number of people.
Research on dengue, antibiotic resistance and road safety shows the advantages of this approach, while the history of mRNA reminds us to protect some basic science.
A [[judicious|judicious]] balance between these goals would serve both present needs and future discoveries.

essays.title: Benefit is too unpredictable to target

paragraphs.text: Some of the most useful knowledge in history came from research that seemed to have no practical purpose at the time.
This fact complicates the recommendation that scientists and other researchers should focus on areas likely to benefit the greatest number of people.

I largely disagree with this recommendation, because the benefits of research are hard to predict and smaller groups also deserve attention, although the rule makes sense for urgent public-health problems.
The unpredictable value of basic research, the moral claims of smaller groups, and the special case of widespread epidemics shape this position.
First, adopting this recommendation would be disadvantageous in basic science, where no one can know in advance which projects will benefit the most people.
Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman spent decades on little-noticed basic research on mRNA.
That work later allowed the COVID-19 mRNA vaccines to be developed in under a year, and it earned them the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
Similarly, GPS was built by the US military, yet once it was opened to civilians, it became the basis of everyday navigation, ride-hailing and delivery apps.
Neither the mRNA researchers nor the engineers who built GPS could have predicted how widely their work would eventually be used.
These examples show that predictions about benefit are [[conjectural|conjectural]] at best.
A [[myopic|myopic]] funding rule based on such predictions would likely cut exactly the research that later helps the most people.
Second, the recommendation would be disadvantageous where a small group faces severe suffering that no one else will address.
Consider a rare genetic disease that affects only a few thousand children worldwide.
By the logic of the recommendation, researchers should ignore it in favor of common conditions, yet for those families, a treatment would change everything.
A rule based only on numbers would leave these children without hope.

Such research has also become more feasible because of shared resources such as the Human Genome Project, a publicly funded international effort completed in 2003 that made the human DNA sequence freely available to all researchers.
This shows that a purely numerical rule would [[marginalize|marginalize]] small groups and treat human need as a matter of headcount.
Research priorities should also reflect severity and fairness, not only scale, especially now that shared data make rare conditions easier to study.
Admittedly, in circumstances where a threat is widespread and resources are scarce, focusing on the greatest number would be advantageous.
Dengue is [[endemic|endemic]] in Vietnam, and a randomized trial in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, showed that releasing mosquitoes carrying Wolbachia bacteria cut dengue cases by 77%.
In such a setting, a health ministry would be wise to fund this kind of research before more specialized projects.
When a disease affects so many people, delaying such research would cost lives.
Nevertheless, this is an argument for setting priorities within a crisis, not for a general rule governing all research.
Even countries facing heavy disease burdens benefit from basic science and from attention to neglected groups, so some funding should continue for questions whose value is not yet clear.
The recommendation therefore works as a guide for emergencies but becomes [[counterproductive|counterproductive]] when applied to science as a whole.
In conclusion, I largely disagree that researchers should focus their work on the areas likely to benefit the greatest number of people.
The surprising value of mRNA and GPS, the needs of patients with rare diseases, and the narrow case of widespread epidemics all shape this position.
Science serves humanity best when it leaves room for curiosity and compassion, not only for counting heads.

essays.title: Consensus usually beats elusive ideals

paragraphs.text: In politics, the perfect plan is often the enemy of the plan that can actually pass.
This tension lies behind the recommendation that politicians should pursue common ground and reasonable consensus rather than elusive ideals.
I largely agree with this recommendation, because consensus usually produces lasting and practical results, although compromise on basic rights would be wrong.
The strength of inclusive governing, the success of cooperation on shared problems, and the special case of fundamental injustice shape my position.
First, in a divided government, seeking common ground is advantageous because it turns opponents into partners.
Abraham Lincoln appointed his political rivals, including William Seward, to his cabinet, choosing able critics over loyal followers.
Rather than surround himself with people who shared his views, he built a team that represented different factions and could test his decisions.
His critics could warn him of mistakes that loyal followers might have hidden.

Similarly, a provincial health director in Vietnam who invites both hospital managers and private pharmacists to design an antibiotic policy is more likely to see it followed than one who issues orders alone.
These cases show that consensus is not weakness; it is a [[pragmatic|pragmatic]] way to make decisions that survive opposition.
Moreover, people who helped shape a policy are more likely to defend it later, whereas ideals that [[alienate|alienate]] half the population rarely become lasting policy.
Second, when a problem crosses borders or parties, adopting this recommendation is advantageous because cooperation is the only path to success.
Smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980 after a coordinated global WHO vaccination campaign that relied on countries sharing data and vaccine.
Governments with very different political systems set aside their disagreements to reach a shared goal.
No single country could have eliminated the disease alone, because the virus did not respect borders.
Likewise, Vietnam's 2007 law requiring motorbike helmets raised helmet use from low levels to over 90% within months, a change that worked only because riders across the country accepted it.
Had the law faced strong public resistance, it would have been far harder to enforce on the roads.
These cases show that reasonable consensus can [[engender|engender]] results that no single faction could achieve on its own.
A leader who insists on ideological purity in such situations risks achieving nothing at all.
Admittedly, there are circumstances in which pursuing consensus would not be advantageous, particularly when basic rights are at stake.
In the Montgomery bus boycott (1955-1956), Black residents refused for over a year to ride segregated buses, and their stand helped end bus segregation in that city.
A "reasonable" middle ground with segregation would have been [[unconscionable|unconscionable]]; in that situation, firm commitment to an ideal of equality was more valuable than any compromise.
Nevertheless, such cases are exceptions that concern fundamental rights, not the everyday business of governing.
Most political decisions involve trade-offs between reasonable interests rather than a choice between justice and injustice.
On most questions, such as budgets, health programs or transport, consensus produces better outcomes than [[quixotic|quixotic]] ideals.
This exception therefore qualifies my position without overturning it: politicians should treat basic rights as limits on compromise while seeking common ground on everything else.
In conclusion, I largely agree that politicians should usually seek common ground rather than chase elusive ideals.
Lincoln's inclusive cabinet, global cooperation against smallpox and the success of Vietnam's helmet law show the value of consensus, while the Montgomery bus boycott marks its moral limit.
Wise politicians should compromise on methods but never on basic human dignity.

essays.title: Ideals, not consensus, drive real progress

paragraphs.text: Many reforms that we now take for granted once seemed unrealistic.
This history challenges the recommendation that politicians should pursue common ground and reasonable consensus rather than elusive ideals.
I largely disagree with this recommendation, because clear ideals are often what move societies forward, although consensus is valuable for carrying out reforms once their direction is set.
The role of principled pressure in ending injustice, the need for bold reform when the status quo fails, and the practical value of consensus shape this view.
First, adopting this recommendation would be disadvantageous when a society faces a clear injustice, because consensus often protects existing arrangements.
In the Montgomery bus boycott (1955-1956), Black residents refused for over a year to ride segregated buses.
They sought an end to segregation, not a moderate middle ground, and the boycott helped end bus segregation in that city.
A compromise that kept segregated seating in a milder form would have left the injustice in place.

Similarly, after the Tuskegee syphilis study withheld treatment from Black men without their informed consent, it was public outrage, not quiet compromise, that led to US rules requiring ethics review boards.
These cases show that on questions of justice, a firm ideal can [[galvanize|galvanize]] citizens far more effectively than a careful compromise.
Consensus is valuable among people who disagree reasonably, but it cannot be the goal when one side defends a clear wrong.
Second, in circumstances where existing policies have clearly failed, politicians should pursue bold change rather than settle for small adjustments.
Before 1986, Vietnam relied on central planning and faced food shortages.

The Doi Moi reforms, an [[audacious|audacious]] break with the past, replaced central planning with market incentives, and the country became one of the world's largest rice exporters as poverty fell dramatically.
A cautious adjustment to central planning would probably not have produced such results.

Likewise, a health minister who wants to end over-the-counter antibiotic sales may find that a compromise with every seller leaves the core problem untouched, because such sales help resistant bacteria spread.
These cases show that a clear goal, firmly pursued, can achieve what [[timorous|timorous]] compromise cannot.
Leaders who seek only consensus risk preserving a failing [[status quo|status quo]], because a politician who waits for everyone to agree may wait forever.
Admittedly, consensus is advantageous when a reform must be carried out over many years by people with different views.
Abraham Lincoln appointed his political rivals, including William Seward, to his cabinet, choosing able critics over loyal followers.
Nevertheless, Lincoln used consensus as a tool to pursue his goals, not as a [[surrogate|surrogate]] for them.
Similarly, a city council may need broad agreement to fund a new metro line, but agreement on the details should not shrink the line until it serves no one.
This shows that consensus works best in service of an ideal; it should shape the methods of reform, not lower its goals.

When consensus becomes the goal itself, politicians tend to choose whatever offends the fewest people, even when it solves nothing; I therefore accept consensus as a means while rejecting it as an end.
In conclusion, I largely disagree that politicians should prefer consensus to ideals.
The Montgomery bus boycott, the outrage after Tuskegee and the Doi Moi reforms show that ambitious goals drive progress, while Lincoln's cabinet shows that consensus is best used to achieve them.
Politicians should therefore hold firmly to their ideals while staying flexible about the means.

essays.title: Think first, especially when others bear risk

paragraphs.text: Bold action is often admired, but its costs usually fall on people who never chose the risk.
This is why the recommendation that people should undertake risky action only after carefully considering its consequences deserves serious attention.
I largely agree with this recommendation, especially when actions affect the health or safety of others, although in true emergencies careful thought must happen in advance.
The dangers of untested medical decisions, the value of testing new ideas before scaling them up, and the special pressure of emergencies shape my position.
First, when an action could harm many people, careful consideration of its consequences is clearly advantageous.
Thalidomide, a sedative given to pregnant women around 1960, caused severe birth defects in thousands of babies in Europe.
In the United States, however, Frances Kelsey of the FDA refused to approve the drug, and the country then passed stricter drug-testing rules in 1962.
Her caution protected many American families from [[grievous|grievous]] harm.
A faster approval might have exposed American mothers and babies to the same tragedy.
Similarly, a doctor who prescribes antibiotics carelessly may help one patient today while helping resistant bacteria spread to many others.
These cases show that the people who bear the consequences of a risky decision are often not the ones who make it, which is exactly why decision-makers must think first.
Careful thought costs a little time, while careless action can cost lives that cannot be restored.
Second, in settings where a new idea is promising but uncertain, testing it carefully before acting on a large scale is advantageous.
Releasing mosquitoes carrying Wolbachia bacteria, which block dengue transmission, was a novel intervention with uncertain effects.
Researchers tested it in a randomized trial in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, where it cut dengue cases by 77%, and the method has also been tested in Vietnam.
Because the consequences were measured first, health officials can now [[advocate|advocate]] the method with confidence.
Likewise, the Wright brothers achieved the first powered flight in 1903 only after years of careful experiments with gliders and a wind tunnel they built themselves.
Each glider test answered a small question before they risked their lives on a powered machine.
Their caution did not prevent bold action; it made bold action survivable.
Careful consideration is therefore not the opposite of risk-taking but its [[prudent|prudent]] companion.
Admittedly, in some circumstances long deliberation would not be advantageous, because delay itself carries risk.
In an emergency department, a physician treating a patient in septic shock must start antibiotics within minutes, not after a long period of reflection.
Waiting to consider every possible consequence would cost the patient's life.
Nevertheless, even in emergencies, good decisions rest on consequences that were considered in advance.
Hospitals prepare protocols, and physicians train for years, precisely so that they can act quickly without acting blindly.
Similarly, disaster teams rehearse evacuation plans long before any flood or storm arrives.

Thus, the emergency case does not reject the recommendation; it shows that careful consideration can happen before the crisis, allowing swift and [[judicious|judicious]] action when the crisis arrives.
In this sense, the recommendation still holds, but its timing changes: the careful thinking is done before the risk appears.
In conclusion, I largely agree that people should take risky action only after carefully weighing its consequences.

Frances Kelsey's caution, the careful testing of Wolbachia and the Wright brothers' experiments show the value of forethought, while emergencies show that this forethought must sometimes happen in advance.
Risk is unavoidable in medicine, science and daily life, but [[foolhardy|foolhardy]] risk is not.

words.meaning_here: careful and sensible about the future

essays.title: Sometimes delay is the greater risk

paragraphs.text: Caution is usually praised as a virtue, but too much caution can be costly.
This tension complicates the recommendation that people should undertake risky action only after they have carefully considered its consequences.

I largely disagree with this recommendation as a general rule, because in many situations delay is more dangerous than action, although careful thought remains essential when others' lives are at stake.
The cost of hesitation in business, the need for quick action in emergencies and moral struggles, and the real value of caution in drug safety shape this position.
First, in fast-changing industries, insisting on full consideration of every consequence would not be advantageous, because opportunities disappear while leaders deliberate.
Kodak engineer Steven Sasson invented the digital camera in 1975.
However, Kodak, protecting its profitable film business, was slow to embrace digital photography and filed for bankruptcy in 2012.
While its leaders [[dithered|dither]] over the risk to film sales, the market moved on without them.
Similarly, a small startup that waits for perfect market research before launching may find that a rival has already captured its customers.
In fast markets, a good decision made today is often better than a perfect decision made next year.
These cases show that in competitive settings, the consequences of inaction can be just as serious as the consequences of risky action.
Careful thought is valuable, but when it becomes endless, it turns into a decision to do nothing.
Second, the recommendation is impractical in emergencies and moral struggles, where the full consequences cannot be known in advance.
In the Montgomery bus boycott (1955-1956), Black residents refused for over a year to ride segregated buses, and the boycott helped end bus segregation in that city.
Had they waited until every consequence was clear, the injustice would have continued.
They chose to act even though they could not predict exactly how the city would respond.
Likewise, during a dengue outbreak in a Vietnamese district, health workers must begin clearing mosquito breeding sites immediately, even before they know how large the outbreak will become.
These cases show that when the cost of waiting is high, an [[inordinate|inordinate]] demand for certainty becomes a form of paralysis.
Courage often means taking [[audacious|audacious]] action on the best available judgment rather than on complete knowledge.
Admittedly, careful consideration is advantageous when an action could cause severe and lasting harm to others.
Thalidomide, a sedative given to pregnant women around 1960, caused severe birth defects in thousands of babies in Europe, while Frances Kelsey of the US FDA refused to approve it.
In that case, careful review clearly protected many families from tragedy.
Nevertheless, this example concerns a special category of decisions, those whose harms are both [[grievous|grievous]] and permanent.
A drug given to pregnant women cannot be taken back once the damage is done.
Drug approval requires deep caution, but most everyday risks, such as starting a business or joining a peaceful protest, do not.
Applying the same standard to all of them would make people [[timorous|timorous]] and slow, so this case narrows my position rather than reversing it.
In conclusion, I largely disagree that people should take risky action only after carefully considering every consequence.
Kodak's decline, the Montgomery bus boycott and outbreak response show that delay can be costly, while thalidomide shows when deep caution is truly necessary.
The wiser rule is to match the depth of deliberation to the size of the possible harm.
