essays.title: Demands forge leaders from ordinary people

paragraphs.text: Few people wake up one day and decide to become leaders; more often, leadership finds them.
This observation supports the statement that leaders are created by the demands that are placed on them.

I largely agree with this statement, because pressure and responsibility develop leadership skills that few people possess beforehand, although demands can only build on qualities a person already has.
The way crises turn ordinary people into leaders, the way responsibility teaches leadership through practice, and the limits set by personal character shape this view.
First, the statement holds true in crises, which often turn ordinary people into leaders.
During the Montgomery bus boycott (1955-1956), Black residents refused for over a year to ride segregated buses.
Keeping a boycott alive for so long demanded organization and courage from community members who were not professional politicians, and the struggle helped end bus segregation in that city.
Similarly, in my experience with dengue outbreaks in Vietnam, junior doctors asked to coordinate village health workers often grow into confident leaders within weeks.
Before the outbreak, many of them had never managed anyone; the demands of the situation taught them how.
These cases show that demands do not merely reveal leadership; they [[elicit|elicit]] and shape it.
People who never sought authority discovered abilities they did not know they had, abilities that might never have developed without the crisis.
Second, leadership is largely learned through practice, and demands provide that practice.
Consider Frances Kelsey of the US FDA, who had to decide whether to approve thalidomide, a sedative given to pregnant women around 1960.
She refused, while in Europe the drug caused severe birth defects in thousands of babies, and the US then passed stricter drug-testing rules in 1962.
The demands of her position required her to stand firm, and her decision made her a model of scientific leadership.
Likewise, a manager promoted to run a struggling clinic learns to set priorities only because the clinic's problems force her to.
She has no formal training in leadership, but each problem gives her a lesson that no course could teach.
This shows that leadership is less an [[inborn|inborn]] gift than a skill developed under pressure.
The more [[exacting|exacting]] the demands, the more fully that skill develops.
Admittedly, the statement does not fully hold true, because demands alone cannot create a leader out of someone who lacks judgment.

Kodak's leaders faced a clear demand when their own engineer, Steven Sasson, invented the digital camera in 1975, yet the company, protecting its profitable film business, was slow to embrace digital photography and filed for bankruptcy in 2012.
Nevertheless, this failure shows that demands are necessary but not sufficient, not that they are unimportant.
A demand creates an opportunity to lead, but a person must still choose to meet it.

Because some people respond to pressure by growing while others [[buckle|buckle]] or [[equivocate|equivocate]], demands are best understood as a [[catalyst|catalyst]] that turns potential into leadership.
This qualification refines my agreement: demands create leaders, but only from the material they are given.
In conclusion, I largely agree that leaders are created by the demands placed on them, provided that those demands meet people with basic judgment and resolve.
The Montgomery boycott, outbreak response in Vietnam and Frances Kelsey's stand show how pressure builds leaders, while Kodak shows that pressure alone is not enough.
Organizations that want strong leaders should therefore give capable people real responsibility early.

essays.title: Demands reveal leaders rather than create them

paragraphs.text: Every crisis produces people who rise to the occasion and people who collapse under it.
This difference challenges the statement that leaders are created by the demands that are placed on them.
I largely disagree with this statement, because demands reveal and test leadership rather than create it, although pressure can sharpen abilities that already exist.
The importance of preparation, the decisive role of judgment, and the real but limited power of crises shape this position.
First, the statement does not hold true because effective leadership usually rests on preparation that comes long before any demand.
Marie Curie won Nobel Prizes in both physics (1903) and chemistry (1911) despite the barriers women faced in science at the time.
Her leadership in a new field did not appear suddenly in response to a single demand; it grew from years of [[sedulous|sedulous]] work and the confidence that such work builds.
Similarly, a hospital director who calmly manages a sudden outbreak is usually someone who spent years learning the hospital's systems and earning the trust of its staff.
When the crisis comes, the director draws on that preparation rather than inventing leadership on the spot.
These cases show that demands call on [[latent|latent]] leadership, but they do not supply it.
A person who has not prepared has little to offer when the moment arrives.
Second, demands frequently fail to create leaders, which suggests that the decisive factor is personal judgment.
Kodak engineer Steven Sasson invented the digital camera in 1975, presenting the company's leaders with an obvious challenge.
Yet Kodak, protecting its profitable film business, was slow to embrace digital photography and filed for bankruptcy in 2012.
The demand was clear, but the leadership needed to meet it never appeared.

By contrast, Abraham Lincoln appointed his political rivals, including William Seward, to his cabinet, choosing able critics over loyal followers, a decision that reflected his own judgment and confidence.
His judgment was not created by the pressures of office; it was what allowed him to handle those pressures.
Both Kodak's executives and Lincoln faced heavy demands, but only Lincoln responded wisely.
If demands alone created leaders, such [[disparate|disparate]] outcomes would be hard to explain; the key variable was the person, not the pressure.
Admittedly, demands can strengthen and refine leadership, and sometimes they draw people into roles they would never have chosen.
Consider a senior nurse who, during a severe flood, is the only experienced staff member able to reach her district hospital and must organize the entire ward.
Within days, she may learn to delegate, negotiate for supplies and comfort frightened families.
Nevertheless, she succeeds because she already has clinical knowledge and a sense of responsibility; another person in the same position might become anxious and [[irresolute|irresolute]].
The flood did not give her these qualities; it gave her a stage on which to use them.
Thus, demands act as a test that [[winnows|winnow]] capable leaders from the rest.
They amplify existing qualities rather than create new ones, which is why I see them as a secondary rather than a primary cause of leadership.
In conclusion, I largely disagree that leaders are created by the demands placed on them.
Marie Curie's long preparation, the contrast between Kodak and Lincoln, and the case of a nurse tested by a flood all show that character and preparation matter more than pressure.
Societies that want good leaders should invest in education and character long before the crisis comes.

essays.title: Costly rescues rarely justify their human price

paragraphs.text: Every society must decide what it values most when its resources are limited.
Few decisions test this more sharply than the choice of whether to spend heavily on protecting endangered animals and plants.

I largely agree that there is little justification for extraordinary efforts to save endangered species, especially at a great cost in money and jobs, as long as basic conservation continues and species with clear value to humans remain protected.
This position rests on the limits of public budgets, the human cost of lost jobs and the existence of cheaper ways to protect nature, although the hidden value of some species qualifies my view.
First, extraordinary conservation efforts are hard to justify because money spent on one species is money not spent on [[pressing|pressing]] human needs.
In my work as an epidemiologist in Vietnam, I have seen provincial health offices struggle to fund basic dengue control, such as larval surveys and community clean-up campaigns.
When budgets are this tight, a program that costs millions to protect a single rare bird competes directly with programs that keep children out of the hospital.
In such settings, every dollar has a visible human cost, and officials who [[countenance|countenance]] large conservation budgets while clinics lack staff will rightly face public anger.
Similarly, a poor district that must choose between a new clinic and an expensive breeding center for an endangered turtle can hardly be blamed for choosing the clinic.
This shows that when the costs are extraordinary, the lost opportunities in human health and welfare make such efforts difficult to defend.
Second, the statement holds true because the burden of extraordinary efforts often falls on the workers who can least afford it.
Consider a logging town whose forest is suddenly closed to protect a rare owl.
Hundreds of families may lose their only source of income overnight, and young people may leave for the cities, leaving behind a community in decline.
Retraining programs can help, but they are slow, and older workers rarely find jobs that pay as well as the ones they lost.
Vietnam's own history shows how much such livelihoods matter: after the Doi Moi reforms of 1986 replaced central planning with market incentives, poverty fell dramatically over the following decades.

These cases suggest that the cost in jobs is not a minor detail but a central reason to [[eschew|eschew]] the most extreme conservation measures, since hard-won gains in rural income can disappear quickly.
Admittedly, the statement does not hold true when a species may offer benefits that we cannot yet see.
In 1928, Alexander Fleming noticed that a mold killed bacteria on a culture plate, and this observation eventually led to penicillin.
Had that organism vanished before anyone studied it, one of the most important drugs in history might never have existed.
Nevertheless, this argument supports reasonable, low-cost protection, such as seed banks, protected areas and scientific surveys, rather than extraordinary efforts at any price.
Modest measures can preserve most of this hidden value while avoiding [[prohibitive|prohibitive]] costs to workers and taxpayers.
Therefore, the possibility of future benefits [[qualifies|qualify]] my position, but it does not overturn it.
In conclusion, society has little reason to make extraordinary and costly efforts to save every endangered species, although it should not abandon conservation altogether.
Limited budgets, the real cost to workers and the availability of cheaper alternatives all point toward a more [[pragmatic|pragmatic]] approach.
The wisest policy, therefore, is to protect nature steadily and sensibly rather than at any price.

essays.title: Saving species is an investment, not a luxury

paragraphs.text: Humans have always depended on the living world for food, medicine and a stable environment.
Yet when protecting that world becomes expensive, some argue that society should simply let endangered species disappear.

I largely disagree with the claim that there is little justification for extraordinary efforts to save endangered species, although such efforts should be designed to limit their cost in money and jobs.
Species may hold medical value that no one can predict, human livelihoods depend on healthy ecosystems, and the cost to jobs is usually more manageable than critics suggest.
First, extraordinary efforts are justified because a single species may hold benefits that no one can foresee.
Alexander Fleming noticed in 1928 that a mold killed bacteria on a culture plate.
Years later, Howard Florey and Ernst Chain's team developed this observation into penicillin during World War II, and the drug went on to save countless lives.
Penicillin did not come from a famous or obviously useful organism; it came from a common mold that most people would have ignored.

Similarly, the Wolbachia bacteria carried by some insects have become a tool against dengue: releasing mosquitoes carrying Wolbachia cut dengue cases by 77% in a randomized trial in Yogyakarta, Indonesia.
No one studying these bacteria decades ago could have predicted that they would one day protect people in tropical cities.
This shows that the value of a living organism is often [[latent|latent]], and once a species is extinct, that value is lost permanently.
Second, the statement overlooks the fact that whole ecosystems, not isolated species, support human welfare.
Consider a coastal province that clears its mangrove forests to build shrimp farms.
If the fish and crabs that breed among the roots disappear, local fishers lose their income, and nearby villages lose a natural barrier against storms.
Fishers in such a province may see their catches shrink without ever learning which species disappeared.
Likewise, when pollinating insects decline, farmers must pay for costly substitutes or accept smaller harvests.
These cases reveal that the loss of one species can [[undermine|undermine]] an entire system on which jobs and health depend, so protecting it is often an investment rather than a luxury.
Protecting endangered species, in this sense, often means protecting the people who live beside them.
Admittedly, the statement holds some truth when the costs fall heavily on poor communities.

A sudden ban on logging or fishing can leave families without income, and in a country like Vietnam, where many people escaped poverty only in recent decades, such losses are [[nontrivial|nontrivial]].
Nevertheless, this problem argues for better policy design, not for abandoning endangered species.
Governments can hire displaced workers as forest rangers, support ecotourism or introduce restrictions gradually so that communities have time to adjust.
In other words, the cost in jobs is a reason to share the burden fairly, but it does not show that the effort itself lacks justification.
Moreover, a well-designed program can turn conservation into a new source of jobs rather than merely a threat to old ones.
In conclusion, society has strong reasons to make serious, even extraordinary, efforts to protect endangered species, provided that it [[mitigates|mitigate]] the costs for workers.
The unpredictable value of species, the dependence of human livelihoods on healthy ecosystems and the availability of fair ways to manage job losses all support this view.
What is truly hard to justify is the permanent loss of a species in exchange for a modest saving in the short term.

essays.title: Machines serve purposes; minds choose them

paragraphs.text: Almost every major technology, from the printing press to the smartphone, has raised the fear that machines might one day replace their makers.
Today, with computers that can write, translate and help diagnose disease, the question of whether the human mind will remain superior feels more urgent than ever.
I largely agree that the human mind will remain superior to machines because machines are tools of human purposes, as long as superiority means judgment and purpose rather than raw speed.
Machines depend on goals that people set, they cannot weigh values in new situations, and even their impressive successes occur within limits that humans define.
First, the human mind remains superior because machines carry out goals that people choose; they do not choose those goals themselves.
GPS was built by the US military, and only after it was opened to civilians did it become the basis of everyday navigation, ride-hailing and delivery apps.
The satellites did not decide to serve taxi drivers; people saw a new use for an existing tool and built entire businesses around it.
A delivery app optimizes routes, but a person still decided that fast delivery was worth building in the first place.
Similarly, a computer program that reads chest X-rays searches only for the patterns its designers trained it to find.
This shows that machines extend human purposes rather than create their own, which is exactly what it means to be a tool.
Second, human judgment is superior when a situation demands weighing values that no data set contains.
In my clinical work, I have treated patients whose test results suggested one treatment, while their poverty, family duties or beliefs made another option wiser.
A good physician combines the numbers with the person, and this kind of judgment is difficult to [[distill|distill]] into a formula.

Likewise, when Frances Kelsey of the US FDA refused to approve thalidomide, a sedative that later caused severe birth defects in thousands of babies in Europe, she relied on careful skepticism rather than a fixed rule.
Her caution, which helped lead the US to pass stricter drug-testing rules in 1962, came from human judgment about risk, not from a calculation.
These cases suggest that the most important decisions require a [[discerning|discerning]] mind that understands what is at stake for real people.
Admittedly, the statement does not hold true for narrow tasks, where machines already outperform the human mind.
A calculator multiplies faster than any mathematician, and a navigation app finds the quickest route through a crowded city better than most drivers.
In some hospitals, software can also flag abnormal scans faster than a busy radiologist.
Nevertheless, speed and accuracy in a defined task are not the same as superiority of mind.
A machine that excels at one task cannot decide whether that task is worth doing, and it cannot take responsibility when it fails.

Therefore, these successes [[qualify|qualify]] my position: machines may be superior instruments, but they remain instruments, and the more powerful they become, the more society needs human minds to decide how to use them.
In conclusion, the human mind is likely to remain superior to machines in the ways that matter most, even if machines surpass us in speed and memory.
Machines pursue goals that humans set, lack the judgment to weigh human values, and excel only within boundaries that we draw.
The real challenge, then, is not to fear machines but to use them [[judiciously|judicious]] in the service of human aims, rather than to surrender those aims to them.

essays.title: Being a tool does not mean inferior

paragraphs.text: The word "always" is a risky one in any prediction about technology.
The claim that the human mind will always be superior to machines, simply because machines are tools, makes exactly this kind of prediction.
I mostly disagree with this statement, because being a tool does not prevent a machine from surpassing its maker, although humans should keep control over the purposes that machines serve.

Tools have long exceeded human abilities, the human mind has systematic weaknesses that machines can avoid, and the word "always" ignores how quickly machines improve, even if they still lack human values.
First, the reason given in the statement is weak, because a tool can be superior to its maker in the very task for which it was built.

The Wright brothers, bicycle makers without college degrees, achieved the first powered airplane flight in 1903 after years of careful experiments with gliders and a wind tunnel they built themselves.
Their airplane was a tool of their minds, yet it could do something that no human body could ever do.
Telescopes see farther than any eye, and microscopes reveal what no unaided observer could detect.
Similarly, GPS, first built by the US military, now guides millions of drivers through unfamiliar cities more reliably than their own memory.
This shows that being a tool and being superior are not [[antithetical|antithetical]]; in fact, people build tools precisely to exceed their own limits.
Second, the statement does not hold true because the human mind has systematic weaknesses that machines can avoid.
In 1847, Ignaz Semmelweis had doctors wash their hands in chlorinated lime, and deaths from childbed fever on his ward fell sharply.
Yet most of his colleagues rejected his idea, because human minds tend to defend [[ingrained|ingrained]] beliefs even against clear evidence.
His idea was vindicated by germ theory only years after his death, long after many more mothers had died.
Likewise, when a large collaboration in 2015 tried to repeat 100 published psychology studies, it reproduced the results of only about a third of them.
Human researchers, eager for striking results, had published findings that did not hold up.
A system that tracks every outcome without pride or fatigue could flag such errors earlier, which suggests that machines may sometimes prove more [[dispassionate|dispassionate]] judges than people.
Admittedly, the statement holds true in one important respect: machines do not choose their own goals or understand why those goals matter.
A program can recommend a treatment, but it cannot feel responsible to a frightened patient or decide what a society owes its poorest members.
Nevertheless, this shows that humans must remain in charge of values, not that the human mind will always be superior overall.
Moreover, machines already help write software and design new molecules, tasks once reserved for human experts.
As machines improve, the range of tasks in which people stay ahead is likely to shrink, so the word "always" is hard to [[substantiate|substantiate]].
This concession therefore narrows my disagreement without reversing it, since the statement confuses the question of who sets the goals with the question of who performs best.
In conclusion, the claim that the human mind will always be superior to machines rests on a weak reason and an overconfident prediction.
Tools routinely exceed their makers, human reasoning has clear flaws, and only in setting goals and values do people hold a firm advantage.
Instead of assuming permanent superiority, we should decide carefully which tasks to give to machines and which to keep for ourselves.

essays.title: True believers make the sharpest critics

paragraphs.text: We often assume that the strongest supporters of an idea are also the least likely to criticize it.
However, the relationship between commitment and criticism may be the reverse, as the statement suggests.

I largely agree that the people most deeply committed to an idea or policy are often its sharpest critics, as long as their commitment is to the idea's purpose rather than to their own status or group.
Committed people know an idea's weaknesses best and care most about its success, although blind loyalty shows where the statement fails.
First, the statement holds true because deep commitment brings deep knowledge, and knowledge reveals flaws that casual supporters miss.
Alexander Fleming noticed in 1928 that a mold killed bacteria, and he became closely identified with penicillin, the drug that grew out of his discovery.
Yet in his 1945 Nobel lecture, at the height of his fame, he warned that misuse would breed resistant bacteria.
He understood better than anyone how powerful the drug was, and for that very reason he saw the danger of careless use.

Similarly, in my own field, the physicians who most strongly [[champion|champion]] antibiotics for serious infections are also the loudest critics of over-the-counter sales, which help resistant bacteria spread in Vietnam and elsewhere.
This shows that the people who understand an idea best are often the first to see how it can go wrong.
Shallow supporters, by contrast, rarely know enough to notice such problems.
Second, committed people criticize an idea because they want it to succeed, not because they want it to fail.
In 2015, a large collaboration tried to repeat 100 published psychology studies and reproduced the results of only about a third of them.
This uncomfortable finding came from researchers who believed in their discipline and wanted its results to be more reliable.
They did not abandon psychology; they pushed it toward more careful methods.
Likewise, a health officer who believes deeply in a vaccination program is usually the first to report a weak supply chain or a missed group of children.
Such criticism is demanding, but its aim is to strengthen the program.
These examples suggest that [[candid|candid]] criticism from committed people is a form of loyalty, because it protects the idea from errors that could later [[discredit|discredit]] it.
Admittedly, the statement does not hold true when commitment turns into blind loyalty.

When Ignaz Semmelweis showed in 1847 that hand washing in chlorinated lime sharply reduced deaths from childbed fever, most of his colleagues, committed to [[orthodox|orthodox]] views of disease, rejected his idea instead of questioning their own.
Their loyalty was to familiar habits, and that loyalty made them [[impervious|impervious]] to evidence that challenged them.
Nevertheless, these doctors were committed less to medicine's real goal, healing patients, than to their own authority and habits.
Their case therefore refines my position rather than refuting it.
People committed to an idea's purpose tend to criticize it, while people committed to their own standing tend to defend it at any cost.
In conclusion, I largely agree that those most deeply committed to an idea or policy are often its most serious critics, provided that their commitment is to its purpose.
Their knowledge exposes flaws, their concern for success motivates honest criticism, and only when loyalty replaces purpose does the pattern break down.
Leaders who want their ideas to last should therefore listen most closely to their most committed critics, not only to those who offer praise.

essays.title: Commitment usually breeds defense, not criticism

paragraphs.text: Most people find it far easier to criticize ideas they dislike than ideas they love.
This common experience raises doubts about the claim that those most deeply committed to an idea or policy are also its harshest critics.
I mostly disagree with this statement, because deep commitment usually leads people to defend an idea rather than question it, although some committed experts are indeed its sharpest critics.

Commitment creates personal stakes, committed groups tend to silence outside criticism, and the most useful critics are therefore often outsiders, even though a few committed insiders prove the exception.
First, the statement often fails because deep commitment gives people a personal stake in an idea's success.
Kodak engineer Steven Sasson invented the digital camera in 1975, but Kodak, protecting its profitable film business, was slow to embrace digital photography.
The company's leaders were deeply committed to film, and that commitment kept them from seeing its weaknesses until Kodak filed for bankruptcy in 2012.
Film had made the company rich for decades, so admitting its decline meant admitting that much of its future was at risk.
Similarly, a researcher who has spent ten years on one hypothesis may [[construe|construe]] every [[ambiguous|ambiguous]] result as support for it.
Such a researcher is not dishonest; rather, years of effort make it painful to accept that the hypothesis may be wrong.
This shows that commitment tends to bend judgment toward defense, which is the opposite of what the statement claims.
Second, groups that are deeply committed to an idea tend to punish critics rather than become critics themselves.
In 1633, the Church forced Galileo to [[recant|recant]] his support for the idea that the Earth moves around the sun.
Those most committed to the established view did not reexamine it; instead, they silenced the person who questioned it.
Their commitment made them less critical, not more.
Likewise, after Ignaz Semmelweis showed in 1847 that hand washing sharply reduced deaths from childbed fever, most doctors rejected his idea, which germ theory vindicated only years after his death.
The cost of their certainty was paid by the patients who continued to die while the debate dragged on.
These cases suggest that strong commitment can harden into [[dogma|dogma]], and dogma treats criticism as a threat rather than a contribution.
Admittedly, some deeply committed people are also sharp critics of their own ideas.
Alexander Fleming, whose discovery led to penicillin, warned in his 1945 Nobel lecture that misuse would breed resistant bacteria.
His warning shows that commitment and criticism can coexist in a single, unusually honest mind.
Nevertheless, such figures are admirable precisely because they are rare.
Abraham Lincoln seemed to understand this, since he appointed political rivals such as William Seward to his cabinet, choosing able critics over loyal followers.

If committed supporters were naturally the most critical, Lincoln would not have needed to look beyond his circle; his choice suggests that useful criticism usually comes from people with some distance from an idea.
Committed critics exist, but they are the exception that a wise leader must seek out, not the rule that the statement describes.
In conclusion, I mostly disagree that those most committed to an idea or policy are its most critical observers.
Commitment creates stakes that bias judgment, committed groups often suppress [[dissent|dissent]], and the few committed critics are notable exceptions rather than the rule.
Anyone who wants honest feedback on an idea should therefore seek out thoughtful skeptics, not only devoted supporters, whose loyalty may blind them to an idea's flaws.

essays.title: Extinction is permanent, so try to save all

paragraphs.text: Extinction is one of the few changes that human beings can never undo.
For this reason, the debate over how much society should spend to save endangered plants and animals deserves careful thought.

My position aligns more closely with the first view, that society should try to save every species despite the cost, as long as "every" is understood as a serious effort for each species rather than unlimited spending on any one of them.
The value of a species is often unpredictable, ambitious collective efforts have succeeded before, and extinction is permanent, although the second view rightly warns about the burden on workers.
First, the first view is persuasive because no one can predict which species will prove valuable to humans.

Wolbachia, a type of bacteria once of interest mainly to specialists, is now used against dengue: releasing mosquitoes carrying it cut dengue cases by 77% in a randomized trial in Yogyakarta, Indonesia.
The method has also been tested in Vietnam, where dengue remains a serious burden on families and hospitals.
Similarly, in 1928 Alexander Fleming noticed that a common mold killed bacteria on a culture plate, an observation that eventually led to penicillin.
Few people would have expected such an ordinary organism to become the source of one of the most important drugs in history.
Extinction would have erased such possibilities before anyone could test them.
This shows that the worth of a living thing often appears only in hindsight, which is why society should hesitate before letting any species disappear.
Second, the first view is realistic because coordinated efforts that seem extraordinary have succeeded before.
Smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980 after a global WHO vaccination campaign that relied on countries sharing data and vaccine.
Few people at the start believed that a disease could be removed from the entire planet, yet patient cooperation achieved it.
Conservation can follow the same model, with countries sharing data on threatened species and funding protection together.
Likewise, Vietnam's 2007 helmet law raised helmet use to over 90% within months, showing that societies can change behavior quickly when they commit to a goal.
These achievements suggest that the cost of saving species is not fixed; with [[assiduous|assiduous]] planning and cooperation, goals that look [[quixotic|quixotic]] can become [[feasible|feasible]].
Admittedly, the second view gets something important right: the costs of conservation often fall on people who can least afford them.
A fishing village banned from its traditional grounds to protect a rare species may lose its main source of income, and promises of future benefits will not feed its children today.
Nevertheless, this problem calls for sharing the cost more fairly, not for giving up on endangered species.
Governments can compensate affected workers, hire them as rangers or develop ecotourism that rewards protection.
Jobs, unlike species, can be replaced, so the second view's concern should shape how society protects species rather than whether it does.
A worker who loses a job can be retrained, whereas a species that disappears is gone forever.
In conclusion, I side more closely with the view that society should try to save every species, even at considerable cost, while making sure that workers do not bear that cost alone.
The hidden value of species, the record of successful global efforts and the permanence of extinction outweigh the second view's valid concerns.
A society that can [[husband|husband]] its resources wisely should be able to protect both its people and the living world they depend on.

words.meaning_here: idealistic to the point of seeming impractical

essays.task_note: The thesis sides with the first view; Bodies 1-2 support it and Body 3 states what the second view gets right (burden on workers) before explaining why the first view is closer to the truth.

essays.title: Protect species wisely, not at any cost

paragraphs.text: Every doctor learns early that resources are limited and that not every patient can receive every possible treatment.
The same hard logic applies when society decides how much to spend on protecting endangered plants and animals.

My position aligns more closely with the second view, that society need not make extraordinary efforts at a great cost in money and jobs to save every species, although it should still protect species of clear ecological or human value.
Resources are finite and must be prioritized, human welfare deserves equal weight, and cheap measures can preserve the hidden value of species that the first view rightly stresses.
First, the second view is more convincing because saving every species is impossible, so society must set priorities.
In epidemiology, we rank health problems by their burden and by how [[feasible|feasible]] they are to control before spending public money.
The global campaign that eradicated smallpox by 1980 succeeded partly because it focused on one achievable target and relied on countries sharing data and vaccine.
Had health workers tried to fight every disease at once, they might have defeated none of them.
Similarly, a conservation agency with a fixed budget will save more species by choosing carefully than by spreading its funds thinly across every case.
This shows that a promise to save every species at any cost is not a moral achievement but a recipe for [[futile|futile]] and wasteful spending.
Second, the second view rightly gives weight to human welfare, which the first view tends to [[slight|slight]].
Vietnam's Doi Moi reforms of 1986 replaced central planning with market incentives, and a country that had faced food shortages became one of the world's largest rice exporters.
That progress depended on farmers, fishers and factory workers being able to earn a living, and many families still depend on that income today.
When such income disappears, families often cut spending on food, schooling and health care, which harms children most.
Likewise, halting a large dam project or closing a fishery to protect a single species can remove the main source of income for an entire region.
These examples suggest that when the cost is counted in jobs and food, extraordinary efforts for every species can harm the most vulnerable people.
Admittedly, the first view makes a fair point: some species turn out to be extremely valuable in ways no one expected.
Wolbachia bacteria, once a narrow topic of research, now help block dengue, and releasing mosquitoes carrying them cut dengue cases by 77% in a trial in Yogyakarta, Indonesia.
Nevertheless, this argues for supporting research and preserving genetic material, which is relatively cheap, rather than for unlimited efforts on behalf of every species.
Seed banks and scientific surveys can capture much of this hidden value at a small fraction of the cost.
Botanical gardens can also preserve living specimens of many plants for future study.
The first view's concern therefore refines my position, but it does not reverse it.
In this way, society can respect the hidden value of species without accepting costs that it cannot bear.
In conclusion, I side with the view that society need not make extraordinary and costly efforts to save every endangered species, while still protecting those of clear value.
Limited resources require priorities, human livelihoods deserve equal concern, and low-cost measures can preserve most of the value that the first view emphasizes.
A [[prudent|prudent]] society protects nature in proportion to its means, not in spite of them.

essays.title: Education exists to set minds free

paragraphs.text: Many people can name a teacher or a book that changed the way they see the world.
Such experiences suggest that education can liberate us, yet critics argue that formal schooling often does the opposite.
My position aligns more closely with the first view, that the purpose of education is to free the mind and the spirit, although formal education fulfills this purpose only when it is well designed.

Education gives people the tools to think independently, it opens opportunities that would otherwise be closed, and the failures that the second view describes come from poor schooling rather than from education itself.
First, the first view is convincing because education provides the tools that independent thinking requires.
My own training in epidemiology taught me to ask how a study was designed before accepting its conclusion.
Before that training, I tended to trust any published result; afterward, I could judge evidence for myself rather than rely on authority.
This habit has made me a more careful [[skeptic|skeptic]] of dramatic health claims, including some that appear in respected journals.

Similarly, when a large collaboration in 2015 repeated 100 published psychology studies and reproduced only about a third of them, it was trained researchers who used their education to expose weak findings.
Their education did not make them obedient; it made them able to [[refute|refute]] weak claims with evidence.
This shows that education, at its best, does not fill the mind with rules but frees it to question them.
Second, education frees the spirit by opening paths that would otherwise remain closed.
Marie Curie won Nobel Prizes in both physics and chemistry despite the barriers that women faced in science at the time.
Her education gave her a way to pursue her curiosity at the highest level, far beyond the limited roles society expected of her.
Learning, for Curie, was not a cage but a way out of the narrow expectations of her society.

Likewise, Finland requires its schoolteachers to hold a master's degree and relies far less on standardized testing than many countries, which allows teachers to encourage curiosity rather than memorization.
Such a system treats students as thinkers rather than test-takers.
These cases suggest that well-designed education can [[kindle|kindle]] ambition and give people real choices about their lives.
Admittedly, the second view correctly observes that formal education often restrains students.
In systems driven by high-stakes exams, students may spend years memorizing answers, learning to fear mistakes rather than to explore ideas.
The Wright brothers, bicycle makers without college degrees, achieved the first powered flight in 1903, a reminder that great minds do not always need formal schooling.
Nevertheless, these problems reveal how education can be poorly delivered, not what its purpose should be.
The remedy for rigid schooling is better education, and the second view's critique is valuable precisely because it shows how schools can [[stymie|stymie]] the very freedom they should foster.
In fact, the very ability to criticize schooling, as the second view does, is itself a product of education that teaches people to think freely.
In conclusion, I side with the view that education exists to free the mind and the spirit, while accepting that formal schooling sometimes falls short of this aim.
Education supplies the tools for independent thought, opens doors to opportunity, and fails mainly when it is reduced to rote testing.
The task, therefore, is not to abandon formal education but to reform it so that it achieves its liberating purpose for every student.

essays.title: Formal schooling too often restrains the mind

paragraphs.text: Children are naturally curious, asking endless questions about how the world works.
Yet by the time many of them finish school, that curiosity seems to have faded, which gives weight to the claim that formal education restrains rather than frees.
My position aligns more closely with the second view, that formal education tends to restrain our minds and spirits, although education in a broader sense can still set people free.
Formal systems reward conformity, institutions of learning often resist new ideas, and the first view, though it describes a worthy ideal, rarely matches what schools actually do.
First, the second view is persuasive because many formal systems reward memorization and conformity rather than independent thought.
When I prepared for my university entrance exam in Vietnam, I spent most of a year memorizing model answers, and asking an unexpected question felt like a waste of valuable time.
I passed, but it took years of research training before I felt comfortable questioning an expert's conclusion.
Many students in exam-driven systems share this experience, learning that the safest strategy is to repeat what the teacher expects.
By contrast, Finland relies far less on standardized testing than many countries, which suggests that heavy testing is a choice rather than a necessity.
Finland also requires its teachers to hold a master's degree, a sign that trusting well-trained teachers can replace rigid control.
This shows that formal education, as it is commonly practiced, often [[inculcates|inculcate]] obedience instead of freeing the mind.
Second, established institutions of learning have often resisted the very ideas that would have expanded human understanding.
In 1847, Ignaz Semmelweis showed that hand washing in chlorinated lime sharply reduced deaths from childbed fever on his ward.
Yet most of his highly educated colleagues rejected his idea, and it was vindicated only years after his death.
Their training had caused their ideas to [[ossify|ossify]], so they could not see the evidence in front of them.
Similarly, the Wright brothers, bicycle makers without college degrees, achieved the first powered flight in 1903 through experiments they designed themselves.
They learned by building, testing and failing, a process that formal schooling rarely encourages.
These cases suggest that formal training can make people [[complacent|complacent]] about what they already know, while freedom from it can encourage original thinking.
Admittedly, the first view captures an important truth: education at its best can be profoundly liberating.
Marie Curie won Nobel Prizes in both physics and chemistry, and her scientific training gave her the means to pursue questions that few people of her time could explore.
Nevertheless, Curie succeeded despite the barriers that women faced in science, which shows how formal institutions restrained even the most gifted students.
Her story therefore shows that the two views are not entirely [[antithetical|antithetical]]: the first describes the goal of education, and the second describes its reality in formal schooling.
A system that frees only the exceptional few who overcome its barriers cannot be said to free the mind in general.
In conclusion, I side with the view that formal education tends to restrain the mind and spirit, even though education in its ideal form should free them.
Exam systems reward conformity, institutions often resist new ideas, and even the liberating ideal of the first view is rarely realized in formal schooling.
Unless schools change how they teach and assess, the liberating purpose of education will remain an ideal rather than a common experience.

uncritically satisfied with oneself or current knowledge

essays.title: Limited, overseen secrecy is sometimes necessary

paragraphs.text: In a democracy, transparency is usually treated as an unquestioned good.
However, leaders sometimes face situations in which releasing information too early or too fully could cause serious harm.

My position aligns more closely with the first view, that it is sometimes necessary for political leaders to withhold information from the public, as long as the secrecy is temporary, limited and subject to independent oversight.
Unverified information can cause panic, some matters of security and negotiation require discretion, and the abuses that the second view fears can be prevented with proper checks.
First, withholding information is sometimes necessary because releasing unverified facts can cause more harm than good.
During a dengue outbreak in my province, early case reports included many patients whose diagnoses were later ruled out.
Had health officials published those raw numbers immediately, they might have triggered panic, crowded hospitals with mild cases and diverted staff from the sickest patients.
In my experience, the most useful message in the first days of an outbreak is a clear, confirmed one, even if it arrives a day later.
Similarly, social media, which let activists organize quickly during the Arab Spring of 2011, also spread misinformation faster than corrections can follow.
Once a false claim spreads, accurate statements struggle to catch up with it.
This shows that a short delay to verify information can be a responsible choice rather than an act of deception.
Second, matters of security and negotiation often require leaders to keep some information private.
Consider a government negotiating the release of citizens held hostage abroad.
If every offer and concession were made public, the other side could exploit the information, and the hostages might pay the price.
Diplomats often need room to explore compromises in private before either side can accept them in public.
Likewise, the details of military operations or of an investigation into a criminal network must often remain confidential until the work is finished.
Revealing the timing of a police raid, for instance, would allow suspects to [[abscond|abscond]] before they could be arrested.
These examples suggest that discretion is sometimes a [[prudent|prudent]] tool of good government, especially when public disclosure would [[abet|abet]] those who mean harm.
Admittedly, the second view raises a serious concern: secrecy can hide abuse.
In the Tuskegee syphilis study, which lasted from 1932 to 1972, treatment was withheld from Black men without their informed consent, and the public learned the truth only decades later.
The harm came not from a short delay but from decades of deliberate deception.
Nevertheless, this case shows the danger of permanent and unchecked secrecy, not of every decision to delay information.
The public outrage that followed led to US rules requiring ethics review boards for research on people, a reminder that oversight can control secrecy without banning it.
The second view, then, correctly demands accountability, but it does not prove that full disclosure is always wise.
Secrecy without oversight invites abuse, but oversight without any secrecy would leave leaders unable to handle real emergencies.

In conclusion, I side with the view that withholding information is sometimes necessary for political leaders, provided that such secrecy is temporary and [[circumscribed|circumscribe]] by independent checks.
Unverified data can cause panic, security and negotiation require discretion, and oversight can prevent the abuses that critics rightly fear.
The real question is not whether leaders may ever withhold information, but who holds them accountable when they do, and for how long.

essays.task_note: The thesis sides with the first view; Bodies 1-2 support it and Body 3 fairly states what the second view gets right (Tuskegee abuse) before explaining why limited, overseen secrecy remains justified.

essays.title: The public's right to know comes first

paragraphs.text: Trust between citizens and their leaders is easy to lose and hard to rebuild.
For this reason, the question of whether leaders may withhold information from the public goes to the heart of democratic government.
My position aligns more closely with the second view, that the public has a right to be fully informed, although a few narrow and temporary exceptions are acceptable.

Secrecy has repeatedly enabled serious abuse, informed citizens cooperate more effectively with public policy, and the first view's valid concerns can be met without abandoning transparency as the rule.
First, the second view is more convincing because secrecy has repeatedly allowed those in power to harm the people they serve.
In the Tuskegee syphilis study, which lasted from 1932 to 1972, researchers withheld treatment from Black men without their informed consent.
The study continued for four decades largely because the public did not know about it, and only public outrage led to rules requiring ethics review boards.
Every year of silence meant more men left without treatment that could have helped them.
Similarly, when information about drug safety is kept from patients, they lose the ability to protect themselves and their families.
Thalidomide, given to pregnant women around 1960, caused severe birth defects in thousands of babies in Europe, which shows how high the stakes of medical information can be.
This shows that the public's right to know is not a luxury but a basic protection against the [[iniquity|iniquity]] of unchecked power.
Second, an informed public cooperates more readily with policies that require collective effort.
Smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980 after a global vaccination campaign that relied on countries sharing data and vaccine.
Countries that hid outbreaks would have allowed the virus to keep spreading across borders.
Without open exchange of information, health workers could not have tracked the disease or persuaded communities to accept vaccination.
Likewise, in my work on dengue control, communities clear mosquito breeding sites far more willingly when officials share accurate case numbers instead of reassuring them with vague statements.
When people understand the risk, they act; when they are kept in the dark, they become [[cynical|cynical]] and stop listening.
These examples suggest that transparency has a [[salutary|salutary]] effect, building the trust on which effective policy depends, while secrecy breeds suspicion and [[apathy|apathy]].
Admittedly, the first view is right that some information must be withheld for a time.
The details of a military operation or a hostage negotiation cannot be published while lives are at risk.
Moreover, social media can spread unverified rumors faster than corrections can follow, so releasing raw information too early may cause confusion.
Nevertheless, these are narrow exceptions that justify a brief delay, not a general license for leaders to decide what citizens should know.
Even in such cases, the information should be released once the danger has passed, and independent bodies should review the decision so that temporary secrecy does not quietly become permanent.
Thus, the first view identifies real exceptions, but they do not overturn the general rule of disclosure.
In conclusion, I side with the view that the public has a right to be fully informed, with only limited and temporary exceptions.
Secrecy has enabled grave abuses, transparency supports cooperation, and the risks that the first view describes can be handled without eroding this right.
Leaders who trust their citizens with the truth are usually rewarded with citizens who trust them in return.

essays.title: Breadth requirements prepare students for real problems

paragraphs.text: Many of today's most difficult problems, from pandemics to climate change, do not respect the boundaries between academic departments.
This reality explains why many people argue that universities should require students to study a variety of fields outside their majors.

I largely agree with the claim that universities should require such courses, and I partly agree with the reason that broad knowledge is the best way to become truly educated, although depth in one field remains essential.

The claim is sound because breadth prepares students for complex problems, the reason is largely valid because broad knowledge improves judgment, and the strongest objection, the cost in time, can be managed.
First, the claim is justified because problems in the real world require knowledge from several disciplines at once.
My own field, epidemiology, combines medicine, statistics, economics and social science, and I have seen projects fail because a team understood the disease but not the community.
For example, a dengue campaign that ignored how families store water would have little effect, however good its science.
In such projects, an anthropologist who understands local habits can be as valuable as a laboratory expert.
Similarly, the Human Genome Project, completed in 2003, required biologists, computer scientists and engineers to work together on one goal.
Its scientists had to understand enough of one another's fields to communicate, and broad training made that possible.
This shows that a requirement for broad coursework is not a burden but a [[pragmatic|pragmatic]] preparation for the work graduates will actually do.
Second, the reason on which the claim is based is largely valid, because exposure to several fields sharpens judgment.
Marie Curie won Nobel Prizes in both physics and chemistry, and her ability to move between disciplines allowed her to see connections that specialists might have missed.
Breadth allows a student to borrow tools from one field to solve problems in another.
Likewise, a physician who has studied ethics and history is better prepared to understand why patients distrust medicine, as many did after the Tuskegee study was revealed.
Knowledge of history helps such a physician respond to distrust with patience rather than frustration.
Even so, the word "best" overstates the case, since depth and practice also make a person truly educated.
These examples suggest that the reason [[bolsters|bolster]] the claim, even if broad knowledge is one essential part of education rather than its sole source.
Admittedly, the most compelling objection is that required courses take time and money away from a student's main field.
A medical student in Vietnam already faces a six-year program, and extra requirements could delay entry into practice.
Moreover, some students find unrelated courses [[irksome|irksome]] and complete them with little effort.
Nevertheless, this problem can be solved by designing requirements carefully rather than abolishing them.
Universities can offer short, focused courses, such as statistics for future doctors or ethics for engineers, that complement the major instead of competing with it.
The cost of breadth is therefore real but [[commensurate|commensurate]] with its benefits, and it does not outweigh the case for the claim.
Indeed, some graduates later say that a course outside their major was the one that changed how they think.
In conclusion, I largely agree that universities should require students to take courses outside their majors, and I partly accept the reason offered for this claim.
Broad coursework prepares students for complex problems and improves their judgment, while careful design can limit its costs.
A truly educated graduate needs both depth and breadth, and universities should ensure that students acquire both.

essays.title: Encourage breadth, but do not require it

paragraphs.text: University tuition and time are among the most valuable resources a young person has.
For this reason, the claim that universities should require every student to take many courses outside the major deserves careful scrutiny.

I largely disagree with the claim that such courses should be required, and I also question the reason that knowledge of various disciplines is the best way to become truly educated, although breadth can certainly be valuable.

Mandatory breadth often wastes students' limited time, being truly educated depends more on how one thinks than on how many subjects one studies, and the benefits of breadth can be achieved without requirements.
First, the claim is questionable because mandatory courses outside the major often consume time that students cannot spare.
Consider a medical student in Vietnam who already faces a six-year program and must master large amounts of clinical knowledge.
Requiring that student to take unrelated courses in, for instance, art history may add cost and delay without improving patient care.
Every semester spent on unrelated courses is a semester not spent on clinical skills that patients will depend on.
Similarly, students from poor families who must work while studying may find that extra requirements push graduation out of reach.
For them, each additional course is not an enriching experience but an [[onerous|onerous]] expense.
This shows that a universal requirement ignores the different needs of students and can turn breadth into a [[perfunctory|perfunctory]] box to check.
Second, the reason behind the claim is flawed, because being truly educated depends more on the quality of one's thinking than on the variety of subjects one has studied.
The Wright brothers, bicycle makers without college degrees, achieved the first powered flight in 1903 through careful experiments with gliders and a wind tunnel they built themselves.
Their success came from disciplined reasoning and testing, not from a broad academic background.
Neither brother held a college degree, yet few people would deny that they thought more rigorously than many graduates.
Conversely, when a 2015 collaboration repeated 100 published psychology studies and reproduced only about a third of them, it showed that highly educated researchers can still be misled.
Years of formal training had not protected them from accepting findings that later failed to hold up.
These cases suggest that a [[discerning|discerning]] mind, rather than a wide range of courses, is the real mark of education.
Admittedly, the most compelling challenge to my position is that broad knowledge helps people solve complex problems.
The Human Genome Project, completed in 2003, needed biologists, computer scientists and engineers to work together.
Each specialist contributed depth, and the project succeeded because the team, not each member, was broad.
Nevertheless, such collaboration shows the value of teams with different expertise, not the need for every individual to study every field.
Universities can encourage breadth through optional courses, joint projects and flexible minors without making them compulsory.
Thus, this challenge [[qualifies|qualify]] my position, since breadth has real benefits, but it does not justify a requirement for every student.
Students who choose breadth freely are also more likely to engage with it seriously than those forced to attend.
In conclusion, I largely disagree with the claim that universities should require courses outside each student's major, and I reject the reason that breadth is the best path to true education.
Requirements waste limited time, true education depends on the quality of thinking, and the benefits of breadth can be gained voluntarily.
Universities would serve students better by fostering curiosity and judgment than by multiplying requirements.

essays.title: Patient work outlasts quick fame

paragraphs.text: Social media has made it possible for a teenager to become famous overnight.
This new reality makes the question of what young people should aim for more important than ever.
I largely agree that young people should be encouraged to pursue long-term, realistic goals rather than seek immediate fame and recognition, as long as "realistic" does not mean small or unambitious.
Lasting achievement usually requires years of patient work, the pursuit of fame can distort judgment, and the most ambitious goals can still be pursued in a realistic, step-by-step way.
First, the statement holds true because most lasting achievements are the result of years of patient effort rather than sudden success.
Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman spent decades on little-noticed basic research on mRNA, work that made it possible to develop the COVID-19 mRNA vaccines in under a year.
Their reward, the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, came long after the work itself.
For years, their work attracted little attention, yet they persisted because they believed in the long-term goal.
Similarly, the Wright brothers achieved the first powered flight in 1903 only after years of careful experiments with gliders and a wind tunnel they built themselves.
Neither achievement would have happened if its creators had needed applause at every stage.
This shows that the young people most likely to make a real difference are those who are [[assiduous|assiduous]] rather than impatient for applause.
Second, chasing immediate fame can distort a young person's judgment and values.

On social media, the posts that spread fastest are often the most dramatic; the same tools that helped activists organize during the Arab Spring of 2011 also spread misinformation faster than corrections can follow.
A young person who measures success by views may learn to value attention over accuracy.
Such habits are hard to [[jettison|jettison]] later, even when the person matures.
Likewise, in research, a young scientist eager for recognition may be tempted to publish striking results too quickly, and many such findings later fail to hold up.
The 2015 effort that could reproduce only about a third of 100 psychology studies shows how often single findings mislead.
These examples suggest that fame is often [[ephemeral|ephemeral]], while habits formed in pursuit of it can do lasting harm.
Admittedly, the statement may not hold true if "realistic" is taken to mean modest or safe.
Vincent van Gogh sold very few paintings during his lifetime, and a purely realistic adviser might have urged him to choose a more secure career.
Ambitious dreams, rather than safe plans, have produced much of human progress.
Nevertheless, van Gogh's story supports long-term commitment, since his greatness lay in the work he produced over years, not in any recognition he received.
Similarly, a young doctor who dreams of eliminating a disease can still set realistic yearly targets, such as improving one clinic's diagnosis rates.
The best advice, therefore, is to pursue ambitious goals through realistic steps, which keeps young people both hopeful and grounded.
This consideration [[qualifies|qualify]] my position but does not reverse it.
In conclusion, I largely agree that young people should be encouraged to pursue long-term goals rather than immediate fame, provided that those goals remain ambitious.
Lasting achievement takes time, fame-seeking can distort judgment, and bold aims are best reached through steady, realistic steps.
Recognition, when it comes, should be the result of meaningful work, not the purpose of it, and young people who learn this early are likely to build careers that last.

essays.title: Aim high, and welcome earned recognition

paragraphs.text: Advice to young people often sounds wise but can quietly limit what they believe they can achieve.
The statement that young people should pursue long-term, realistic goals rather than seek immediate recognition is a clear example of such advice.
I mostly disagree with this statement, because it sets up a false choice and undervalues both bold ambition and early recognition, although seeking fame for its own sake is clearly unwise.
Many great achievements began as unrealistic goals, early recognition can provide the support that long-term work requires, and the real danger lies in empty fame rather than recognition itself.
First, the statement does not hold true for many great achievements, which began as goals that seemed unrealistic.
The Wright brothers, bicycle makers without college degrees, set out to build a flying machine at a time when many experts considered powered flight impossible.
Through years of experiments with gliders and a wind tunnel they built themselves, they achieved the first powered flight in 1903.
Had they accepted the [[prudent|prudent]] advice of their time, they would have stayed in the bicycle business.
Similarly, Marie Curie pursued a scientific career despite the barriers women faced at the time and went on to win Nobel Prizes in both physics and chemistry.
By the standards of her era, her goal was hardly realistic, yet her persistence changed science.
This shows that urging young people to be "realistic" may stifle the very ambition that produces breakthroughs.
Second, early recognition is often not a distraction but a source of support for long-term goals.
Vincent van Gogh sold very few paintings during his lifetime, and the lack of recognition left him struggling to continue his work.
Had he received earlier attention, he might have gained the security to paint for many more years.
Many talented people abandon their work not from lack of ability but from lack of support.
Likewise, a young researcher who wins an early award may attract funding and mentors, while equally talented peers without such recognition leave science.
Recognition, in such cases, acts as a [[catalyst|catalyst]] for long-term work rather than a replacement for it.
These cases suggest that recognition and long-term goals are [[complementary|complementary]], since early success can make sustained effort possible.
Admittedly, the statement holds true when young people seek fame for its own sake.

On social media, attention often rewards dramatic content over accurate content, and misinformation can spread faster than corrections can follow, rewarding those who care more about attention than truth.
Nevertheless, this danger argues for teaching young people to seek recognition for meaningful work, not for avoiding recognition altogether.
The same platforms that spread rumors also allowed activists during the Arab Spring of 2011 to organize quickly and draw attention to their cause.
Recognition, in other words, can serve good causes as well as empty ones.
The problem, therefore, is hollow fame, and the statement's sweeping advice misses this distinction.
Young people should learn to [[eschew|eschew]] attention that is unearned while welcoming recognition that rewards real accomplishment.
In conclusion, I mostly disagree that young people should be steered toward realistic goals instead of recognition, although fame pursued for its own sake deserves the warning.
Bold goals often produce the greatest achievements, early recognition can sustain long-term work, and only empty fame poses a real threat.
Young people should be encouraged to aim high and to welcome recognition that comes from work worth doing, since such recognition often makes further work possible.

words.meaning_here: something that speeds up or triggers progress

essays.title: Fund research whose risks can be judged

paragraphs.text: Every public budget is a bet on the future, and some bets are far riskier than others.
This raises the question of whether governments should fund scientific research whose consequences are unclear.
I largely support the policy of withholding public money from such research, as long as "unclear" means that neither its possible harms nor its likely benefits can be reasonably assessed in advance.
Implementing the policy would protect citizens from unpredictable harm and direct scarce funds toward pressing needs, although it would occasionally sacrifice a valuable discovery.
First, implementing this policy would protect citizens from harms that nobody can predict, because research with unclear consequences can injure the very people it aims to help.
The sedative thalidomide, used before its effects in pregnancy were understood, is a clear warning.
Around 1960 it was given to pregnant women, and it caused severe birth defects in thousands of babies in Europe.
In the United States, Frances Kelsey of the FDA refused to approve it, and the country then passed stricter drug-testing rules in 1962.
Similarly, a gene-editing trial launched before its risks are understood could harm volunteers in ways that no one could later reverse.
These cases show that when the consequences of research are unclear, the people who bear the risk are rarely the people who decide.
A government that refuses to fund such work is not hostile to science; it is simply being [[prudent|prudent]] with human lives.
Second, the policy would direct scarce public funds toward research whose benefits are already likely, which matters most in countries with limited budgets.
Consider the use of Wolbachia mosquitoes against dengue.

Releasing mosquitoes carrying Wolbachia bacteria, which block dengue transmission, cut dengue cases by 77% in a randomized trial in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, and the method has also been tested in Vietnam.
Funding such a project is a sound investment, because its goal, method and expected result are all defined in advance.
In my own work on dengue control in Vietnam, I have seen that every dollar spent on a vague project is a dollar not spent on testing, mosquito control or community education.
This shows that requiring clear consequences is not a bureaucratic preference but a way to fund [[efficacious|efficacious]] interventions when health needs are [[pressing|pressing]].
A ministry that funds clearly defined projects can also measure their results and correct course, which unclear research rarely allows.
Admittedly, some of the most valuable research in history began with consequences that no one could foresee.

Decades of little-noticed basic research on mRNA by Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman allowed COVID-19 vaccines to be developed in under a year, and the two scientists won the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
Nevertheless, such success stories are memorable precisely because they are rare.
In 2015, a large collaboration tried to repeat 100 published psychology studies and reproduced the results of only about a third of them.
If even published findings fail so often, then open-ended projects with no defined purpose are an even more [[tenuous|tenuous]] use of taxpayers' money.

This consequence shapes my position rather than reversing it: governments should fund work whose outcomes they can explain, while leaving most purely exploratory research to universities and private foundations.
In conclusion, governments should generally decline to fund research whose consequences are unclear, especially when those consequences may include serious harm.
Such a policy protects people from unpredictable risks and channels limited budgets toward projects with defined goals, even though it may occasionally miss a rare breakthrough.
On balance, this cost is acceptable, and it can be [[mitigated|mitigate]] as long as other funders remain free to pursue bolder ideas.

words.meaning_here: careful and sensible about avoiding risk
weak and poorly supported; unlikely to pay off

essays.task_note: Body 1 and 2 describe consequences of implementing the policy (fewer harms, better use of funds); Body 3 weighs the lost-breakthrough consequence and states how it shapes the position.

essays.title: Uncertain research deserves funding, with oversight

paragraphs.text: Many great discoveries looked useless, or even strange, at the moment they were first made.
For this reason, the proposal that governments should not fund any scientific research whose consequences are unclear deserves careful scrutiny.
I strongly oppose this policy, because its likely consequences would harm both science and the public, although I accept that risky research needs strict oversight.
Such a policy would block future breakthroughs, push basic science into profit-driven hands, and answer genuine risks with the wrong tool.
First, implementing the policy would cut off the unpredictable breakthroughs on which modern medicine depends, because nearly every major discovery began with unclear consequences.
In 1928, Alexander Fleming noticed that mold had killed bacteria on a culture plate, an observation whose practical value was far from clear at the time.
Only when Howard Florey and Ernst Chain's team developed penicillin during World War II did it become a usable drug.
Similarly, Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman spent decades on little-noticed basic research on mRNA, which later allowed COVID-19 vaccines to be developed in under a year.
These cases show that the value of research often remains [[latent|latent]] for many years.
A rule that funds only work with clear consequences would have starved exactly the projects that later transformed medicine.
Basic research, by its nature, cannot state its consequences in advance, so the policy would effectively end it.
Second, the policy would push basic research into private hands, with the consequence that knowledge becomes narrower and less widely shared.
The Human Genome Project, a publicly funded international effort completed in 2003, made the human DNA sequence freely available to all researchers.
Because the public paid for it, its results belonged to everyone rather than to a single company.
Likewise, GPS was built by the US military, and once it was opened to civilians, it became the basis of everyday navigation, ride-hailing and delivery apps.
Neither project could promise its final uses in advance, yet both produced benefits that a cautious, [[myopic|myopic]] funding rule would have blocked.
Private firms, which must [[garner|garner]] quick profits for their investors, rarely make such long bets on their own.
In practice, the policy would leave the most open-ended questions to companies whose first duty is to shareholders, not to the public.
Admittedly, implementing the policy might prevent some harm, because research with unclear consequences can hurt the very people who take part in it.
The Tuskegee syphilis study, which ran from 1932 to 1972, withheld treatment from Black men without their informed consent.
Nevertheless, the lesson of that tragedy is not that uncertain research should go unfunded, but that it should be carefully supervised.
Indeed, the public outrage over Tuskegee led to US rules requiring ethics review boards for research on people.
This consequence shapes my position: the real danger lies in [[lax|lax]] oversight, not in uncertainty itself.
Ethics review can [[mitigate|mitigate]] harm far more precisely than a blanket ban on funding ever could.
Under such a system, researchers can still explore uncertain questions, while the people who take part in studies are protected.
In conclusion, refusing to fund all research with unclear consequences would do far more harm than good.
It would choke off unexpected breakthroughs, leave basic science to private interests, and treat the problem of risk with a blunt instrument when careful oversight already works.
Governments should therefore keep funding uncertain research, while insisting that every study involving people pass strict ethical review.

words.meaning_here: present but hidden; not yet visible or developed
