essays.title: The past alone is an unreliable guide

paragraphs.text: People often say that those who forget history are doomed to repeat it.
Yet the opposite danger is discussed less often: people who remember history too faithfully may apply old lessons to new problems.

I largely agree with the statement, because knowing about the past cannot, by itself, guide important decisions today, especially when conditions have changed, although it can still offer useful warnings.
Past success can blind decision-makers to change, lessons from the past are often less reliable than they appear, and history helps only when present evidence confirms it.
First, knowledge of the past can actively mislead people when circumstances have changed, because it tempts them to repeat what once worked.
Kodak is a clear example.
In 1975, its own engineer Steven Sasson invented the digital camera, but the company, protecting its profitable film business, was slow to embrace digital photography.
It filed for bankruptcy in 2012.
Similarly, a physician trained in an era when antibiotics cured most infections may still prescribe them freely, even though resistant bacteria now make many of those drugs fail.
These cases show that the past can become a trap rather than a guide.
Decision-makers who [[venerate|venerate]] what worked before may cling to [[obsolete|obsolete]] methods and miss the very changes that matter most today.
The more successful a past strategy has been, the harder it becomes to abandon when conditions change.
Second, the lessons people draw from the past are often less reliable than they seem, so relying on them can lead to poor decisions.
In 2015, a large collaboration tried to repeat 100 published psychology studies and reproduced the results of only about a third of them.
Before that effort, any of those findings could easily have been cited to justify a school program or a clinical decision.
Likewise, history itself is often recorded in [[ambiguous|ambiguous]] terms, so two leaders can read the same event and draw opposite conclusions.
This shows that knowing about the past is not the same as knowing the truth about it.
When the historical record is [[dubious|dubious]], it cannot safely settle anything important today.
Leaders who treat such findings as settled truth may build important policies on foundations that later collapse.
Admittedly, some lessons from the past remain valid and clearly help people make decisions today.
In 1847, Ignaz Semmelweis had doctors in Vienna wash their hands in chlorinated lime, and deaths from childbed fever on his ward fell sharply.
Nevertheless, his own colleagues rejected that evidence, and the lesson was widely accepted only after germ theory vindicated it years after his death.
Hospital staff today wash their hands because modern microbiology explains why it works, not merely because of a record from 1847.
Without that explanation, hospitals would have had little reason to trust his results over the beliefs of the majority.
This consideration qualifies my position: the past can suggest the right questions, but present evidence must answer them.
The statement therefore holds largely true when it refers to knowledge of the past on its own.
In conclusion, knowledge of the past is a weak and sometimes dangerous guide when people rely on it alone.
Old successes can blind people to new conditions, historical lessons are often shaky, and even the best of them need present evidence before they can be trusted.
The most [[pragmatic|pragmatic]] decision-makers therefore treat history as a source of questions rather than answers, and they make important choices on the basis of what is true today.

out of date; no longer useful
open to more than one interpretation
practical; focused on what works in reality

essays.title: History supplies tested lessons for today

paragraphs.text: Every new decision is made by people who carry memories, records and stories from earlier times.
The claim that knowing about the past cannot help people make important decisions today therefore seems difficult to accept.
I strongly disagree with the statement, because the past offers tested evidence and warnings that improve present decisions, although its lessons must be adapted to new conditions.

History supplies hard-won rules that prevent old mistakes, it shows which large-scale policies actually work, and its occasional failures as a guide come from misreading it rather than from the past itself.
First, knowledge of the past helps people avoid repeating disasters, because many of today's safeguards were written in response to earlier harm.
Around 1960, the sedative thalidomide was given to pregnant women and caused severe birth defects in thousands of babies in Europe.
Frances Kelsey of the US FDA refused to approve it, and the US then passed stricter drug-testing rules in 1962, so regulators today inherit a clear lesson about testing drugs before approval.
Similarly, the outrage over the Tuskegee syphilis study, which withheld treatment from Black men without their informed consent, led to US rules requiring ethics review boards for research on people.
These examples show that the past is not a museum but a set of working rules.
Without that memory, every generation would be forced to discover the same dangers again, at the same [[grievous|grievous]] cost.
Every new drug approved today passes through rules shaped by that history.
Second, the past shows which policies actually work, which is exactly what leaders need when the stakes are high.
In 1986, Vietnam's Doi Moi reforms replaced central planning with market incentives.
A country that had faced food shortages became one of the world's largest rice exporters, and poverty fell dramatically over the following decades.
Policymakers in other developing countries can study this record when they weigh their own economic choices.
On a smaller scale, in my work on dengue control in Vietnam, records of earlier outbreaks help us decide when and where to send limited teams.
This shows that historical evidence is often the most [[empirical|empirical]] guide available, because it records what happened to real people rather than what a theory predicted.
No laboratory experiment could test an entire economic transformation, but history already has.
Admittedly, knowledge of the past can mislead when conditions change, and in such cases the statement seems to hold.
Kodak engineer Steven Sasson invented the digital camera in 1975, but Kodak, protecting its profitable film business, was slow to embrace digital photography and filed for bankruptcy in 2012.
Nevertheless, Kodak's failure came from a narrow reading of its own past, not from knowing too much history.
Had its leaders studied how earlier technologies replaced older ones, they might have recognized the threat sooner.
This consideration qualifies my position only slightly: the past helps most when people read it in a [[discerning|discerning]] way and adapt its lessons to present conditions.
A [[myopic|myopic]] reading of history is a problem of interpretation, not of history itself.
Kodak's mistake, in fact, has itself become a lesson from the past for firms facing new technologies today.
In conclusion, knowing about the past is one of the most valuable aids to important decisions today.
It supplies safeguards born of earlier tragedies, provides evidence about which policies succeed, and misleads only when people read it narrowly.
Rather than [[dismiss|dismiss]] history, decision-makers should study it carefully and ask how today's conditions differ from yesterday's.

words.meaning_here: based on observation and real experience

essays.task_note: Body 1 and 2 show ways the statement does not hold (safeguards from past harm, tested policies); Body 3 admits a case where it seems to hold (Kodak) and explains why that only slightly qualifies the position.

essays.title: Media scrutiny leaves few living heroes

paragraphs.text: A century ago, most people knew their leaders only through speeches, photographs and carefully edited newspaper stories.
Today, by contrast, cameras and social media follow public figures everywhere, which raises the question of whether any living person can still be regarded as a hero.
I largely agree with the statement, because intensive media coverage exposes every flaw and divides public opinion, although a few people can still earn admiration for specific acts.
Constant exposure makes flaws impossible to hide, modern media turns admiration into partisan conflict, and the exceptions that remain tend to be narrow and short-lived.
First, intensive coverage makes it nearly impossible for a living person to remain a hero, because heroism depends partly on distance and the media removes that distance.
Consider a popular national leader whose every speech, old message and private joke can now be found online within minutes.
Even if she has served her country well, a single careless remark from twenty years ago can be replayed millions of times.
Her achievements remain, but the public image of a flawless figure does not.
Similarly, a celebrated athlete may be admired on Monday and [[disparaged|disparage]] by Friday after one angry post.
These cases show that the media does not simply report on public figures; it constantly tests them.
Few human beings can survive such [[exhaustive|exhaustive]] scrutiny, so the living hero has nearly disappeared.
Second, modern media tends to divide societies, so even admirable figures are admired by only part of the public.
During the Arab Spring of 2011, smartphones and social media let activists organize quickly, but the same tools also spread misinformation faster than corrections could follow.
In such conditions, an activist praised as a hero by one group can be attacked as a traitor by another within hours.
A single misleading post can undo years of trust before any correction appears.
In Vietnam, too, I have seen respected doctors praised online one week and accused of greed the next, often on the basis of rumors.
This shows that heroism requires broad agreement, yet a [[polarized|polarized]] media environment rarely allows a society to agree on anyone.
The statement therefore holds strongly when it refers to society as a whole.
Admittedly, some living people still receive wide admiration, which suggests that the statement may go too far.
When Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman won the 2023 Nobel Prize for the mRNA research behind COVID-19 vaccines, many news stories celebrated their persistence.
Nevertheless, this admiration focused on their research rather than on their whole lives, and public attention soon moved elsewhere.
Moreover, the same media that praised them could just as easily search their past for mistakes.
Such praise is real but [[ephemeral|ephemeral]]; it honors a specific achievement rather than creating a lasting hero for society.
Admiration of this kind rarely survives the next news cycle.
This exception therefore qualifies my position without overturning it: individuals can be admired for heroic acts, but they are rarely regarded as heroes in the traditional sense.
In conclusion, intensive media coverage has made it extremely difficult, though not entirely impossible, for a society to regard a living person as a hero.
Constant exposure reveals ordinary flaws, divided audiences rarely agree on anyone, and the praise that survives is usually brief and limited to particular acts.
The age of the flawless hero may be over, and societies should learn to admire good actions without needing to [[lionize|lionize]] perfect people.

complete and thorough; covering every detail

essays.title: Media can make heroes, not just destroy them

paragraphs.text: Heroes have always been ordinary people who did something extraordinary when it mattered.
Some argue, however, that in this age of intensive media coverage, no living man or woman can still be regarded as a hero.
I mostly disagree with this statement, because the media can create and spread heroism as easily as it destroys it, although constant scrutiny has made heroic reputations more fragile.
Media coverage brings hidden heroes to public attention, modern heroism rests on specific acts rather than flawless lives, and media scrutiny, while real, filters heroes rather than eliminating them.
First, intensive media coverage often makes heroes rather than destroying them, because it reveals courage and dedication that would otherwise remain unseen.
For decades, Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman carried out little-noticed basic research on mRNA.

When that research allowed COVID-19 vaccines to be developed in under a year, and the two scientists won the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, news outlets around the world told their story of persistence.
Similarly, a nurse who rescues patients during a flood may become known across a whole country within hours because someone shared a video.
These cases show that the media can [[elevate|elevate]] people who would once have stayed in obscurity.
Coverage, in this sense, is a [[catalyst|catalyst]] for heroism, not its enemy.
Without modern media, their story might have remained known only to a few colleagues.
Second, the statement assumes that a hero must be flawless, yet societies today increasingly honor people for particular acts of courage or service.
During the COVID-19 pandemic in Vietnam, doctors, nurses and volunteers who worked in isolation wards were widely praised as heroes, even though the public knew little about their private lives.
In my own work with frontline health staff, I saw how this public recognition strengthened morale and encouraged exhausted colleagues to keep going.
This shows that a modern hero is defined by what he or she does, not by a perfect record.
Media exposure of minor flaws does not [[negate|negate]] the courage of such acts, and most people understand this distinction.
Indeed, the public's knowledge of a hero's ordinary weaknesses can make his or her courage seem more human and more admirable.
A hero, in this modern sense, is someone who acts well when it counts, not someone who never makes mistakes.
Admittedly, [[ubiquitous|ubiquitous]] cameras and constant scrutiny can damage reputations quickly, and in this respect the statement holds some truth.

As the Arab Spring of 2011 showed, smartphones and social media let people organize quickly but also spread misinformation faster than corrections can follow, so a respected figure can be attacked unfairly overnight.
Nevertheless, this pressure tends to filter heroes rather than eliminate them.
People whose courage is genuine, such as frontline health workers, usually keep public respect even after critics examine them closely.
Intense coverage makes heroism harder to fake, so the reputations that survive it are arguably more [[warranted|warranted]] than those of the past.
This consideration qualifies my view: heroic status is more fragile today, but it is far from impossible.
In conclusion, modern media has not made living heroes impossible; it has changed how they are made and tested.
Coverage can bring hidden heroes to light, today's societies honor specific acts rather than perfect lives, and harsh scrutiny mainly separates real heroes from false ones.
A society that looks carefully can still find living people worth admiring, and the media often helps it look.

words.meaning_here: raise to a higher position or status
something that causes or speeds up a change

essays.title: Shared foundations make learning deeper

paragraphs.text: Most of us choose our friends, our news and even our colleagues from among people who see the world as we do.
Critics call this habit [[insular|insular]], but the statement suggests that we usually learn much more from people whose views we share than from people whose views contradict our own.
I largely agree with this statement, as long as "shared views" means shared basic goals and methods rather than identical opinions on every question.

Shared foundations allow deep and efficient learning, people absorb lessons more readily from those they trust, and opposing views, though valuable, teach most when they come from within a shared framework.
First, people who share our basic views can teach us more because they let us skip arguments about first principles and move quickly to details.
The Wright brothers, bicycle makers without college degrees, shared the same practical belief in careful testing.
Working together through years of experiments with gliders and a wind tunnel they built themselves, they achieved the first powered airplane flight in 1903.
Similarly, in my research group, epidemiologists who agree on basic methods can spend an hour improving a dengue model instead of debating whether models are useful at all.
These cases show that agreement on foundations is not a weakness but a [[precursor|precursor]] to deeper learning.
When we share core assumptions, each conversation can build on the last rather than starting again.
Two scientists who must first argue about whether evidence matters will rarely reach the point of learning anything new.
Second, people learn more readily from those they trust, and trust usually grows from shared views.
Consider a mother in rural Vietnam who doubts vaccines.
If a doctor from the city lectures her, she may become defensive and [[dismiss|dismiss]] his evidence.
If a neighbor who shares her values explains why she vaccinated her own child, however, the mother is far more likely to listen and change her mind.
Likewise, on social media, arguments between strangers with opposing views usually harden positions instead of changing them.
This shows that information alone does not produce learning; learning also requires a listener who is willing to accept it, and shared views create that willingness.
Shared views, in other words, open the door through which new information can enter.
Admittedly, people who disagree with us can expose mistakes that our allies would never notice.
Abraham Lincoln appointed his political rivals, including William Seward, to his cabinet, choosing able critics over loyal followers.
Nevertheless, these rivals worked inside his own government and shared his duty to lead the country, so their disagreement took place within a common purpose.
Each rival could disagree with him openly because all of them wanted the government to succeed.
This suggests that opposing views teach most when they come from people who share our deeper goals.
Such cases therefore refine my position rather than [[refute|refute]] it: the most useful critics usually stand on common ground with us.
Far from weakening my view, Lincoln's example highlights the value of a shared foundation.
In conclusion, we usually learn more from people who share our fundamental views, even if we sometimes need their disagreement on details.
Shared foundations make learning efficient, trust makes it possible, and the most productive disagreements occur among people with common goals.
The best strategy, then, is not to avoid those who think like us but to choose companions who share our values while remaining [[candid|candid]] enough to challenge our conclusions.

essays.title: Opposing views reveal our blind spots

paragraphs.text: It is comfortable to spend time with people who agree with us, but comfort is rarely how we grow.
The statement nevertheless claims that we usually learn much more from people whose views we share than from people whose views contradict our own.
I mostly disagree, because those who challenge our views expose errors that like-minded people overlook, although shared views do make some kinds of learning easier.
Opposing views reveal our blind spots, disagreement drives the progress of knowledge, and shared views, while helpful for building on a foundation, cannot tell us whether that foundation is sound.
First, people who contradict us are often the only ones who can reveal our blind spots, because those who share our views usually share our mistakes as well.
In 1847, Ignaz Semmelweis had doctors in Vienna wash their hands in chlorinated lime, and deaths from childbed fever on his ward fell sharply.
Yet most of his colleagues, who held the same medical beliefs as one another, rejected his idea, and germ theory vindicated him only years after his death.
By listening mainly to one another, those doctors reinforced a shared error instead of learning from the man who challenged it.
This shows that a group of like-minded people can become [[complacent|complacent]] precisely because no one inside it raises doubts.
The person whose views contradict ours is often the one carrying the lesson we most need.
Their shared views did not protect them from error; they protected the error itself.
Second, the progress of knowledge depends on disagreement, because ideas improve when they are tested by people who doubt them.
In 2015, a large collaboration tried to repeat 100 published psychology studies and reproduced the results of only about a third of them.
That effort came from researchers willing to question their own field, and it taught the field more than many confirming studies had.
Similarly, Abraham Lincoln appointed political rivals, including William Seward, to his cabinet, choosing able critics over loyal followers.
Both cases show that [[dissent|dissent]] is not an obstacle to learning but one of its main sources.
Without critics, a research field or a government simply repeats its assumptions more confidently.
A scientist who only reads studies that confirm her views will never discover which of them are wrong.
Admittedly, people who share our views can help us learn efficiently, especially when we are beginners in a field.
A new medical resident learns faster from senior doctors who share her basic training than from a critic who rejects medicine altogether.
Nevertheless, this kind of learning only builds on an existing foundation; it cannot tell us whether that foundation is sound.
Galileo's critics held the [[orthodox|orthodox]] view of their time, and in 1633 the Church forced him to recant his support for the idea that the Earth moves around the sun.
Agreement helped those critics learn more of the same, but only disagreement could have taught them something new.
This consideration qualifies my position without reversing it: shared views make learning comfortable, while opposing views keep it honest.
In conclusion, we usually learn more from those who contradict us than from those who agree with us.
Opposing views expose shared errors, drive the testing of knowledge, and reveal flaws in the very foundations that like-minded people take for granted.
Seeking out [[cogent|cogent]] critics may be uncomfortable, but it is the surest way to avoid the [[insular|insular]] thinking that kept Semmelweis's colleagues from accepting a lifesaving idea.

essays.title: Youth trends are culture's earliest signals

paragraphs.text: Every culture changes, and the first signs of change usually appear among the young.
This observation lies behind the claim that the most effective way to understand contemporary culture is to analyze the trends of its youth.
I largely agree with this claim, because young people adopt new technologies and values first, although their trends must be read alongside the habits of older generations.
Youth trends reveal how new technology reshapes daily life, they foreshadow where a culture is heading, and, despite including many passing fads, they remain the clearest window into the present.
First, analyzing youth trends is effective because young people are usually the first to adopt the technologies that reshape a culture.
During the Arab Spring of 2011, smartphones and social media let activists organize quickly.
Observers who followed how young people used these tools understood the political mood far better than those who read only official newspapers.
Similarly, in Vietnam, young city residents were quick to embrace ride-hailing and delivery apps built on GPS, changing how urban families travel and eat.
These cases show that youth trends are not [[trifling|trifling]] details but [[salient|salient]] signals of how a culture is changing.
To study contemporary culture without them would be to study yesterday's culture.
Young people, in effect, test new ways of living before the rest of society adopts them.
Second, youth trends foreshadow the direction of a whole society, so they explain not only the present but also the near future.
Kodak engineer Steven Sasson invented the digital camera in 1975, but Kodak, protecting its profitable film business, was slow to embrace digital photography and filed for bankruptcy in 2012.
Had its leaders watched closely how younger consumers were changing the way they took and shared pictures, they might have adapted in time.
In my own field, younger Vietnamese doctors often look up medical information online and share it in group chats, a habit their senior colleagues are now beginning to adopt.
This shows that the trends of the young often become everyone's habits within a few years, which makes them a [[prescient|prescient]] guide to culture.
Studying them closely is like reading the first chapter of a culture's next decade.
Admittedly, many youth trends are fads that disappear before they reveal anything lasting.
A dance or fashion that spreads across social media one summer may be forgotten by the next, and it may say little about the values of the society as a whole.
Nevertheless, a careful analyst can separate [[ephemeral|ephemeral]] fads from durable shifts by watching which habits persist and spread to older groups.
Social media, for example, spread first among the young but is now [[ubiquitous|ubiquitous]], used even by grandparents in Vietnamese villages.
This consideration qualifies my position: youth trends are the most effective starting point, but they must be checked against the behavior of other generations.
In other words, the analyst's task is to filter youth trends, not to ignore them.
Most of the habits that pass this test began among the young, which is why their trends deserve first attention.
In conclusion, analyzing the trends of young people is, in most cases, the most effective way to understand contemporary culture.
Young people adopt new technology first, their habits foreshadow society's direction, and although some of their trends are passing fads, the lasting ones reveal where a culture truly stands.
Anyone who wants to understand the present should therefore watch the young closely, while remembering that culture belongs to every generation.

essays.task_note: Body 1 and 2 show where the statement holds (early adoption, foreshadowing); Body 3 names where it may not (passing fads) and explains how that qualifies the position.

essays.title: Culture lives in institutions, not fads

paragraphs.text: Culture is the shared set of habits, beliefs and institutions that shapes how a whole society lives.
It is therefore surprising to claim that the most effective way to understand contemporary culture is to analyze the trends of its youth.
I mostly disagree with this claim, because youth trends are often fleeting and unrepresentative, although they do offer early signs of technological change.

Youth trends change too quickly to define a culture, the deepest features of a culture are found in its institutions and its majority, and the real value of youth trends lies only in their role as early signals.
First, youth trends are a poor guide to contemporary culture because they are [[transitory|transitory]] and often reflect a small, urban minority.
Consider an analyst who studies Vietnamese culture by tracking which songs, slang and fashions are popular on social media among teenagers in Hanoi.
Within a year, most of those trends will be replaced, and they will have told the analyst little about the values of farmers, factory workers or older citizens.
Similarly, a viral online challenge may reach millions of screens without changing anyone's beliefs about family, work or religion.
These cases show that popularity among the young is not the same as cultural depth, and young people themselves are hardly a [[homogeneous|homogeneous]] group.
An analysis built on such trends risks mistaking noise for meaning.
Second, the most important features of a culture are found in its laws, institutions and majority behavior, which youth trends rarely capture.
Vietnam's 2007 law requiring motorbike helmets raised helmet use from low levels to over 90% within months and reduced head injuries and deaths.
This change in everyday behavior came from a government policy that applied to every age group, not from a youth trend.
Likewise, Vietnam's Doi Moi reforms of 1986 replaced central planning with market incentives, and the culture of enterprise that followed was shaped largely by adults running farms and businesses.
These examples show that culture is [[ingrained|ingrained]] in institutions and shared practices, so analyzing them reveals more than analyzing the tastes of the young.
Laws, markets and family traditions shape the lives of every generation, whereas youth trends touch only part of one.
Such changes last for decades, while a teenage fashion may last only a season.
Admittedly, young people often adopt new technologies first, and their habits can signal broader change.
During the Arab Spring of 2011, smartphones and social media let activists organize quickly, and observers who watched young users understood the speed of the protests.
Nevertheless, those same tools also spread misinformation faster than corrections could follow, so youth activity online gave an incomplete and sometimes misleading picture.
This consideration shapes my position: youth trends are useful as early signals, but they are only one lens among several.
An effective analysis must [[juxtapose|juxtapose]] them with the habits, laws and institutions of the whole population.
Without such a comparison, an analyst could easily mistake the loud voices of a few young users for the views of an entire society.
In conclusion, analyzing youth trends is not the most effective way to understand contemporary culture.
Such trends are fleeting and narrow, the core of a culture lies in its institutions and majority behavior, and even the genuine signals that youth provide must be confirmed by broader evidence.
Anyone seeking to understand a society should therefore study all of its generations, with youth trends serving as one [[complementary|complementary]] source rather than the main one.

essays.title: Immediate surroundings shape attitudes most

paragraphs.text: A doctor who moves from one hospital to another often finds that her habits change within weeks.
This common experience supports the statement that people's attitudes are determined more by their immediate situation or surroundings than by society as a whole.
I largely agree with this statement, because the people and pressures closest to us shape our attitudes most directly, although [[pervasive|pervasive]] national laws and norms set the outer limits.

Local workplace cultures outweigh distant rules, close communities can lead people to resist the attitudes of the wider society, and society's influence, while real, usually reaches people through their immediate surroundings.
First, attitudes are shaped mainly by immediate surroundings because people imitate the colleagues they see every day rather than the rules written far away.
In my work on antibiotic resistance in Vietnam, I have seen two hospitals under the same national guidelines prescribe antibiotics very differently.
Young doctors in each hospital simply followed the habits of the senior colleagues on their ward.
Similarly, in 1847, Ignaz Semmelweis cut deaths from childbed fever on his ward by having doctors wash their hands in chlorinated lime, yet most colleagues around him rejected his idea.
These cases show that the [[milieu|milieu]] of a ward or a team can [[eclipse|eclipse]] both official rules and strong evidence.
People adopt the attitudes that earn approval from those immediately around them.
A guideline from the ministry rarely changes practice unless a respected local doctor adopts it first.
Second, close communities can lead people to adopt attitudes that differ sharply from those of society as a whole.
During the Montgomery bus boycott of 1955-1956, Black residents refused for over a year to ride segregated buses, even though segregation was the accepted law of their society at the time.
Their resolve was sustained by neighbors and families who supported one another day after day, and the boycott helped end bus segregation in that city.
Likewise, a teenager in a conservative town may hold progressive views if her circle of friends does.
This shows that local [[solidarity|solidarity]] can be strong enough to override the attitudes of the wider society.
The boycotters' attitude toward segregation was formed in their own community, not handed down by the society around it.
Teenagers, in particular, often care more about the approval of a few close friends than about the opinions of millions of strangers.
Admittedly, society as a whole can sometimes change attitudes on a large scale.
Vietnam's 2007 law requiring motorbike helmets raised helmet use from low levels to over 90% within months and reduced head injuries and deaths.
Nevertheless, even this national law worked largely through local channels: police on street corners, parents insisting that children wear helmets, and neighbors who noticed those who did not.
The same law that changed behavior in one neighborhood might have been ignored in another without that local pressure.
Society set the rule, but immediate surroundings turned it into a personal attitude.
This consideration qualifies my position: society defines the options, while immediate surroundings [[inculcate|inculcate]] the attitudes that people actually hold.
In conclusion, people's attitudes depend more on their immediate surroundings than on society as a whole, although the two often work together.
Workplace habits outweigh distant guidelines, close communities can resist national norms, and even successful national policies take hold through local pressure.
Anyone who hopes to change attitudes, whether about antibiotics or road safety, should therefore start with the small groups in which people live and work.

essays.title: Society sets the attitudes surroundings transmit

paragraphs.text: No one grows up in a vacuum; each of us absorbs the language, values and expectations of a whole society.
The statement nevertheless claims that people's attitudes are determined more by their immediate situation or surroundings than by society as a whole.
I mostly disagree, because laws, economic systems and widely shared norms shape attitudes more deeply than any single setting, although immediate surroundings can modify them.

National laws can transform attitudes across very different local settings, a society's economic system shapes how people think about work and success, and local influence, while real, usually operates within society's broader frame.
First, society-wide laws can change attitudes in every local setting at once, which suggests that society, not immediate surroundings, is the stronger force.
Vietnam's 2007 law requiring motorbike helmets raised helmet use from low levels to over 90% within months and reduced head injuries and deaths.
Local differences in wealth, education and custom did not prevent the change, which shows how powerful a national rule can be.
Such a rapid national shift cannot be explained by any single neighborhood, family or workplace.
Similarly, a national anti-smoking campaign can make smoking unfashionable in offices, schools and homes at the same time.
These cases show that society can [[permeate|permeate]] every local setting.
When a broad norm changes, immediate surroundings change with it rather than resisting it.
Neighbors and families did help enforce the rule, but they were responding to a national decision rather than creating their own.
Second, the economic system of a society shapes how its members think about work, wealth and success.
Vietnam's Doi Moi reforms of 1986 replaced central planning with market incentives.
A country that had faced food shortages became one of the world's largest rice exporters, and poverty fell dramatically over the following decades.
Along with these changes, attitudes toward private enterprise shifted for millions of families, whatever their village or neighborhood.
Likewise, Singapore's government housing program now houses about 80% of the country's residents, most of whom own their flats, so national policy frames how residents think about owning a home.
This shows that broad institutions shape deeply [[ingrained|ingrained]] attitudes in ways that no single household or workplace could [[counter|counter]].
A family's attitude toward business today reflects decisions made at the national level decades ago.
Admittedly, immediate surroundings can sometimes lead people to resist the attitudes of their wider society.
During the Montgomery bus boycott of 1955-1956, Black residents refused for over a year to ride segregated buses, and their local unity helped end bus segregation in that city.
Nevertheless, such resistance usually draws on ideals already present in the broader society, such as fairness and equal citizenship, and it succeeds by changing society's rules.
Local communities can [[galvanize|galvanize]] people, but they rarely invent attitudes from nothing.
This consideration qualifies my view: surroundings influence how strongly people hold an attitude, while society largely determines which attitudes are available.
Even the most determined local communities, in other words, work with ideas that society has already supplied.
In conclusion, society as a whole shapes people's attitudes more powerfully than their immediate surroundings do.
National laws change behavior everywhere at once, economic systems reshape attitudes toward work and wealth, and even local resistance relies on ideas drawn from the wider society.
Immediate surroundings can [[attenuate|attenuate]] or strengthen that influence, but they usually work as channels for society's values rather than as independent sources of belief.

essays.title: In real crises, food before the arts

paragraphs.text: When a family runs short of money, it buys rice before it buys concert tickets.
The same logic underlies the recommendation that nations should suspend government funding for the arts when significant numbers of their citizens are hungry or unemployed.
I largely agree with this recommendation, particularly in severe crises, as long as the suspension is temporary and the savings go directly to food and jobs.
Adopting it would be advantageous during acute food shortages and when arts funding serves mainly wealthy audiences, although it would be unwise where arts spending itself supports poor workers.
First, in a setting where many citizens lack enough food, suspending arts funding would be advantageous because every available resource should go toward survival.
Consider Vietnam before the Doi Moi reforms of 1986, when the country faced food shortages.
In such conditions, a government that spent money on a new opera house rather than on food or seed would have neglected its most basic duty.
The reforms, which replaced central planning with market incentives, later turned Vietnam into one of the world's largest rice exporters, showing where attention needed to go first.
Similarly, a provincial health office facing a dengue outbreak should buy test kits before it sponsors a festival.
These cases show that when hunger is widespread, [[pressing|pressing]] human needs must come before cultural projects.
A government cannot ask its citizens to enjoy culture while they are still waiting in line for food.
Second, the recommendation would be advantageous in countries where state arts funding benefits mainly wealthy urban audiences.
Imagine a national theater in a capital city whose tickets are too expensive for most citizens.
If thousands of factory workers have lost their jobs, a subsidy for that theater effectively transfers public money from the struggling to the comfortable.
Redirecting the same funds toward job training or meal programs would reach far more people and [[alleviate|alleviate]] real suffering.
This shows that suspending such funding is not hostile to culture; it is a matter of [[equitable|equitable]] priorities during hard times.
Few citizens would miss a subsidized premiere if their neighbors were eating again.
A budget, after all, reveals a government's priorities, and during a crisis those priorities should favor the many.
Admittedly, in some circumstances suspending arts funding would not be advantageous, because the arts budget also supports poor workers.
Vincent van Gogh sold very few paintings during his lifetime, and many artists today also live close to poverty.
In a town where a public craft program employs hundreds of local artisans, cutting it would simply add to the number of unemployed citizens.
Nevertheless, such programs could be treated as employment support and protected, while purely ceremonial arts spending is paused.

This circumstance refines my position: the recommendation is wise for arts spending that serves few people, but [[counterproductive|counterproductive]] when the arts themselves provide jobs for the poor.
The aim of the suspension is to reduce hardship, so any cut that increases hardship defeats its own purpose.
Even in a crisis, then, the government should protect spending that keeps artists employed and pause only the spending that serves a privileged few.
In conclusion, suspending government arts funding during widespread hunger or unemployment is generally a sound policy.
It is clearly advantageous during acute food shortages and when subsidies serve mainly the wealthy, though it should not eliminate programs that employ struggling artists.
A [[prudent|prudent]] government that pauses its arts budget temporarily, and spends the savings on food and work, ultimately protects the citizens whom culture is meant to serve.

essays.title: Cutting the arts rarely feeds anyone

paragraphs.text: In hard times, the arts are often the first item that budget officials cut.
The recommendation that nations should suspend government funding for the arts whenever significant numbers of citizens are hungry or unemployed reflects this instinct.
I largely disagree with this recommendation, because in most circumstances the savings would be small and the losses large, although a brief pause may be justified during an extreme emergency.
Suspending arts funding would rarely feed anyone, it would add artists and cultural workers to the unemployed, and only in an acute famine might it offer a real advantage.
First, in most countries adopting this recommendation would not be advantageous, because arts budgets are too small to make a meaningful difference to hunger or unemployment.
Consider a middle-income country that spends a tiny fraction of its budget on museums, theaters and orchestras while millions of its people are poor.
Canceling that spending might fund a few weeks of meals, but it would not address the causes of poverty, such as a lack of jobs or low wages.

Vietnam's experience supports this point: its Doi Moi reforms of 1986 replaced central planning with market incentives, and poverty fell dramatically over the following decades, a gain that came from economic reform rather than from cuts to culture.
This shows that hunger and unemployment require economic reform, and cutting the arts is at best a [[token|token]] gesture.
Such a cut would deliver a symbolic victory while leaving the real problem untouched.

Second, in a setting where unemployment is high, suspending arts funding would be counterproductive, because artists and cultural workers are among the most [[precarious|precarious]] members of the workforce.
Vincent van Gogh sold very few paintings during his lifetime, yet he is now regarded as one of the greatest painters in history.
Talented artists in difficult times often face the same struggle, and modest public support can keep them working.

Similarly, a provincial theater employs not only actors but also carpenters, ticket sellers and lighting technicians, so closing it would add dozens of families to the very group the policy aims to help.
This shows that arts funding is often a form of employment support, so cutting it would [[exacerbate|exacerbate]] the problem it claims to solve.
A policy meant to reduce unemployment should not begin by creating more of it.
Admittedly, there are rare circumstances in which a temporary suspension would be advantageous.
In an acute famine, when people are dying of hunger within weeks, every available resource should go toward food, and even small savings matter.

Nevertheless, such emergencies are exceptional, while the recommendation would apply whenever "significant numbers" of citizens are hungry or unemployed, which describes many countries most of the time.
Moreover, even during a famine, the savings from the arts budget would be small compared with emergency aid from other sources.
This circumstance shapes my position: I would accept a brief pause during a true famine, but not a standing rule that [[relegates|relegate]] culture to permanent second place.
The arts also help people endure hardship, and hard times are precisely when societies need them most.
In conclusion, nations should generally not suspend arts funding simply because many citizens are hungry or unemployed.
The savings are usually too small to help, the cuts would push cultural workers out of work, and only an extreme famine justifies even a temporary pause.

Governments should fight hunger and unemployment with economic policy, while recognizing that a [[modest|modest]] investment in the arts is part of a healthy society rather than an [[extraneous|extraneous]] luxury.

essays.title: Flexible parent volunteering strengthens schools

paragraphs.text: A school is not only a building with teachers; it is a community that depends on families.
This idea leads to the recommendation that all parents should be required to volunteer time to their children's schools.
I largely agree with this recommendation, as long as the requirement is flexible enough for parents with heavy work or family burdens.
Required volunteering would be advantageous in schools with limited resources and would strengthen children's learning, although it would need adjustment for parents who cannot easily spare time.
First, in a setting where schools lack staff and money, requiring parents to volunteer would be advantageous because it would add skilled help at almost no cost.
Consider a primary school in a rural province of Vietnam with one teacher for forty children.
If each parent gave two hours a month, the school could run reading groups, repair classrooms and organize simple health checks.
As a physician, I could teach the children basic handwashing and explain why it prevents disease.
Similarly, a parent who works as an accountant could help the school manage its small budget.
These examples show that parents bring a [[plethora|plethora]] of skills that most schools leave unused.
For a school with almost no budget, such contributions are worth far more than their cost.
A requirement turns this [[latent|latent]] resource into real support for children.
Second, required volunteering would be advantageous for students themselves, because children tend to value school more when they see their parents involved.
Imagine a teenager who sees his father helping at the school library every month.
He learns that education matters to his family, and his father learns what the teachers expect, which makes conversations about homework easier at home.
Likewise, when parents meet teachers regularly, small problems such as falling grades or bullying are noticed early instead of being ignored.
This shows that volunteering builds a partnership between home and school, and children who see adults take school seriously often follow their example.
Unlike a voluntary scheme, which attracts only parents who are already engaged, a requirement ensures that the children of busy or [[indifferent|indifferent]] parents benefit as well.
Over time, these small contacts can turn a distant institution into a place where parents feel welcome.
Admittedly, in some circumstances a strict requirement would not be advantageous, especially for parents who already struggle to meet basic needs.
A single mother working two factory shifts may be unable to give even an hour, and punishing her would only add to her burden.
A rule that ignores such cases would drive struggling parents away from the school.
Nevertheless, this problem calls for flexibility, not for abandoning the idea altogether.
Schools could allow parents to contribute in many ways, such as weekend tasks, short online sessions or a single talk about their work.

This circumstance qualifies my position: the requirement should be universal in principle but [[malleable|malleable]] in practice, so that it supports families rather than [[alienates|alienate]] them.
In this way, the requirement would still reach every family without punishing those with the least time.
In conclusion, requiring parents to volunteer at their children's schools would generally be beneficial.
It would bring valuable skills to schools with scarce resources and show children that their education matters, provided that schools adapt the requirement for parents with heavy burdens.
With such flexibility, the policy could turn every parent into a partner in education rather than a distant observer.

essays.title: Encourage parent volunteering; do not require it

paragraphs.text: Most parents care deeply about their children's education, but caring and having free time are not the same thing.
The recommendation that all parents should be required to volunteer time to their children's schools overlooks this difference.

I disagree with this recommendation, because a universal requirement would burden the poorest families and distract from what truly improves schools, although encouraging voluntary help is often wise.

The requirement would be unfair to parents with demanding jobs, school quality depends mainly on trained teachers rather than parental labor, and the benefits of involvement can be achieved without compulsion.
First, in communities where many parents work long hours for low pay, a volunteering requirement would be harmful rather than advantageous.
Consider a factory worker in an industrial zone near Ho Chi Minh City who works long shifts six days a week.
For her, two hours at school means lost wages or lost sleep, and failing to meet the rule may expose her to penalties or [[stigma|stigma]].
Meanwhile, a wealthy parent with flexible hours can comply easily, so the rule falls most heavily on those least able to bear it.
This shows that a universal requirement would be [[onerous|onerous]] for exactly the families who most need support.
Far from being [[equitable|equitable]], it could deepen the divide between rich and poor parents.
Rules that look equal on paper can be deeply unequal in practice.
A policy meant to bring families closer to schools would instead make some of them feel unwelcome.
Second, the quality of a school depends mainly on skilled professional teachers, so requiring parental labor addresses the wrong problem.
Finland requires schoolteachers to hold a master's degree, makes teaching a respected and selective profession, and relies far less on standardized testing than many countries.
Its approach centers on the quality and status of its teachers, not on the labor of parents.
Similarly, a hospital improves patient care by training nurses, not by requiring patients' relatives to work shifts on the ward.
This shows that a mandate on parents would [[deflect|deflect]] attention from the investment that actually matters: well-trained, well-paid teachers.
Parents can support learning at home, but they cannot replace the professional skills of a trained teacher.
Requiring them to volunteer would treat the symptom of a weak school system rather than its cause.
Admittedly, there are circumstances in which parental involvement would be highly advantageous.
In a small village school with few staff, parents who help with reading, repairs or health checks can make a real difference to children's learning.
Nevertheless, these benefits come from willing parents, and they can be achieved through encouragement, flexible schedules and recognition rather than through a requirement.
A school that invites parents to share their professional skills once a year, for example, will attract many who would resent a compulsory schedule.

This circumstance shapes my position: parental involvement is valuable, but making it compulsory risks turning goodwill into resentment, which would [[undermine|undermine]] the very partnership the policy hopes to build.
In many communities, parents already help schools informally when they are asked politely and given choices.
A voluntary approach keeps the benefits of involvement while avoiding the costs of compulsion.
In conclusion, requiring all parents to volunteer at their children's schools would do more harm than good.
Such a rule would burden working families unfairly, distract from the central role of trained teachers, and gain nothing that voluntary participation cannot achieve.
Schools should therefore welcome parents warmly and make involvement easy, but leave the decision to each family.

essays.title: A funded semester abroad prepares global professionals

paragraphs.text: Some of the most important lessons in a person's education happen far from the lecture hall.
For this reason, many people argue that colleges and universities should require their students to spend at least one semester studying in a foreign country.
I largely agree with this recommendation, as long as universities provide financial support so that the requirement does not exclude poorer students.
A semester abroad prepares students for global problems, exposes them to different ways of working, and, despite real costs, can be made fair through careful planning.
First, requiring study abroad would be advantageous in fields where the most pressing problems cross national borders, because students need to see these problems from more than one country.
Consider the eradication of smallpox, which was declared in 1980 after a coordinated global WHO vaccination campaign.
That campaign succeeded only because countries shared data and vaccine, and the people who led it had to work across languages, health systems and political interests.
A young doctor who has studied in another country is far better prepared for this kind of cooperation than one who has never left home.

Similarly, antibiotic resistance spreads easily across borders, so a pharmacy student in Vietnam who spends a semester in a country with strict prescription rules would return with practical ideas for reform.
This shows that, for disciplines facing global challenges, a required semester abroad is not a luxury but a sound investment in professional skill.
Second, a semester abroad would be valuable for students who might otherwise remain [[insular|insular]], because living in another culture challenges habits that seem natural at home.
In my own training as a physician in Vietnam, I assumed that the way my hospital organized ward rounds was the only reasonable way.
When I later observed colleagues in another country, I saw nurses speak openly to senior doctors, a practice that caught errors my own team might have missed.
That experience still shapes how I lead clinical teams today, more than any lecture I attended at home.
Likewise, a business student who studies in Japan may learn how long-term relationships with suppliers shape company decisions in ways that no textbook fully conveys.
Such experiences make graduates more [[cosmopolitan|cosmopolitan]] and more willing to question their own assumptions, which is exactly what a university education should achieve.
Admittedly, a mandatory semester abroad would not be advantageous in every circumstance, especially for students with limited money or heavy family duties.

A student from a poor rural family who works part-time to support younger siblings could not easily leave for four months, and an [[onerous|onerous]] requirement might push such a student to abandon college altogether.
Nevertheless, this problem argues for better design rather than for rejecting the recommendation.
Universities could offer scholarships, partner with institutions in nearby and less expensive countries, or allow short, intensive programs as an alternative for students in genuine hardship.

With these measures in place, the requirement would [[alleviate|alleviate]] rather than [[exacerbate|exacerbate]] inequality, since poorer students are often the ones who would never go abroad without institutional support.
A well-funded requirement would give them the same chance as their wealthier classmates.
In conclusion, I believe that universities should generally require a semester of study in a foreign country, provided they make it affordable for all.
Such a policy prepares students for problems that cross borders and broadens their habits of mind, and its main drawback, cost, can be reduced through planning.
The value of the requirement therefore depends less on the idea itself than on whether institutions are willing to fund it fairly.

essays.title: Encourage study abroad; do not require it

paragraphs.text: Travel is often praised as the best teacher, but not every valuable lesson needs to be compulsory.
Some argue that colleges and universities should require their students to spend at least one semester studying in a foreign country.
I mostly disagree with this recommendation: study abroad should be strongly encouraged and funded, but making it a requirement for all students would do more harm than good.

A universal requirement would burden students with fewer resources and disrupt programs with tight training sequences, and although study abroad is valuable, its benefits can be achieved through more flexible options.
First, a mandatory semester abroad would be disadvantageous in circumstances where students lack money or carry family duties, because the requirement would turn an opportunity into a barrier.
Consider a first-generation student in Vietnam whose parents are farmers and whose tuition is paid through loans.
For her, four months in Europe or the United States would mean extra costs for housing, flights and visas, as well as lost income from her part-time job.
Faced with this [[onerous|onerous]] condition, she might delay graduation or leave school entirely.
Similarly, a student who cares for an ill parent cannot simply move abroad for a semester, no matter how much he might benefit from the experience.
This shows that a universal rule, however well meant, would [[exacerbate|exacerbate]] inequality, since it would fall hardest on the students whom universities most need to keep.
Second, the recommendation would be impractical in fields with tightly sequenced training, where a semester away can interrupt the development of essential skills.
In medical school, clinical rotations follow a strict order, and each one depends on supervised practice with local patients, local diseases and local laws.

A Vietnamese medical student who spent a semester abroad might learn interesting theory but would miss months of hands-on work with conditions such as dengue, which he will treat daily after graduation.
Likewise, engineering programs that require accredited laboratory courses may find that foreign credits do not transfer, forcing students to repeat work and delay their careers.
In such programs, the requirement would [[impede|impede]] rather than enrich professional preparation, and the cost would be paid later by the patients and clients these graduates serve.
Admittedly, studying abroad can be transformative, and the strongest case for the recommendation is that many students would never go unless they were required to.
A student who spends a semester in another country often returns more [[cosmopolitan|cosmopolitan]], more confident and more aware that familiar practices are not the only reasonable ones.

Nevertheless, students who would not otherwise go abroad are usually held back by cost or family duties rather than by the lack of a rule, so these benefits can be extended to them without forcing every student to leave.

Universities could offer generous scholarships, short summer programs and joint online courses with foreign partners, and they could invite international students and visiting scholars to their own campuses.
These measures would bring the advantages of global exposure to many students while respecting those whose circumstances make a long stay abroad unwise.
A [[pragmatic|pragmatic]] policy of encouragement is therefore better than a blanket rule.
In conclusion, although study abroad has real value, colleges should not make it a requirement for graduation, at least not for every student in every program.
A mandatory semester would penalize poorer students and disrupt programs with strict training sequences, and its benefits can be achieved through more flexible means.
The best policy is to make study abroad possible for every student who wants it, rather than compulsory for those who cannot afford it.

essays.title: Reward teachers for student progress, carefully measured

paragraphs.text: In most professions, people who do excellent work expect to be rewarded for it.
This principle lies behind the recommendation that teachers' salaries should be based on the academic performance of their students.
I agree with this recommendation in a limited form: part of a teacher's pay should depend on students' academic progress, as long as progress is measured fairly and not by raw test scores alone.
Such a system would reward effective teaching, would direct attention to struggling students, and, despite the risk of gaming, can be designed to avoid its worst abuses.

First, linking some pay to student progress would be advantageous in school systems where pay depends only on years of service, because such systems give teachers little [[incentive|incentive]] to improve.
Consider a secondary school in which a dedicated young mathematics teacher spends her evenings redesigning lessons, and her students' scores rise steadily over two years.
Under a seniority scale, she earns less than a colleague who has taught from the same notes for twenty years and whose students make little progress.
Over time, she may leave teaching for a better-paid job in business.
Similarly, a district hospital that rewards its wards for lowering infection rates gives nurses a clear reason to follow hand-washing rules consistently.
This shows that when pay ignores results, the most capable teachers feel undervalued, and a modest link to student performance can help keep them in the classroom.
Second, performance-based pay would be beneficial where struggling students tend to be neglected, provided that the measure rewards improvement rather than final scores.
If a teacher's bonus depended on how much each student gained over the year, a child who began far behind would count as much as a top student.
A teacher in a poor rural district could then earn as much as one in a wealthy city school by helping weak readers catch up.
Likewise, a teacher with a class of recent immigrants would be rewarded for the students' rapid progress in a new language, even if their final scores remained modest.
Such a design makes the policy [[equitable|equitable]], because it measures what the teacher adds rather than what the student brought from home.
It also tells teachers that the children who need the most help are worth the most effort.
Admittedly, the strongest objection is that tying pay to test results can encourage teaching to the test or even dishonesty.
When scores alone determine rewards, some teachers may narrow their lessons to exam drills and neglect subjects such as art or history, and a few may be tempted to inflate grades.
Nevertheless, these risks argue for careful design rather than for abandoning the idea, just as the risk of side effects argues for careful dosing rather than for refusing all medicine.
A [[prudent|prudent]] system would use performance for only part of a salary, combine test gains with classroom observation and student feedback, and audit unusual jumps in scores.
With such safeguards, the [[pernicious|pernicious]] effects of purely test-based pay could be [[mitigated|mitigate]] while the benefits of rewarding good teaching are preserved.
In conclusion, I support basing a meaningful share of teachers' salaries on the academic progress of their students, but not on raw scores alone.
This approach would reward effective teachers, draw attention to students who are falling behind, and limit the risk of gaming through balanced measures.
Whether the policy helps or harms education depends on what it measures, so the measure must be designed as carefully as the reward.

essays.title: Test-based pay punishes teachers of poor students

paragraphs.text: What gets measured gets managed, but what gets measured is not always what matters most.
This warning applies directly to the recommendation that teachers' salaries should be based on the academic performance of their students.
I mostly disagree with this recommendation, because in most circumstances it would reward teachers for the advantages of their students rather than for the quality of their teaching.
Such a policy would penalize teachers in poor schools, would narrow what students learn, and, although it rightly values accountability, could be replaced by better ways of supporting good teaching.

First, performance-based pay would be disadvantageous in settings where students' results depend heavily on factors outside the classroom, because teachers would be judged on things they cannot control.

Consider two equally skilled teachers, one in a wealthy city school and one in a remote mountain district where many children are hungry, miss school during the harvest, and speak a minority language at home.
The first teacher's students will almost certainly score higher, so she would earn more even if her colleague worked twice as hard.
Over time, teachers would learn that the easiest way to raise their pay is to move to a richer school.
Similarly, in public health, judging a clinic only by its patients' outcomes would unfairly punish doctors who serve the sickest communities.
This shows that tying salaries to student performance would drive capable teachers away from the schools that need them most, an outcome that would [[exacerbate|exacerbate]] existing inequality.
Second, the recommendation would be harmful wherever performance is measured by standardized tests, because teachers would reasonably focus on what is tested and neglect what is not.

Finland offers a useful contrast: it requires schoolteachers to hold a master's degree, makes teaching a respected and selective profession, and relies far less on standardized testing than many countries.
Its approach treats teachers as trusted professionals rather than as workers paid by output, and it gives them room to teach subjects that no exam can easily measure.
By contrast, a pay system based on scores would push many teachers toward [[perfunctory|perfunctory]] drills and away from projects, discussion and creative work.
Such narrowing would [[undermine|undermine]] the very purpose of education, which is to develop curious and independent thinkers, not merely good test takers.
Admittedly, the recommendation responds to a real problem: in systems where pay depends only on seniority, weak teachers face little pressure to improve.
A teacher who has delivered the same [[lackluster|lackluster]] lessons for years earns as much as an inspiring colleague, and students bear the cost.
Nevertheless, the solution to this problem is better evaluation and support, not salaries tied to student scores.

Schools could use regular classroom observation, peer mentoring and professional training, and they could reward teachers for taking on difficult assignments, guiding new colleagues or leading improvements in their departments.
These measures hold teachers accountable without blaming them for poverty or tempting them to teach only to the test, so the concern about accountability qualifies but does not reverse my position.
In conclusion, paying teachers according to their students' academic performance would, in most circumstances, do more harm than good.
It would punish teachers who serve disadvantaged children and narrow the curriculum, while the legitimate goal of accountability can be met through more [[equitable|equitable]] means.
If a society wants better teaching, it should invest in teachers, as Finland does, rather than turn their salaries into a gamble on test results.

words.meaning_here: make an already bad situation worse
done routinely with little care or thought

essays.task_note: The essay names circumstances (poor rural schools, test-based measurement) where the recommendation would be disadvantageous and one (seniority-only pay) where its goal has merit, then explains why these examples lead to rejecting it in favor of other accountability tools.

essays.title: Shared heroes now mostly belong to history

paragraphs.text: Every age needs figures who show what human beings can achieve at their best.
Yet some argue that it is no longer possible for a society to regard any living man or woman as a hero.
I largely agree with this claim, at least when "society" means a whole nation rather than a small community, because modern conditions make shared admiration of a living person extremely fragile.

Constant media exposure reveals every flaw, deeply divided societies rarely agree on anyone, and although some living people still earn wide respect, that respect seldom becomes lasting, shared hero status.
First, it has become very difficult to view a living person as a hero, because smartphones and social media expose every mistake to millions of people within hours.
In the past, a leader's private failings might remain hidden until long after death.
Today, an old post, a careless remark or a leaked recording can circulate worldwide in a single day, and smartphones and social media spread misinformation faster than corrections can follow.
A respected scientist or athlete can therefore be [[lionized|lionize]] on Monday and [[disparaged|disparage]] on Friday.
Similarly, any public figure who speaks on a contested issue quickly attracts organized critics who search for past errors.
This shows that the constant scrutiny of modern media makes the spotless image of a hero almost impossible to sustain while the person is still alive.
Second, modern societies are often so [[polarized|polarized]] that no living figure can win the admiration of a whole population.

Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman spent decades on little-noticed mRNA research that allowed COVID-19 vaccines to be developed in under a year, and they won the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
Yet their recognition did not end public suspicion of the vaccines their work made possible.
In many countries, debates over masks and lockdowns turned public health officials into heroes for some citizens and enemies for others.
Likewise, political leaders admired by one party are routinely portrayed as villains by the other, so even genuine achievements are judged through the lens of loyalty.
When admiration divides along group lines, a person may be a hero to a faction but not to the society, which is precisely what the claim describes.
Admittedly, the most compelling challenge to my position is that ordinary people still perform heroic acts and are honored for them.
Doctors and nurses who worked long shifts during the pandemic were applauded in many countries, and firefighters who rescue children from burning buildings are still praised in local news.
Nevertheless, such recognition is usually [[ephemeral|ephemeral]] and local rather than lasting and shared by an entire society.
The applause for health workers faded within months, and few people remember the names of individual rescuers.
Full recognition often comes only after death, as with Ignaz Semmelweis, whose idea of hand washing most colleagues rejected in his lifetime and germ theory vindicated only years after he died.
These cases show that heroic acts still exist, but they do not [[negate|negate]] the claim, since brief local praise is not the lasting, shared admiration that makes someone a society's hero.
In conclusion, I largely agree that a modern society can no longer regard a living person as a hero in the full sense of the word.
Relentless media exposure and deep social divisions prevent lasting, shared admiration, even though individual acts of courage are still honored briefly.
Heroism has not disappeared, but its full recognition increasingly belongs to the dead, whose lives can finally be judged as a whole.

words.meaning_here: treated as a celebrity; praised highly

essays.task_note: Body 3 states the strongest challenge (ordinary people are still honored for heroic acts) fairly with examples, then answers it by showing such recognition is brief and local.

essays.title: Living heroes survive, though judged more realistically

paragraphs.text: It is fashionable to say that we live in a [[cynical|cynical]] age that no longer believes in heroes.
Following this view, some claim that it is no longer possible for a society to regard any living man or woman as a hero.

I mostly disagree with this claim: although modern scrutiny has made heroes harder to sustain, societies still recognize living people as heroes when their courage or service is clear and widely shared.

Living heroes still emerge in moments of crisis and in science and public service, and the strongest challenge to my view, the power of modern media to expose flaws, changes how heroes are seen but does not make them impossible.
First, societies continue to honor living people as heroes during crises, when the value of courage becomes obvious to everyone.
During the COVID-19 pandemic, doctors and nurses in Vietnam left their families for weeks to staff isolation hospitals, and many citizens wrote letters and sent food to thank them.
In my own field, I watched epidemiologists work through the night to trace contacts, and their communities thanked them openly.
Newspapers and neighbors described these health workers as heroes, and the word did not seem exaggerated.
Similarly, after natural disasters, rescuers who risk their lives to save strangers are widely praised as heroes while they are very much alive.
This shows that when a society faces a common threat, it readily treats the [[laudable|laudable]] sacrifices of its protectors as heroic, so the claim overstates the loss of public admiration.
Second, living scientists and public servants can earn heroic status when their work saves lives on a large scale.
Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman spent decades on little-noticed research on mRNA, and that work made it possible to develop COVID-19 vaccines in under a year.
When they won the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, they were celebrated not merely as skilled researchers but as people whose persistence helped protect the world.
Their story is admired precisely because they continued their work when few people believed it mattered.

Likewise, a provincial health officer whose quick decisions stop a dengue outbreak may be publicly honored by the people she protected, which shows that careful judgment, not only dramatic courage, can still make someone a hero.
Such figures show that admiration for living people remains possible when their contribution is concrete and their motives seem [[disinterested|disinterested]].
Admittedly, the most compelling challenge to my position is that modern media make it easy to expose and exaggerate the flaws of any public figure.
Smartphones and social media spread misinformation faster than corrections can follow, so a respected person can be [[disparaged|disparage]] by thousands of strangers in a single day.
Even admired leaders now face constant criticism, and old mistakes can be revived at any moment.
Nevertheless, this scrutiny makes heroism more demanding, not impossible, because it tests whether admiration is deserved.
In fact, a hero who survives close examination may deserve more trust than the distant, idealized heroes of the past, whose failings were simply hidden.
Thus, the challenge [[qualifies|qualify]] my position: today's living heroes may be admired for specific acts rather than worshipped as perfect people, but they are still heroes.
In conclusion, I reject the claim that a society can no longer regard any living person as a hero.

Crises still produce widely admired figures, scientists and public servants still earn gratitude for lifesaving work, and media scrutiny, though intense, mainly forces societies to judge heroes more realistically.
What has changed is not our capacity for admiration but our demand that heroes be human rather than flawless.
