essays.title: A shared national core serves every student

paragraphs.text: Where a child is born should not decide what that child has the chance to learn.
This principle supports the claim that a nation should require all of its students to study the same national curriculum until they enter college.
I largely agree with this claim, provided that the common curriculum sets a shared core of knowledge while leaving teachers room to adapt how it is taught.

A national curriculum promotes equal opportunity, it creates a shared foundation for citizens, and, although critics argue that it ignores local needs and stifles creativity, this risk can be managed.
First, a common curriculum promotes fairness because it guarantees that rural and poor students are taught the same essential content as wealthy urban students.
In Vietnam, a student in a mountain district and a student in central Hanoi follow the same national program, so both are prepared for the same university entrance examinations.
Without that shared standard, schools in poorer areas might quietly lower their expectations, leaving their students with a disadvantage they could never [[surmount|surmount]].
Similarly, a child whose family moves from one province to another can continue learning without gaps or repetition.
This continuity matters in a country where many families move to cities in search of work.
These cases show that a national curriculum makes education more [[equitable|equitable]], which is the strongest reason to require it for all students.
Equal content does not guarantee equal results, but it removes one important source of inequality.
Second, a shared curriculum gives citizens a common foundation of knowledge, which a nation needs in order to function as a community.
When every student learns the same basic biology, for instance, public health campaigns about vaccination or dengue prevention can build on knowledge that the whole population shares.
In my work on disease control, explaining risk is far easier when people already understand how infections spread.
Likewise, a common history course gives young people from different regions a shared story and a common vocabulary for discussing their country's future.
This shows that a national curriculum does more than transmit facts; it helps citizens from different backgrounds [[coalesce|coalesce]] into a society that can understand one another.
Such shared understanding is difficult to build if every school teaches entirely different content.
The most compelling challenge to my position is that a single curriculum may ignore local needs and limit creativity.
Finland, often admired for its schools, gives its highly trained teachers considerable freedom and relies far less on standardized testing than many countries.
Nevertheless, this example shows the value of flexible teaching methods, not the danger of shared content, since Finland still sets national goals for what students should learn.
A national curriculum can likewise define core subjects while allowing schools to add local languages, crafts or electives.
This challenge therefore refines my position: the content of the core should be national, but the methods and the extras should remain local.
Shared goals and local freedom, in other words, are not opposites but partners.
In conclusion, I largely agree that all students should study the same national curriculum before college, as long as it defines a core rather than [[circumscribing|circumscribe]] every lesson.
A common curriculum promotes equal opportunity and a shared civic foundation, and flexibility in teaching can answer the concern about local needs.
Such a balance gives every child the same starting line without forcing every classroom into the same mold.

essays.title: One curriculum cannot fit every student

paragraphs.text: Students form a [[heterogeneous|heterogeneous]] group, differing in talents, interests and goals as much as in height.
Yet the claim holds that a nation should require all of its students to study the same national curriculum until they enter college.

Although some shared standards are useful, I mostly disagree with this claim, because a single required curriculum ignores students' different needs and discourages the variety that drives better teaching.
A uniform curriculum fails students with different abilities and goals, it limits teachers' freedom to innovate, and, admittedly, common standards do help ensure fairness.
First, a single curriculum fails many students because it assumes that all of them need the same knowledge at the same pace.
Consider a sixteen-year-old in rural Vietnam who wants to become a mechanic or a farmer using modern techniques.
Requiring him to follow exactly the same academic program as a student preparing for medical school may leave him bored, unprepared for his chosen work and more likely to drop out.
Vocational programs in many countries keep such students engaged by linking lessons to real jobs.
Similarly, a student gifted in mathematics may lose interest when forced to [[dawdle|dawdle]] at the pace set for everyone else.
These cases show that uniformity, however well meant, can [[impede|impede]] the very students it claims to serve.
A curriculum that serves the average student well may serve the individual student poorly.
Second, a required national curriculum limits innovation by preventing schools and teachers from trying new approaches.
Finland, often admired for its schools, requires teachers to hold a master's degree and then trusts them with considerable freedom, relying far less on standardized testing than many countries.
This trust allows teachers to adjust lessons to the students in front of them rather than follow a script set by distant officials.

Likewise, the Wright brothers, bicycle makers without college degrees, learned through their own experiments with gliders and a homemade wind tunnel, a reminder that valuable learning often happens outside a fixed program.
This suggests that a nation benefits more from many experiments in teaching than from a single, [[ossified|ossify]] curriculum.
If one method fails, a nation with many methods can learn from the others; a nation with one method cannot.
The most compelling challenge to my position is that, without a common curriculum, schools in poor areas may offer weaker education, widening inequality.
In many countries, wealthy districts can afford richer programs, while poorer schools struggle to teach even basic subjects.
Wealthier families can also pay for private tutoring, which widens the gap further.
Nevertheless, this problem can be solved with national minimum standards in core subjects such as reading, mathematics and science, rather than with one curriculum for every subject and every year.
Vietnam, for example, could keep a national standard in core subjects while letting schools design vocational and advanced courses for different students.
This challenge therefore shapes my position: the state should guarantee a floor of essential knowledge, but above that floor, students and schools should be free to choose their own paths.
Fairness requires a common minimum, not a common maximum.
In conclusion, I mostly disagree that every student should follow the same national curriculum until college.
Such uniformity fails students with different goals and limits innovation, while the legitimate concern for fairness can be met by minimum standards.
A nation serves its young people best by setting a common foundation and then allowing many different paths to be built on it.

essays.title: Require a semester abroad, and fund it

paragraphs.text: Some lessons cannot be learned from a textbook, only from living among people who see the world differently.
This is the main argument for the claim that colleges and universities should require their students to spend at least one semester studying in a foreign country.
I largely agree with this claim, as long as universities provide financial support so that the requirement does not exclude poorer students.
Studying abroad builds the international outlook that modern problems demand, it develops independence and adaptability, and, although cost is a serious objection, it can be addressed.
First, a semester abroad is valuable because many of today's most important problems cross national borders.
The eradication of smallpox, declared in 1980, depended on a coordinated WHO campaign in which countries shared data and vaccine.
The people who led such efforts needed to understand other countries' health systems, languages and customs.
The Human Genome Project, a publicly funded international effort completed in 2003, also showed how much researchers from different countries can achieve together.

Similarly, antibiotic resistance spreads today partly through the overuse and over-the-counter sale of antibiotics in many countries, including Vietnam, so tackling it requires professionals who can work across borders.
These cases show that global problems demand an international outlook, and a required semester abroad is one reliable way to [[engender|engender]] it.
Graduates who have lived abroad are better prepared to join such cooperation.
Second, living in a foreign country develops independence and adaptability that classroom learning rarely provides.
Consider a Vietnamese medical student who spends a semester at a hospital in another country.
She must work in an unfamiliar language, adapt to different routines and ask for help, and she returns with greater confidence and a broader view of how health care can be organized.
Likewise, a business student who spends a semester abroad learns firsthand that markets and customers differ, a lesson that no case study conveys as vividly.
In my experience, colleagues who trained abroad adapt quickly to new teams and unfamiliar problems.
Such experiences make students less [[insular|insular]] and more [[cosmopolitan|cosmopolitan]], qualities that employers and societies increasingly need.
These are skills that matter in every career, not only in international ones.
The most compelling challenge to this position is cost: travel, housing and tuition abroad can be [[prohibitive|prohibitive]] for students from poor families.
A student from a farming family in the Mekong Delta might be unable to pay for a semester in Europe, and a strict requirement could even prevent her from graduating.
Even with a partial scholarship, airfare and rent in a foreign city could exceed what her family can manage.
Nevertheless, this problem argues for funding the requirement, not for abandoning it.
Universities can offer scholarships, sign exchange agreements that keep tuition at home rates, and partner with nearby countries where living costs are lower.
This challenge therefore shapes my position: the requirement is justified only when universities make it affordable for every student.
A requirement without funding would be unjust, but a funded requirement would open doors that many students could never open alone.
In conclusion, I largely agree that universities should require students to study abroad for at least one semester, provided they make it financially possible for all.
Such a semester prepares graduates for global problems and builds independence, while scholarships and exchanges can answer the concern about cost.
A requirement backed by real support would turn a privilege of the few into an opportunity for everyone.

words.meaning_here: open to and familiar with many cultures
so high that it prevents action

essays.task_note: Body 3 states the strongest challenge (cost excludes poor students), concedes it, and answers it by making funding a condition of the requirement.

essays.title: Encourage study abroad, but do not require it

paragraphs.text: An experience that transforms one student may be a heavy burden for another.
This is the main problem with the claim that colleges and universities should require all students to spend at least one semester studying in a foreign country.

Although studying abroad can be valuable, I mostly disagree that it should be required, because a universal mandate would be unfair to many students and is unnecessary for gaining international understanding.
The requirement would exclude students with limited money or heavy responsibilities, its benefits can be achieved in other ways, and, admittedly, time abroad does offer real advantages.
First, a required semester abroad would be unfair because many students cannot afford it or cannot leave home.
Consider a student in Vietnam whose parents are farmers and who works part-time to pay her tuition; a semester in another country could cost more than her family earns in a year.
Other students care for sick relatives, have children of their own, or have disabilities that make travel difficult.
Similarly, students in demanding programs such as medicine may find that a semester abroad delays their clinical training and graduation.
A requirement that ignores these situations would force some students to choose between their families and their degrees.
For such students, the requirement would be not an opportunity but an [[onerous|onerous]] barrier, which [[undermines|undermine]] the claim that it should apply to everyone.
A rule that only some students can meet is not a fair graduation requirement.
Second, the benefits of studying abroad can often be achieved without leaving one's own country.
International collaboration increasingly happens online and in mixed teams at home.
Many of my own international collaborations in epidemiology, for instance, began with online meetings rather than travel.

The Human Genome Project, a publicly funded international effort completed in 2003, made the human DNA sequence freely available to all researchers, so a student almost anywhere can now take part in global science.
Likewise, universities can invite visiting professors, enroll international students and offer joint online courses, bringing foreign perspectives to students who stay home.
This suggests that a mandate is unnecessary, since the goal of a [[cosmopolitan|cosmopolitan]] education can be reached by many [[feasible|feasible]] paths.
Universities can therefore pursue international understanding without making travel compulsory.
The most compelling challenge to my position is that living abroad teaches lessons that no online course can, such as independence and the ability to adapt to an unfamiliar culture.
A medical student who spends a semester in a foreign hospital, for instance, must solve daily problems in another language and returns with a confidence that is hard to gain at home.
Nevertheless, recognizing these benefits supports encouraging and funding study abroad, not forcing it on every student.
Scholarships, exchange agreements and short summer programs can bring these experiences within reach of students who want them.

This challenge therefore shapes my position: universities should make study abroad widely available through scholarships and exchanges, while allowing students to choose it when it fits their circumstances.
Choice, not compulsion, is what makes such experiences meaningful.
In conclusion, I mostly disagree that universities should require every student to study abroad.
Such a requirement would burden students with limited resources, and international understanding can also be gained at home, even though time abroad has real value.
Universities should therefore open the door to study abroad as widely as possible, without pushing every student through it.

essays.task_note: Body 3 states the strongest challenge (living abroad builds independence that nothing else can), concedes it, and answers that this supports funding study abroad, not requiring it.

essays.title: Guiding students toward jobs helps everyone

paragraphs.text: Graduating with a degree but no job is one of the most discouraging experiences a young person can face.
To prevent it, some propose that educational institutions should actively encourage students to choose fields of study in which jobs are plentiful.
I support this policy, as long as encouragement means giving students clear information and incentives rather than forbidding them to follow other interests.

The policy would reduce graduate unemployment, it would help societies meet urgent needs, and, although it might discourage some talented students from less practical fields, that consequence can be limited.
First, implementing the policy would likely reduce unemployment and wasted investment among graduates.
In Vietnam, many families make great sacrifices to send their children to university, yet some graduates in crowded fields struggle for years to find work related to their degree.
If schools showed students data on job prospects before they chose a major, more of them could enter fields where their effort would be rewarded.
Graduates with stable jobs can also repay their families' sacrifices, a responsibility many young Vietnamese take seriously.
Similarly, a student who learns early that demand for nurses or data analysts is high may choose a path that leads to stable employment and independence.
This consequence strongly shapes my support, because a policy that spares young people [[futile|futile]] years of searching for work is a [[pragmatic|pragmatic]] form of care.
Students remain free to choose, but they choose with better knowledge.
Second, the policy would help societies meet their most [[pressing|pressing]] needs.
During the COVID-19 pandemic, countries with too few nurses, laboratory technicians and epidemiologists struggled to test and treat patients.
In my own work in public health, I have seen a shortage of trained staff delay a dengue response even when money and equipment were available.
When jobs go unfilled in such fields, patients wait longer and outbreaks spread further.
Likewise, as smartphones and digital services spread, societies need far more engineers and programmers than they once did.
This shows that guiding students toward fields with plentiful jobs serves not only individuals but also the public, since those jobs are plentiful precisely because the work is needed.
Encouraging students to fill such gaps is therefore a public good as well as a private benefit.

Admittedly, the policy could have a negative consequence: talented students might be discouraged from fields such as art, history or basic science, where jobs are scarce but contributions can be [[profound|profound]].
Vincent van Gogh sold very few paintings during his lifetime and is now regarded as one of the greatest painters in history.
A policy that steered every young artist toward accounting might have cost the world such work.
Nevertheless, this risk arises only if encouragement becomes pressure, and a well-designed policy can avoid that.
Schools can provide job information and scholarships for high-demand fields while still supporting students who, fully informed, choose a different path.
This consequence therefore qualifies my support: the policy is beneficial as long as it informs students' choices rather than dictating them.
Information widens choices; only coercion would narrow them.
In conclusion, I support encouraging students to choose fields with plentiful jobs, provided the encouragement respects their freedom.
Such a policy would reduce graduate unemployment and help meet urgent social needs, and its risks to less practical fields can be limited.
Clear information, offered early, allows students to follow their interests with open eyes rather than discover the job market too late.

essays.task_note: Bodies 1 and 2 trace positive consequences of implementing the policy; Body 3 weighs a negative consequence (lost talent in arts and basic science) and explains how it limits the support.

essays.title: Steering students toward jobs can backfire

paragraphs.text: The job market of today is rarely the job market of tomorrow.
This uncertainty raises doubts about the policy that educational institutions should actively encourage students to choose fields of study in which jobs are plentiful.

Although students deserve accurate information about careers, I oppose this policy, because steering them toward currently popular fields would likely create future surpluses, waste individual talent and neglect work whose value appears only later.
Job markets change faster than degrees can be completed, students do their best work in fields that suit them, and, admittedly, the policy could reduce short-term unemployment.
First, implementing the policy could backfire because today's plentiful jobs may become tomorrow's crowded fields.

If every school pushed students toward a profession that is in demand today, large numbers of graduates might enter the market at the same time several years later, when demand may already have fallen.
Students who chose a field for its job prospects alone would then face the very unemployment that the policy was meant to prevent.
In my own field, for instance, the demand for epidemiologists rose sharply during the COVID-19 pandemic and then eased once the emergency passed.
Kodak's story shows how quickly an industry can change: its engineer Steven Sasson invented the digital camera in 1975, yet the company clung to film and filed for bankruptcy in 2012.
These consequences suggest that the policy rests on a [[myopic|myopic]] view of the job market, which is one reason I oppose it.
Guidance based on today's vacancies may simply move unemployment a few years into the future.
Second, the policy would likely waste talent, because students perform best in fields that match their abilities and interests.
Marie Curie won Nobel Prizes in both physics and chemistry despite the barriers women faced in science at the time, a career few advisers would have called a safe choice.
Her achievements came from [[ardent|ardent]] commitment to her subject, not from a calculation about available jobs.
Likewise, Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman spent decades on little-noticed mRNA research, work that later made rapid COVID-19 vaccines possible and won the 2023 Nobel Prize.
This consequence shapes my opposition: a policy that pushes students away from their interests would [[sap|sap]] the motivation that produces excellence.
Societies need such people, and they rarely appear on lists of plentiful jobs.
Admittedly, the policy could reduce short-term unemployment and help students avoid degrees that lead nowhere.
In Vietnam, some families invest heavily in degrees that leave graduates searching for work for years, and clearer guidance might prevent such losses.
Nevertheless, this benefit can be achieved by giving students honest information about job prospects rather than actively steering them.
A university that publishes employment rates for each program and offers career counseling respects students' choices while still protecting them from uninformed decisions.
This consequence therefore refines my position: institutions should inform students, but they should not encourage them to [[abdicate|abdicate]] their own judgment in favor of the latest job report.
Honest information protects students; active steering replaces their judgment with someone else's.
In conclusion, I oppose the policy of actively encouraging students to choose fields in which jobs are plentiful.
It could create future surpluses, waste talent and neglect fields whose value emerges slowly, while its benefits can be gained through honest career information.
Schools serve students best by informing their choices, not by making those choices for them.

essays.task_note: Bodies 1 and 2 trace harmful consequences of implementing the policy (future gluts, lost talent); Body 3 weighs a benefit (less short-term unemployment) and explains how it shapes the position toward information rather than steering.

bank: Ignaz Semmelweis (Vienna, 1847) had doctors wash their hands in chlorinated lime; deaths from childbed fever on his ward fell sharply, yet most colleagues rejected his idea, which germ theory vindicated only years after his death.

Alexander Fleming noticed in 1928 that mold killed bacteria on a culture plate; penicillin became a usable drug only when Howard Florey and Ernst Chain's team developed it during World War II. In his 1945 Nobel lecture Fleming warned that misuse would breed resistant bacteria.

Antibiotic resistance today: overuse and over-the-counter sales of antibiotics, common in many countries including Vietnam, help resistant bacteria spread, so drugs that once cured infections now often fail.
Smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980 after a coordinated global WHO vaccination campaign that relied on countries sharing data and vaccine.

The COVID-19 mRNA vaccines were developed in under a year because of decades of earlier, little-noticed basic research on mRNA by Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman, who won the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

Thalidomide, a sedative given to pregnant women around 1960, caused severe birth defects in thousands of babies in Europe; Frances Kelsey of the US FDA refused to approve it, and the US then passed stricter drug-testing rules in 1962.
The Tuskegee syphilis study (1932-1972) withheld treatment from Black men without their informed consent; the public outrage led to US rules requiring ethics review boards for research on people.

Wolbachia mosquitoes: releasing mosquitoes carrying Wolbachia bacteria, which block dengue transmission, cut dengue cases by 77% in a randomized trial in Yogyakarta, Indonesia; the method has also been tested in Vietnam.
Vietnam's 2007 law requiring motorbike helmets raised helmet use from low levels to over 90% within months and reduced head injuries and deaths.

Vietnam's Doi Moi reforms (1986) replaced central planning with market incentives; a country that had faced food shortages became one of the world's largest rice exporters, and poverty fell dramatically over the following decades.
Galileo was forced by the Church in 1633 to recant his support for the idea that the Earth moves around the sun.
The Human Genome Project, a publicly funded international effort completed in 2003, made the human DNA sequence freely available to all researchers.
In 2015 a large collaboration tried to repeat 100 published psychology studies and reproduced the results of only about a third of them, revealing how often single findings mislead.
GPS was built by the US military; once it was opened to civilians, it became the basis of everyday navigation, ride-hailing and delivery apps.
Kodak engineer Steven Sasson invented the digital camera in 1975, but Kodak, protecting its profitable film business, was slow to embrace digital photography and filed for bankruptcy in 2012.
Wikipedia, launched in 2001 and written by unpaid volunteers, grew into the largest encyclopedia in history.
Abraham Lincoln appointed his political rivals, including William Seward, to his cabinet, choosing able critics over loyal followers.
Vincent van Gogh sold very few paintings during his lifetime and is now regarded as one of the greatest painters in history.

The Wright brothers, bicycle makers without college degrees, achieved the first powered airplane flight in 1903 after years of careful experiments with gliders and a wind tunnel they built themselves.
Marie Curie won Nobel Prizes in both physics (1903) and chemistry (1911) despite the barriers women faced in science at the time.
The Montgomery bus boycott (1955-1956), in which Black residents refused for over a year to ride segregated buses, helped end bus segregation in that city.
Finland requires schoolteachers to hold a master's degree, makes teaching a respected and selective profession, and relies far less on standardized testing than many countries.
Singapore's government housing program now houses about 80% of the country's residents, most of whom own their flats.
Smartphones and social media let activists organize quickly, as during the Arab Spring of 2011, but they also spread misinformation faster than corrections can follow.

concepts.sentence: Almost all basic research has indeterminate consequences at the outset; demanding certainty before funding would have blocked the early studies of bacterial immunity that later yielded CRISPR gene editing.

synonyms.note: harmful in a gradual, hidden way

concepts.sentence: Some technologies prove deleterious only decades later, as the slow damage done by leaded gasoline illustrates.

synonyms.note: beneficial, often in an unwelcome way ('a salutary lesson')
effective at producing a result; not merely 'good'
caution: harmless rather than actively helpful

concepts.sentence: Moderate oversight can be salutary for science itself, since the public trusts research more when it knows dangerous experiments are reviewed.

synonyms.note: just beginning to develop; used of fields and ideas

concepts.sentence: Novel ideas often come from outsiders precisely because they have not yet learned which questions are considered closed.
Fleming's discovery of penicillin was fortuitous, but only a trained eye would have noticed that the mold had killed the surrounding bacteria.
Each advance in genetics has made heredity seem more intricate, not less: the single 'gene for' a trait has given way to networks of thousands of interacting variants.

synonyms.note: reinforce; same as bolster, more formal

concepts.sentence: A single striking study proves little until independent teams corroborate its results with different samples and methods.

synonyms.note: widespread, usually of something bad ('rife with')

concepts.sentence: Smartphones are now so ubiquitous that the question is no longer whether young people use them but how.
An online friendship can be genuine, but for many teenagers it becomes an ersatz substitute for the harder work of face-to-face conversation.

synonyms.note: deck headword: aesthetic; value as beauty or art

concepts.sentence: A song enjoyed by millions may still lack lasting merit, while a difficult novel may be valued for centuries.

synonyms.note: clear and simple; usually of prose style

concepts.sentence: Clarity is a virtue in an argument, but demanding that every poem be immediately intelligible would rule out much of the best poetry ever written.

synonyms.note: meant for a small inner circle

concepts.sentence: Much modern art first struck audiences as opaque; Stravinsky's Rite of Spring provoked an uproar at its 1913 premiere, yet it is now a concert-hall staple.

synonyms.note: overused to the point of meaninglessness

concepts.sentence: An artist who merely imitates the masters produces derivative work; one who studies them and then breaks their rules may produce something new.
Folk festivals in rural villages often preserve a nation's heritage more faithfully than urban museums, which display traditions rather than live them.

synonyms.note: make impure by adding inferior elements

concepts.sentence: When a ministry dictates which themes an artist may address, state funding begins to compromise the integrity of the very work it pays for.
Cities nurture new cultural forms because their heterogeneous populations bring traditions into contact and friction.
Before public arts councils existed, the munificence of a few wealthy patrons decided which composers prospered and which starved.

synonyms.note: deck headword: fecund; prolific generation of ideas

concepts.sentence: In fields such as design, imagination outweighs knowledge only when enough knowledge disciplines it into something feasible.
Talent may open the door to a creative career, but only assiduous practice sustains one over decades.
A principled leader who refuses to trade away civil rights for a short-term bump in the polls may lose an election but win the verdict of history.

synonyms.note: deck headword: vacillate; switching back and forth

concepts.sentence: Voters rarely trust a leader whose positions vacillate with every news cycle, because they cannot predict what he will do next.

synonyms.note: combined effect greater than the parts
unity of purpose within a group

concepts.sentence: The most productive research consortia run on collaboration: no single laboratory has the samples, skills, and funding to answer a global question alone.
Healthy competition sharpens performance, but a leader who is merely combative treats colleagues as rivals and drives talented staff away.

synonyms.note: proven honesty, esp. in public office

concepts.sentence: Probity matters in public office not because leaders must be saints but because a single exposed lie can destroy the trust that every policy depends on.

synonyms.note: deck headword: eminent; distinction in a field

concepts.sentence: Young people chasing instant renown on social media may gain thousands of followers but rarely build the skills that sustain a career.

synonyms.note: bold; can be admiring rather than critical

concepts.sentence: Risk-taking is not the problem; impetuous risk-taking, without any estimate of what could go wrong, is.

synonyms.note: wary of risks; considers all sides

concepts.sentence: A judicious investor does not avoid risk altogether; she accepts it only after weighing the plausible worst case.
Term limits can revitalize an organization, but forcing out a capable leader after exactly five years may sacrifice hard-won expertise for mere novelty.

synonyms.note: generous, esp. toward rivals or the less powerful

concepts.sentence: Even if volunteers feel good when they help, that warm feeling does not make their act any less magnanimous, since the benefit to others is real.

synonyms.note: eager to acquire wealth or things

concepts.sentence: A corporation may grow by pursuing profit alone, but an acquisitive culture that ignores pollution eventually pays in lawsuits and lost trust.
Group identity offers belonging, but it can also demand conformity, pressuring members to adopt views they have never examined.

synonyms.note: challenge the truth or integrity of

concepts.sentence: A society in which citizens freely question authority catches its leaders' mistakes early, before they harden into disasters.

synonyms.note: odd in behavior; not necessarily principled

concepts.sentence: Many celebrated scientists began as mavericks, as Barry Marshall did in the early 1980s when his claim that bacteria cause stomach ulcers was widely dismissed.

synonyms.note: a perfect example of a quality

concepts.sentence: The heroes a society celebrates reveal its ideals: a culture that lionizes billionaires values wealth, whereas one that honors nurses values care.
Tabloids that denigrate public figures for minor slips make it harder to recognize genuine heroism when it appears.

synonyms.note: attractive on the surface but without value

concepts.sentence: In an age of curated online profiles, an ostentatious lifestyle can attract more attention than quiet competence.
Convenience does not automatically weaken character; a person can rely on a washing machine and still be self-reliant in the decisions that matter.

synonyms.note: deck headword: warranted; give good reason for

concepts.sentence: A worthy goal cannot warrant every means; no cure for a disease would justify testing it on unwilling patients.

concepts.concept: Relevance (of the past to the present)
concepts.sentence: History is germane to modern policy not because events repeat exactly but because human motives such as fear and greed recur.

synonyms.note: belonging to a much earlier period
deck headword: anachronism; out of its time
neutral: of the past, not necessarily useless

concepts.sentence: Some knowledge does become obsolete, yet the reasoning that produced it, such as the habit of testing claims against evidence, rarely does.
Remaining wary of a new leader's promises is sensible, but treating every newcomer as a suspect can poison a team before it has even begun.

synonyms.note: based on facts rather than feelings

concepts.sentence: Facts may be objective, but the choice of which facts to present rarely is, so even a statistics-heavy argument is never fully dispassionate.
The best test of an argument may not be whether it converts opponents, since even a cogent case can fail against listeners committed to their views.

synonyms.note: deck headword: tenable; cannot be defended
plausible on the surface but wrong

concepts.sentence: The reasoning that a fact may someday be revised, so all facts should be mistrusted, is fallacious: it confuses provisional with unreliable.
Progress in medicine has often come when clinicians with divergent assumptions were forced to test their claims against the same data.

synonyms.note: expert judge, esp. in the arts or taste

concepts.sentence: Expert critics notice technical flaws that ordinary viewers miss, but the connoisseur's judgment is not the only one that counts for art made for the public.
A neophyte may ask the naïve question that experts stopped asking years ago, and occasionally that question exposes a hidden assumption.

synonyms.note: deck headword: predisposed; make more likely

concepts.sentence: Poverty does not dictate a child's future, but it engenders constraints, such as hunger and unstable housing, that make some outcomes far more likely.
